phases.t: Armenia Interior with Theodosiopolis, Satala, Nicopolis, Colonia, Trapezus and Cerasus
enlarged after Maurice's peace with Khosrow II (591) brought most of Persarmenia under Rome; Arab raids from 640 (Dvin sacked October 640)

provinces.summary: Justinian's reorganisation of 536 created four Armenian provinces in place of the old military district, putting Roman Armenia under normal civil government for the first time. Its proconsul's province reached from the Black Sea at Trapezus to Theodosiopolis.

provinces.name: Armenia Quarta
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Armenian satrapies (Sophene, Anzitene, Ingilene, Asthianene, Balabitene), whose hereditary satraps lost their privileges after backing Illus' revolt (484)
province under Novel 31; Martyropolis betrayed to the Persians (589), returned 591

provinces.summary: The old Armenian satrapies south of the Euphrates, ruled by local dynasts under Roman suzerainty until Zeno stripped them after 484. Martyropolis (Mayyafariqin), filled with the relics gathered by its bishop Marutha, was its capital and a frequent Persian target.

provinces.name: Asia (proconsularis, late)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641
provinces.governor: proconsul, outside the authority of the vicar of Asiana

phases.t: the coast from the Troad to the Maeander; Councils of Ephesus (431, 449)

provinces.summary: The reduced Asia of late antiquity, still under a proconsul of high rank. Ephesus hosted the councils of 431 (which condemned Nestorius) and 449 (the 'Robber Council'), and Justinian rebuilt the basilica of St John on a monumental scale. It became the core of the Thrakesion theme in the 7th century.

provinces.name: Hellespontus
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Troad and the Asian shore of the Hellespont and Propontis

provinces.summary: The Asian side of the straits: Cyzicus with its colossal temple of Hadrian and imperial mint, Ilium, Lampsacus, and Abydos, where Justinian set up a customs station to tax shipping through the Hellespont.

provinces.name: Lydia
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: inland western Anatolia: Sardis, Philadelphia, Thyatira
Sardis devastated, probably in a Persian raid (c. 616)

provinces.summary: The old Lydian kingdom, its capital Sardis rich enough to house the largest synagogue known from antiquity, attached to the city's bath-gymnasium complex. The destruction layer of c. 616 at Sardis marks the end of classical urban life there.

provinces.name: Caria
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641
provinces.governor: praeses; under the quaestura exercitus from 536

phases.t: separated from Caria et Phrygia
part of the quaestura exercitus (Novel 41), appeals later referred to Constantinople (Novel 50)

provinces.summary: Aphrodisias, the capital, preserves the most complete copies of Diocletian's Price Edict and Currency Edict (301) and an outstanding school of sculpture; its late antique inscriptions are a major source for provincial government. Justinian attached Caria to the quaestor of the army to feed the Danube troops.

provinces.name: Insulae (the Islands)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641
provinces.governor: praeses; under the quaestura exercitus from 536

phases.t: Rhodes, Cos, Samos, Chios, Lesbos, Tenedos and the Cyclades
part of the quaestura exercitus
Persian raid on Rhodes (c. 622-623)

provinces.summary: An island province whose maritime resources Justinian harnessed in 536 by joining it to Moesia II and Scythia under the quaestor of the army, so that ships could carry supplies to the Danube.

provinces.name: Phrygia Prima / Pacatiana
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: western Phrygia: Laodicea, Hierapolis, Colossae, Eumeneia

provinces.summary: Western Phrygia, with Laodicea and Hierapolis, where the martyrium of the apostle Philip drew pilgrims. Its 3rd-century tombstones with the formula 'Christians for Christians' are among the earliest public Christian inscriptions.

provinces.name: Phrygia Secunda / Salutaris
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: eastern Phrygia: Synnada, Docimium, Nacoleia, Dorylaeum

provinces.summary: Eastern Phrygia, home of the imperial quarries of Docimium, source of the purple-veined pavonazzetto marble. Valens defeated the usurper Procopius at Nacoleia in 366.

provinces.name: Pisidia
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: Pisidian highlands with Antioch, Sagalassos, Termessos
praetor Iustinianus against brigandage

provinces.summary: A highland province of fortified cities and bandits. Sagalassos, excavated since 1990, flourished until earthquakes and plague in the 6th-7th centuries. Justinian gave its governor military powers to deal with the brigands.

provinces.name: Lycaonia
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: created by Valens from Pisidia and Isauria
praetor Iustinianus

provinces.summary: The plain round Iconium, carved out around 371-373 when Basil's correspondence shows the new province forming. Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium from 373, was one of the champions of Nicene orthodoxy.

provinces.name: Pamphylia
provinces.createdNote: separated from Lycia by the early 4th century
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Pamphylian plain: Perge, Side, Aspendos, Attaleia

provinces.summary: A coastal plain of rich cities with some of the best-preserved theatres and aqueducts of Asia Minor (Aspendos, Side). Attaleia was the port for the sea route from the Aegean to Syria and Egypt.

provinces.name: Lycia
provinces.createdNote: separated from Pamphylia by the early 4th century
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Lycian peninsula: Myra, Xanthos, Patara, Limyra

provinces.summary: In 392 the prefect Rufinus, persecuting the family of his predecessor Tatianus, had all Lycians barred from public office; the ban was lifted in 396. The bishop Nicholas of Myra became the most popular saint of the Christian world, and the Sion treasure of church silver from a Lycian monastery is a rare survival of 6th-century liturgical plate.

provinces.name: Europa
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the European shore of the Propontis
Constantinople founded within it (dedicated 11 May 330), under its own urban prefect from 359; Long Walls of Anastasius

provinces.summary: The province in which Constantine founded his new Rome. Its governor sat at Heraclea, since Constantinople had its own urban prefect. Anastasius' Long Walls, running some 56 km from the Black Sea to the Propontis, made the hinterland of the capital a fortified enclave; the Avars and Persians besieged the city itself in 626.

provinces.name: Thracia (late province)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641, though much of the countryside was insecure

phases.t: the upper Hebrus valley; Gothic war (376-382), Hunnic invasions (441-447)
praetor Iustinianus Thraciae with military powers

provinces.summary: The Thracian plain round Philippopolis, repeatedly devastated by Goths, Huns, Bulgars and Slavs. Justinian abolished the vicar of Thrace and gave the governor of this province his powers and a military role.

provinces.name: Haemimontus
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: from Hadrianopolis to the Black Sea ports of Anchialus and Mesembria

provinces.summary: The province of Adrianople, where on 9 August 378 the Goths destroyed Valens and two-thirds of the eastern field army, the worst Roman defeat since Cannae in Ammianus' judgement.

provinces.name: Rhodope
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Aegean coast of Thrace: Aenus, Maroneia, Traianopolis, Maximianopolis

provinces.summary: The Aegean coast of Thrace along the Via Egnatia, a quieter province sheltered by the Rhodope mountains.

provinces.name: Moesia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Roman hold collapsed in the early 7th century; the Bulgar state was founded here in 680-681
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Moesiae secundae; under the quaestura exercitus from 536

phases.t: lower Danube between the Iskar and the Dobruja; Valens' Gothic war base (367-369)
Goths admitted (376); Ulfila's 'lesser Goths' settled near Nicopolis ad Istrum
part of the quaestura exercitus
Roman control collapses under Avar and Slav pressure

provinces.summary: The province where the Gothic crisis began: the Tervingi crossed into it in 376, and Lupicinus' botched banquet at Marcianopolis turned refugees into rebels. Ulfila, translator of the Gothic Bible, led his community to settle near Nicopolis ad Istrum.

provinces.name: Scythia (Minor)
provinces.endedNote: Roman control lost in the early 7th century
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Scythiae; under the quaestura exercitus from 536

phases.t: the Dobruja; Tropaeum Traiani rebuilt by Constantine and Licinius (316); revolt of Vitalian (513-515)
part of the quaestura exercitus
Danube forts abandoned in the early 7th century

provinces.summary: The Dobruja between the Danube delta and the sea, a militarised province of fortress towns. Its 'Scythian monks' stirred the theopaschite controversy at Constantinople and Rome in 519-520, and its comes foederatorum Vitalian marched on the capital three times against Anastasius.

provinces.name: Dacia Ripensis
provinces.endedNote: lost in the Avar-Slav invasions of the early 7th century (date approximate)

phases.t: Danube bank of Aurelian's Dacia; legio XIII Gemina at Ratiaria, V Macedonica at Oescus; Constantine's bridge at Oescus (328)
Hunnic destruction of Ratiaria (441-447)
Justinianic restoration; Avar and Slav invasions

provinces.summary: The riverbank half of Aurelian's Dacia. Constantine built a stone bridge across the Danube from Oescus to Sucidava in 328, the last Roman bridge over the river. Ratiaria, with its arms factory, was sacked by Attila.

provinces.name: Dacia Mediterranea
provinces.endedNote: lost in the early 7th century (date approximate)

phases.t: Serdica and Naissus; Galerius' edict of toleration issued at Serdica (311); Council of Serdica (343)
Attila takes Naissus and Serdica (441-443)
restored by Justinian; overrun by Avars and Slavs

provinces.summary: The interior of Aurelian's Dacia, with Serdica (Constantine's 'my Rome') and Naissus, Constantine's birthplace and site of the imperial villa at Mediana. The Council of Serdica (343) split along East-West lines over Athanasius.

provinces.name: Moesia Prima (Moesia Superior Margensis)
provinces.endedNote: lost in the early 7th century (date approximate)

phases.t: the Danube from Singidunum to the Iron Gates
Huns destroy Viminacium (441); later Gepid and Ostrogothic control of Singidunum
Justinianic restoration; Avars take Singidunum (584); Priscus' campaigns beyond the Danube (599-602)

provinces.summary: The Verona List calls it Moesia Superior Margensis, after the Margus (Morava). The treaty of Margus with the Huns (435 or 439) and the fall of Viminacium to Attila in 441 began the destruction of the Danube cities.

sources.r: fragment on the treaty of Margus

provinces.name: Dardania
provinces.endedNote: abandoned in the early 7th century (date approximate)

phases.t: upland mining province; Scupi destroyed by earthquake (518)
Justiniana Prima founded near Justinian's birthplace, with an archbishopric (Novel 11, 535)

provinces.summary: A province of mines (metalla Dardanica) and hill-country recruits. Justinian, born at nearby Tauresium, built the new city of Justiniana Prima (Caricin Grad) and made its archbishop head of the church in northern Illyricum.

provinces.name: Praevalitana
provinces.endedNote: lost in the early 7th century (date approximate)

phases.t: carved from southern Dalmatia: Scodra, Doclea, Lissus

provinces.summary: Split off from Dalmatia by Diocletian, perhaps because tradition made Doclea his birthplace. It sat in the eastern empire after 395 although it bordered western Dalmatia.

provinces.name: Thessalia
provinces.endedNote: Larisa and the coast still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Thessalian plain
Kotrigur raid reaches Thermopylae (559); Slav settlement (Belegezitai) from c. 600

provinces.summary: The Thessalian plain, separated from Macedonia by Diocletian. Justinian rebuilt the walls at Thermopylae and garrisoned the pass. By the early 7th century Slav groups were settled around its cities.

provinces.name: Epirus Nova
provinces.endedNote: Dyrrachium still Roman in 641

phases.t: the Adriatic end of the Via Egnatia: Dyrrachium, Apollonia, Lychnidus

provinces.summary: The western end of the Via Egnatia, with Dyrrachium, birthplace of the emperor Anastasius, who gave it new walls. Theoderic the Amal seized it in 479 during his wanderings in the Balkans.

sources.r: fragments on Theoderic Strabo and the Amal

provinces.name: Macedonia Salutaris (Secunda)
provinces.createdNote: by c. 386-400 (Notitia); later called Macedonia II
provinces.endedNote: abandoned by the early 7th century (date approximate)

phases.t: upper Axios valley: Stobi, Heraclea Lyncestis; the Notitia places part of it in the diocese of Dacia

provinces.summary: A small province of the upper Vardar. Theodosius I issued laws from Stobi in 388; Theoderic the Amal sacked it in 479. Stobi was abandoned by the early 7th century amid Slav settlement.

provinces.name: Pannonia Prima
provinces.endedNote: ceded to or occupied by the Huns c. 433 (disputed)
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Pannoniae primae et Norici ripensis

phases.t: northwestern Pannonia: Savaria, Scarbantia, Carnuntum, Vindobona
Quadic and Sarmatian invasions; federate settlements after 380

provinces.summary: The western half of Upper Pannonia. Martin of Tours was born at Savaria around 316; by Ammianus' day Carnuntum was 'a deserted town'. Aetius is generally thought to have ceded Pannonian territory to the Huns around 433 in return for their support.

provinces.name: Savia (Pannonia Savensis)
provinces.endedNote: lost after the Avar arrival of 568 (date approximate)

phases.t: the Sava valley with Siscia and its mint
Ostrogothic: Cassiodorus' Variae include letters to its governor (4.49; 5.14)
contested by Lombards, Gepids and the empire; Avars after 568

provinces.summary: The Sava valley, with the mint and martyr-shrine of Siscia (Quirinus, martyred 309). Unusually, Theoderic's administration kept governing it as a Roman province, and Cassiodorus' letters deal with its tax abuses.

provinces.name: Pannonia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Sirmium surrendered to the Avars in 582

phases.t: Sirmium an imperial residence; battles of Cibalae (316) and Mursa (351)
Hunnic capture of Sirmium (441), then Gepids
Ostrogothic, then Gepid
Roman again under Justin II; Sirmium surrendered to the Avars after a siege of 580-582

provinces.summary: Sirmium was one of the tetrarchic capitals and the birthplace of several emperors (Probus among them); Constantius II held councils there. Two of the bloodiest battles of the civil wars were fought in the province, at Cibalae (316) and Mursa (351). Its fall to the Avars in 582 broke the Danube frontier.

sources.r: fragments on the siege of Sirmium

provinces.name: Valeria (Pannonian)
provinces.endedNote: given up to the Huns c. 433 (disputed)

phases.t: named after Galerius' wife Valeria; the Danube bend with Aquincum
Quadi and Sarmatians invade (374); Valentinian I dies of a stroke while receiving Quadic envoys (375)

provinces.summary: Galerius drained Lake Pelso and cleared forests here and named the new province after his wife, Diocletian's daughter Galeria Valeria (Aurelius Victor 40.10). Valentinian I fortified its riverbank heavily; he died in 375 in a fit of rage at Quadic envoys at Brigetio.

provinces.name: Noricum Ripense
provinces.endedNote: evacuated by order of Odoacer, 488
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Pannoniae primae et Norici ripensis

phases.t: the Danube bank of Noricum with Lauriacum, Favianis and Batavis
the world of St Severinus: garrisons unpaid, towns defended by their bishops and citizens

provinces.summary: Eugippius' Life of Severinus (511) is the most vivid account of a Roman frontier province dying: unpaid soldiers walking to Italy for their wages, towns paying tribute to the Rugi, and finally Odoacer ordering the evacuation of the Roman population to Italy in 488, carrying Severinus' body with them.

provinces.name: Noricum Mediterraneum
provinces.endedNote: Frankish overlordship from c. 536-539; Slav settlement from c. 590

phases.t: inland Noricum (Carinthia)
Ostrogothic

provinces.summary: The mountain valleys of Carinthia, more sheltered than the Danube bank; Teurnia with its bishop's church became the provincial centre in the 5th century. It passed from the Ostrogoths to Frankish overlordship in the 530s and was settled by Slavs from the 590s.

provinces.name: Venetia et Histria
provinces.endedNote: Byzantine maritime Venetia and Istria still Roman in 641

phases.t: Aquileia one of the great cities of the West; its mosaic cathedral of Bishop Theodore (after 313)
Attila sacks Aquileia (452); refugees in the lagoons
Lombard invasion; Byzantine control reduced to the lagoons (Grado, later Venice) and Istria

provinces.summary: The northeastern gateway to Italy. Attila's destruction of Aquileia in 452 drove refugees into the lagoons, and Cassiodorus' letter of 537-538 to the 'tribunes of the maritime people' describes the lagoon dwellers and their salt-pans. When the Lombards entered Italy in 568 at Forum Iulii, the patriarch fled to Grado, and Byzantine Venetia began.

provinces.name: Aemilia
provinces.endedNote: eastern part still Roman (exarchate) in 641

phases.t: the Via Aemilia from Placentia to Bononia
partly Lombard after 569; Bononia and the eastern towns held from Ravenna

provinces.summary: The towns of the Via Aemilia, many of which Ambrose described in 387 as 'corpses of half-ruined cities'. Divided between Lombards and the exarchate after 568.

provinces.name: Liguria (late, with Milan)
provinces.endedNote: Lombard conquest 569

phases.t: Mediolanum an imperial capital (from Maximian); Constantine and Licinius' agreement at Milan (313); Ambrose bishop (374-397)
court moves to Ravenna (402); Milan sacked by the Goths in 539; Ticinum the Ostrogothic second capital
Milan taken by the Lombards (September 569)

provinces.summary: Late antique 'Liguria' was the northwest of the Po plain, not the Riviera: Milan, Ticinum, Augusta Taurinorum and Comum. Milan was the western capital for a century, the city of Ambrose and of Augustine's conversion. In 539 the Goths and Burgundians sacked it after it went over to Belisarius, killing, Procopius says, all the men.

provinces.name: Flaminia et Picenum (Annonarium)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman (exarchate) in 641; Ravenna fell to the Lombards in 751

phases.t: the Adriatic coast from Ravenna to Ancona
Ravenna the western capital (402-476), then Odoacer's and Theoderic's, then seat of the praetorian prefect
core of the exarchate (Ravenna and the Pentapolis)

provinces.summary: Honorius moved the court to Ravenna in 402, protected by marshes and with a fleet base at Classe. The province's monuments, from Galla Placidia's mausoleum to Theoderic's tomb and Justinian's San Vitale, are the best surviving ensemble of late antique art. It remained the heart of Byzantine Italy until 751.

provinces.name: Raetia Prima
provinces.endedNote: ceded to the Franks by Vitiges, 536-537
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Raetiae primae et secundae

phases.t: the Alpine Rhine and the Grisons passes
under Odoacer and the Ostrogoths (Cassiodorus' letters to the dux Raetiarum)

provinces.summary: The Alpine part of Raetia with Chur, controlling the passes between Italy and the upper Rhine. Theoderic treated it as 'the bulwark of Italy' (Variae 7.4). Vitiges ceded it to the Franks in 536-537.

provinces.name: Raetia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration lapsed in the later 5th century
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Raetiae primae et secundae

phases.t: the Danube-Iller-Rhine frontier
Alamannic and Iuthungian pressure; Roman control fades

provinces.summary: The Bavarian plain between the Iller and the Inn behind the late Roman Danube-Iller-Rhine line, defended by Valentinian's forts. Roman authority dissolved in the later 5th century.

provinces.name: Alpes Cottiae (late, Ligurian)
provinces.endedNote: conquered by the Lombard king Rothari, c. 643
provinces.capitalName: Segusio in the 4th century; Genua the main city later

phases.t: Italian province; by the 6th century it lay along the Ligurian Apennines and coast
Genua and the Riviera held by the empire after the Lombard invasion

provinces.summary: Paul the Deacon defines the Cottian Alps as the Ligurian Apennines with Genua, Savona and Bobbio; the archbishop of Milan took refuge at Genua from the Lombards. Rothari conquered the coast around 643.

provinces.name: Tuscia et Umbria
provinces.endedNote: Perusia corridor and south Etruria still Roman in 641

phases.t: Etruria and Umbria; battle of Busta Gallorum (Taginae) in 552
mostly Lombard after c. 570; the Byzantine corridor through Perusia linked Rome to Ravenna

provinces.summary: Etruria and Umbria, the hinterland of Rome. Narses destroyed Totila at Busta Gallorum in the Apennines in 552. After the Lombard invasion only the corridor along the Via Amerina through Perusia kept Rome in contact with Ravenna.

provinces.name: Picenum Suburbicarium
provinces.endedNote: absorbed by the Lombard duchy of Spoleto, c. 570s-580s

phases.t: southern Picenum, separated from Flaminia

provinces.summary: Southern Picenum, separated from Flaminia et Picenum in the later 4th century and assigned to the vicar of Rome. Ravaged in the Gothic war (Auximum besieged 539) and absorbed by the Lombard duchy of Spoleto.

provinces.name: Campania
provinces.endedNote: Naples and the coast still Roman in 641

phases.t: the richest part of Italia Suburbicaria: Capua, Neapolis, Puteoli; Vesuvius erupts (472)
Belisarius takes Naples through an aqueduct (536); Totila retakes it (543)
inland Campania Lombard (duchy of Benevento); Naples, Cumae and the coast Byzantine

provinces.summary: The Bay of Naples remained a playground of the Roman aristocracy into the 5th century; the last western emperor, Romulus, was pensioned off to the Castellum Lucullanum at Naples in 476. Belisarius took Naples in 536 by sending men through a disused aqueduct. The duchy of Naples survived as a Byzantine enclave.

provinces.name: Samnium
provinces.endedNote: Lombard duchy of Benevento founded c. 570-571

phases.t: separated from Campania; earthquake of 346 and rebuilding

provinces.summary: The Samnite uplands, separated from Campania in the mid-4th century. Inscriptions record the rebuilding of its towns after the great earthquake of 346. It became the core of the Lombard duchy of Benevento.

provinces.name: Valeria (Italian)
provinces.endedNote: absorbed by the Lombard duchy of Spoleto, c. 570s

phases.t: the central Apennines: Reate, Nursia, Alba Fucens, Corfinium

provinces.summary: A mountain province carved from Picenum and Samnium in the later 4th century. Benedict was born at Nursia around 480. Gregory the Great's Dialogues are full of its hermits and its sufferings at the hands of the Lombards.

provinces.name: Apulia et Calabria
provinces.endedNote: the Salento ports still Roman in 641

phases.t: Apulia and the Salento (ancient Calabria)
Lombard expansion from Benevento; Tarentum, Brundisium, Hydruntum and Gallipolis remain Byzantine

provinces.summary: Grain and wool country of southeast Italy, with the Adriatic crossing at Brundisium and Hydruntum. The Salento ports remained in Byzantine hands, and the name Calabria later migrated to the toe of Italy.

provinces.name: Lucania et Bruttii
provinces.endedNote: still largely Roman in 641

phases.t: the toe of Italy
Alaric dies at Consentia (410); Cassiodorus' Vivarium at Scyllaceum (c. 554); largely Byzantine after the Lombard advance

provinces.summary: The far south, a land of pastoralism and great estates. Alaric died at Consentia in 410 and, Jordanes says, was buried in the bed of the Busentus. Cassiodorus retired to his estate at Scyllaceum and founded the monastery of Vivarium, a key link in the copying of classical texts.

provinces.name: Africa Proconsularis (Zeugitana)
provinces.endedNote: Carthage fell to Hassan ibn al-Numan in 698
provinces.governor: proconsul (outside the vicar's authority); consularis under Justinian's prefect

phases.t: the hinterland of Carthage; Donatist schism and Augustine's polemics; Conference of Carthage (411)
Vandal invasion
Vandal kingdom; Carthage taken on 19 October 439
Justinianic province under the praetorian prefect of Africa
under the exarch of Carthage

provinces.summary: The reduced proconsular province of Carthage, still the second city of the West in 400. The Conference of Carthage (411) brought 286 Catholic and 279 Donatist bishops face to face and ended with an imperial ban on Donatism. Gaiseric's capture of Carthage in 439 was the greatest single blow to the western empire's finances.

provinces.name: Byzacena (Byzacium)
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 647-670

phases.t: the olive belt of southern Tunisia
Vandal; Moorish revolts from the 480s
Justinianic; Moorish wars of Solomon and John Troglita (546-548)
Arab invasion; exarch Gregory killed at Sufetula (647); Kairouan founded (670)

provinces.summary: The great olive-oil country, whose amphorae fed Rome and later Constantinople. The Moorish wars of the 540s are told in Corippus' Latin epic Iohannis. The exarch Gregory, who had rebelled against Constans II, died fighting the Arabs at Sufetula in 647.

provinces.name: Tripolitania
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest 643

phases.t: the three cities (Leptis, Oea, Sabratha); Austurian raids of 363-365 and the scandal of the comes Romanus
Vandal and Moorish control
recovered by the local revolt of Pudentius (533); Amr ibn al-As takes Tripoli (643)

provinces.summary: Septimius Severus' homeland. Ammianus tells how the comes Romanus refused to defend Leptis against the Austuriani unless supplied with 4,000 camels, then covered up his failure at court. Justinian's Leptis shrank behind a new wall enclosing a fraction of the old city.

provinces.name: Mauretania Sitifensis (Mauretania Prima)
provinces.endedNote: Arab conquest, late 7th century (approximate)

phases.t: eastern part of Caesariensis
Vandal
returned to Rome by the treaty of 442
Vandal and Moorish
Byzantine Mauretania Prima

provinces.summary: The high plains round Sitifis, separated from Caesariensis by Diocletian (the Verona List garbles its name). It changed hands repeatedly in the 5th century; under Justinian it was the westernmost securely held province of Africa.

provinces.name: Numidia Cirtensis
provinces.endedNote: reunited by c. 314; Cirta renamed Constantina

phases.t: northern, civilian Numidia

provinces.summary: One half of Diocletian's divided Numidia, attested in the Verona List. The Great Persecution's surrender of scriptures at Cirta (303), recorded in the Gesta apud Zenophilum, fed the Donatist schism.

provinces.name: Numidia Militiana
provinces.endedNote: reunited by c. 314

phases.t: southern, military Numidia with Lambaesis

provinces.summary: The southern half of Diocletian's Numidia, centred on the legionary base at Lambaesis. Its name advertised its military character.

provinces.name: Tarraconensis (late)
provinces.endedNote: Visigothic conquest 472-475

phases.t: the Ebro valley and the northeast
Bagaudae (440s-450s); last Roman province in Spain, taken by Euric (472-475)

provinces.summary: The northeast of Spain, the last part of the peninsula under Roman government. Hydatius records Bagaudic risings in the Ebro valley in the 440s-450s. Euric's generals took Pamplona, Caesaraugusta and Tarraco in 472-475.

provinces.name: Carthaginiensis
provinces.endedNote: Roman government effectively ended by c. 460 (approximate)

phases.t: the centre and southeast, including the Balearics
Balearics separated
Vandals sack Carthago Nova (425); Majorian's invasion fleet destroyed at Portus Illicitanus (460)

provinces.summary: Central and southeastern Spain. Majorian assembled his fleet here in 460 for an invasion of Vandal Africa, only to have it captured by Gaiseric through treachery. Toledo, in its interior, became the Visigothic capital, while the coast round Cartagena was Byzantine Spania from 552.

provinces.name: Gallaecia
provinces.endedNote: Suevic kingdom from 411

phases.t: the northwest with its gold districts and legio VII Gemina
allotted to the Sueves and Hasding Vandals (411)

provinces.summary: The northwest, home of the ascetic movement of Priscillian, the first Christian executed for heresy (Trier, 385), and of the chronicler Hydatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, who recorded the Suevic kingdom that replaced Roman rule from 411.

provinces.name: Insulae Balearum
provinces.endedNote: still Roman in 641

phases.t: separated from Carthaginiensis
Vandal
recovered by Apollinaris for Justinian (534); attached to Africa, later to Spania

provinces.summary: The Balearic Islands, separated from Carthaginiensis between 369 and 385. Bishop Severus' letter on the forced conversion of the Jews of Minorca (418) is a rare document of island life. They remained Byzantine long after Spania was lost.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Prima
provinces.endedNote: Burgundian from the 460s-470s (approximate)

phases.t: Lyon, Autun, Langres, Chalon
Burgundian control from the 460s

provinces.summary: Lyon and Burgundy. Autun's panegyrics to Constantius I and Constantine (c. 297-312) are the voice of a Gallic city rebuilding after the 3rd-century crisis. The Burgundians made Lyon one of their capitals in the 460s-470s.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Secunda
provinces.endedNote: absorbed into the Frankish kingdom by c. 486 (approximate)

phases.t: Normandy; Saxon Shore forts on the Channel coast

provinces.summary: Coastal Normandy, part of the Channel defence against Saxon raiders (the litus Saxonicum per tractum Gallicanum). Its Roman administration merged into the Frankish world by the 480s.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Tertia
provinces.createdNote: split from Lugdunensis II in the later 4th century
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration gone by the 480s (approximate)

phases.t: Touraine, Anjou and Armorica; the tractus Armoricanus command

provinces.summary: Tours, Angers and the Armorican peninsula. Martin, bishop of Tours (371-397), made the city the religious centre of Gaul. Armorica was repeatedly in revolt against Roman officials in the 5th century and received British settlers who made it Brittany.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Senonia
provinces.endedNote: Frankish conquest, 486 onwards

phases.t: Sens, Paris, Orleans, Auxerre, Chartres

provinces.summary: The Paris basin. Julian was proclaimed Augustus at Lutetia in 360, and in 451 bishop Anianus held Orleans against Attila until Aetius arrived. It belonged to the realm of Aegidius and Syagrius until Clovis conquered it.

provinces.name: Belgica Prima
provinces.endedNote: Frankish by the 470s-480s (approximate)

phases.t: Trier an imperial capital (Constantius I, Constantine, Valentinian I, Gratian)
court and prefecture leave for Italy and Arles; Trier sacked repeatedly in the 410s-440s

provinces.summary: Trier was the capital of the West for most of the 4th century, its Aula Palatina and imperial baths still standing. Ausonius' Mosella celebrates its river landscape c. 371. Salvian says Trier was sacked four times in his lifetime; Arbogast, a Frankish count of Trier, still governed it in Roman style around 470.

provinces.name: Belgica Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Clovis defeats Syagrius, 486

phases.t: Reims, Soissons, Amiens, Tournai
kingdom of Aegidius and Syagrius at Soissons beside the Frankish kingdom of Tournai

provinces.summary: Reims and Soissons. The Frankish king Childeric, buried at Tournai around 481 with a Roman general's brooch and a signet ring, was in effect a federate ruler within this province. Syagrius, 'king of the Romans' at Soissons, was defeated by Clovis in 486.

provinces.name: Germania Prima
provinces.endedNote: Alamannic and Frankish control by the mid-5th century (approximate)

phases.t: the Upper Rhine frontier
Rhine crossing of Vandals, Alans and Sueves (31 December 406); Burgundian kingdom at Worms (413-436)

provinces.summary: The Upper Rhine from Mainz to Strasbourg. The great crossing of 406 began here (Jerome lists Mainz among the cities destroyed). The Burgundian kingdom at Worms, destroyed by Aetius' Huns in 436, is the historical kernel of the Nibelungenlied.

provinces.name: Germania Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Frankish by c. 459 (approximate)

phases.t: the Lower Rhine; Constantine's bridge and fort at Deutz (c. 310)
Cologne taken by the Franks (355) and recovered by Julian (356)
Frankish settlement; Cologne Frankish by c. 459

provinces.summary: The Lower Rhine, where Franks had been settled within the frontier since the 3rd century. Julian's recovery of Cologne in 356 was his first success as Caesar. By the mid-5th century the city was the seat of a Rhineland Frankish king.

provinces.name: Maxima Sequanorum
provinces.endedNote: Burgundian and Alamannic by the 470s (approximate)

phases.t: the Jura and the Swiss plateau: Besancon, Aventicum, Augusta Raurica, Vindonissa

provinces.summary: The Swiss plateau and the Jura, behind the late Roman Rhine forts from Basel to Lake Constance. Julian describes Besancon as a small town rebuilt within its old walls. The Burgundians absorbed it in the later 5th century.

provinces.name: Viennensis
provinces.endedNote: Arles taken by Euric, 476

phases.t: the Rhone valley: Vienne, Arles, Valence, Geneva, Grenoble
Arles seat of the prefecture of the Gauls and of the Council of the Seven Provinces (418); Burgundians take Vienne (c. 470)

provinces.summary: The Rhone valley. Arles, Constantine's favourite residence in Gaul, became the seat of the Gallic prefecture around 407, and Honorius' edict of 418 ordered an annual council of the Seven Provinces to meet there. The rival claims of the bishops of Vienne and Arles were adjudicated by Pope Leo in 450.

provinces.name: Narbonensis Prima
provinces.endedNote: Narbonne ceded to the Visigoths, 462

phases.t: Narbonne and Toulouse
Ataulf marries Galla Placidia at Narbonne (414); Toulouse the Visigothic capital (418); Narbonne surrendered to Theoderic II (462)

provinces.summary: Languedoc. Ataulf married Galla Placidia at Narbonne in January 414 in a Roman ceremony, wearing Roman dress. Toulouse became the Visigothic capital after 418, and the count Agrippinus handed Narbonne to the Goths in 462.

provinces.name: Narbonensis Secunda
provinces.endedNote: ceded to the Visigoths, 476

phases.t: eastern Provence: Aix, Forum Iulii, Antipolis, Apt; monastery of Lerins (c. 410)

provinces.summary: Eastern Provence. The monastery founded by Honoratus on the island of Lerins around 410 produced a generation of Gallic bishops, including Hilary of Arles and Faustus of Riez. Ceded to Euric in 476.

provinces.name: Novempopulana
provinces.createdNote: by the early 4th century (Verona List: Novem populi)
provinces.endedNote: Visigothic by the 470s (approximate)

phases.t: the Nine Peoples between the Garonne and the Pyrenees
partly within the Visigothic settlement of 418; Roman administration lapsed by the 470s

provinces.summary: The southwest corner of Gaul, whose separation from the Gauls was obtained by the delegate commemorated in the Hasparren inscription. Partly assigned to the Visigoths in 418.

provinces.name: Aquitanica Prima
provinces.endedNote: ceded to the Visigoths, 475

phases.t: Bourges, Clermont, Limoges, Cahors, Rodez
Clermont, led by Sidonius Apollinaris and Ecdicius, holds out against Euric; ceded by Julius Nepos (475)

provinces.summary: The Massif Central, the land of the Arverni. Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Clermont and son-in-law of the emperor Avitus, led its resistance to the Visigoths in 471-474, and wrote bitterly when Nepos' envoys ceded the Auvergne to Euric in 475.

provinces.name: Aquitanica Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Visigothic settlement of 418

phases.t: Bordeaux, Poitiers, Saintes, Angouleme, Perigueux, Agen
assigned to the Visigoths of Wallia as federates

provinces.summary: The Atlantic southwest, a land of great villas and rhetorical schools: Ausonius, teacher of Gratian and consul in 379, came from Bordeaux. It became the core of the Visigothic federate settlement of 418, the first barbarian kingdom on Roman soil.

provinces.name: Maxima Caesariensis
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration ended in 409-410

phases.t: the southeast with London and the Saxon Shore forts

provinces.summary: The southeast of Britain, with London, renamed Augusta in the 4th century (Ammianus 27.8.7), seat of the vicarius. Its coast was defended by the forts of the Saxon Shore under their own count.

provinces.name: Britannia Prima
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration ended in 409-410

phases.t: the west: Cirencester, Gloucester, Wroxeter, Wales

provinces.summary: The west of Britain, its capital fixed by an inscription from Cirencester naming L. Septimius, governor of Britannia Prima, who restored a Jupiter column. Villa life in the Cotswolds peaked in the 4th century.

provinces.name: Flavia Caesariensis
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration ended in 409-410

phases.t: the east Midlands and Lincolnshire

provinces.summary: Probably the east Midlands with Lincoln, whose bishop attended the Council of Arles in 314. The name honours the Flavian dynasty of Constantius I.

provinces.name: Britannia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration ended in 409-410

phases.t: the north with Hadrian's Wall

provinces.summary: The north of Britain, held by the dux Britanniarum and the garrisons of Hadrian's Wall, which the Notitia lists fort by fort. Constantine was proclaimed emperor at York in July 306.

provinces.name: Valentia
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration ended in 409-410

phases.t: named for Valens by Theodosius the Elder after the 'barbarian conspiracy' of 367

provinces.summary: Ammianus says Theodosius the Elder recovered a province and renamed it Valentia in honour of Valens after the barbarian conspiracy of 367-368. Its location is unknown: the Wall zone, Wales, or a renamed existing province have all been proposed.

provinces.name: Praetorian prefecture of Oriens
provinces.createdNote: prefects attached to emperors since 2 BC; territorial prefectures took shape under Constantine and his sons (c. 330s-340s)
provinces.endedNote: still functioning in 641; attested into the later 7th century

phases.t: regional prefecture of the East under Constantius II and his successors; at times also over the Illyrian dioceses
dioceses of Oriens, Aegyptus, Pontica, Asiana and Thracia; the regent-prefect Anthemius builds the Theodosian land walls (413)
John the Cappadocian's fiscal and administrative reforms; the Nika rioters demand his dismissal (532)
plague and Persian wars; prefecture continues as the empire's treasury and supply office

provinces.summary: The largest administrative machine of the ancient world: the prefect of the East assessed and collected the annona that fed and paid the army, ran the public post and the courts of appeal, and drew up the annual tax indiction for Thrace to Egypt. John Lydus, who served in its offices for forty years, wrote an insider's lament on its decline under John the Cappadocian. Its civil structure outlived the Arab conquests by decades as the themes grew up beside it.

provinces.name: Praetorian prefecture of Illyricum
provinces.endedNote: the prefect still functioned at Thessalonica in 641

phases.t: separate prefecture at intervals (Anatolius 357-360), often combined with Italy
eastern Illyricum (Dacia, Macedonia) transferred to Theodosius I
eastern; claimed by Stilicho for the West (395-408); seat at Sirmium
seat at Thessalonica after Sirmium fell to the Huns; Justinian's plan to move it to Justiniana Prima (Novel 11)

provinces.summary: The Balkan prefecture, a prize contested between the two halves of the empire: Stilicho's attempts to take eastern Illyricum for the West (395-408) poisoned relations between the courts of Honorius and Arcadius. Novel 11 (535) recalls how the prefect had fled from Sirmium to Thessalonica in Attila's time. In the 7th century the prefect at Thessalonica appears in the Miracles of St Demetrius organising the defence of the city against Slavs.

provinces.name: Praetorian prefecture of Italy (Italiae, Illyrici et Africae)
provinces.endedNote: still attested under the exarchate in 641
provinces.capitalName: Mediolanum, then Ravenna (402); the prefect also sat at Rome

phases.t: Italy and Africa, with Illyricum at times
dioceses of Italia (two vicariates), Africa and western Illyricum (Pannoniae)
kept by Odoacer and the Ostrogoths: Liberius and Cassiodorus served as prefects
Gothic war
restored by the Pragmatic Sanction (554)
civil prefect subordinate to the exarch of Ravenna

provinces.summary: The western prefecture of Italy and Africa, whose civil service survived the end of the western emperors almost unchanged: Theoderic's prefects, including Cassiodorus (533-c.537), ran the same offices, and Cassiodorus' Variae preserve their correspondence. Justinian's Pragmatic Sanction of 554 restored it after the Gothic war; it lingered under the exarchs into the 7th century.

provinces.name: Praetorian prefecture of the Gauls
provinces.endedNote: Roman prefecture ended in 476; the Ostrogothic revival lasted until Provence was ceded to the Franks (536-537)

phases.t: Gaul, Spain, Britain and Tingitana from Trier
seat at Arles; Council of the Seven Provinces (418); prefects Agricola, Avitus, Arvandus (condemned for treason, 469)
lapsed with Euric's capture of Arles
revived by Theoderic for Ostrogothic Provence (Liberius prefect c. 510-534)

provinces.summary: The prefecture that governed the whole Atlantic West from Trier, where Ausonius held it in 378-379 for his pupil Gratian. Its move to Arles marked the abandonment of the Rhine as the centre of gravity. The trial of the prefect Arvandus in 469, caught writing to Euric to divide Gaul between Goths and Burgundians, shows how far the Gallic aristocracy had moved.

provinces.name: Praetorian prefecture of Africa
provinces.endedNote: ended with the fall of Carthage (698)

phases.t: seven provinces: Zeugi (Carthage), Byzacium, Tripolis under consulares; Numidia, Mauretania, Sardinia under praesides; plus Tingi
subordinate to the exarch of Carthage

provinces.summary: Created by Justinian's law of April 534 even before the Vandal war was fully over, laying down the salaries of every official from the prefect to the clerks. It was the institutional sign that Justinian meant to restore Africa exactly as it had been before 429, including the return of confiscated property to the Catholic church and descendants of Roman landowners.

provinces.name: Diocese of Oriens
provinces.endedNote: core lost 634-640
provinces.governor: vicarius, styled comes Orientis from the 330s

phases.t: Palestine to Mesopotamia, with Egypt and Libya
Egypt separated; fifteen provinces in the Notitia
the comes Orientis' powers curtailed in Justinian's reforms
Persian occupation
restored; lost to the Arabs, leaving only Cilicia and Isauria

provinces.summary: The diocese of the East, run from Antioch by a vicar so grand that he was titled comes Orientis. It included the richest and most urbanised provinces of the empire and the whole Persian frontier. The Arab conquests of 634-640 erased it.

provinces.name: Diocese of Aegyptus
provinces.endedNote: dissolved by Edict 13 (c. 539)

phases.t: six provinces: Aegyptus, Augustamnica, Arcadia, Thebais, Libya Superior, Libya Inferior

provinces.summary: Egypt was detached from Oriens and given its own head, the Augustal prefect, between 367 and 382. Justinian's Edict 13 (c. 539) dismantled the diocese, giving each Egyptian unit a duke with civil and military powers.

provinces.name: Diocese of Pontica
provinces.endedNote: still a unit in 641
provinces.governor: vicarius; abolished 535, restored with military powers 548

phases.t: northern and eastern Anatolia: eleven provinces in the Notitia
vicariate abolished by Justinian
vicar restored with civil and military powers against brigandage (Edict 8)

provinces.summary: Northern Anatolia from Bithynia to Armenia. Justinian abolished its vicar in 535 to cut costs and strengthen provincial governors, then restored him in 548 because brigandage was out of control.

provinces.name: Diocese of Asiana
provinces.endedNote: vicariate abolished 535
provinces.governor: vicarius (the proconsul of Asia outside his authority); abolished 535

phases.t: western and southern Anatolia: ten provinces plus proconsular Asia
vicariate abolished; several governors upgraded to praetors and counts

provinces.summary: Western and southern Asia Minor. Justinian's 535 reforms abolished its vicar and gave the governors of Pisidia and Lycaonia combined civil and military power.

provinces.name: Diocese of Thracia
provinces.endedNote: vicariate merged in 535
provinces.governor: vicarius; merged with the governorship of Thracia in 535

phases.t: six provinces from the Danube delta to the Propontis
vicariate merged into the praetor of Thrace (Novel 26)

provinces.summary: The European hinterland of Constantinople, devastated by Goths (376-382), Huns (441-447), Bulgars and Slavs. Novel 26 merged its vicar with the governor of Thracia province.

provinces.name: Diocese of Moesiae
provinces.endedNote: divided into Dacia and Macedonia (by c. 327; date disputed)

phases.t: the central and southern Balkans from the Danube to Crete

provinces.summary: The Verona List's diocese of the Moesias stretched from the Danube to Crete. It was soon divided into Dacia and Macedonia.

provinces.name: Diocese of Dacia
provinces.endedNote: Roman control collapsed in the early 7th century

phases.t: five provinces of the central Balkans
eastern; northern Illyricum under Justiniana Prima's archbishop from 535

provinces.summary: The inland Balkans: Dacia Ripensis, Dacia Mediterranea, Moesia I, Dardania and Praevalitana. It was the homeland of the soldier-emperors and of Justinian, and the first part of the empire to be overwhelmed by the Avar and Slav invasions.

provinces.name: Diocese of Macedonia
provinces.endedNote: Thessalonica and the coasts still Roman in 641

phases.t: Macedonia, Achaea, Thessaly, the Epiruses and Crete

provinces.summary: Greece and Macedonia. The Thessalonica massacre of 390, after which Ambrose forced Theodosius I to do penance, happened in its capital.

provinces.name: Diocese of Pannoniae (Illyricum)
provinces.endedNote: largely lost by c. 441 (Dalmatia and Noricum held longer)

phases.t: Pannonias, Noricums and Dalmatia
western Illyricum under the prefecture of Italy

provinces.summary: The middle Danube and Dalmatia, the recruiting heartland of the 3rd- and 4th-century army. After 395 it was the western rump of Illyricum, crumbling under Hunnic pressure from the 420s.

provinces.name: Diocese of Italia
provinces.createdNote: Diocletianic provincialisation; diocese in the Verona List
provinces.endedNote: dissolved in practice after the Lombard invasion of 568
provinces.governor: two vicars: vicarius Italiae (Milan) and vicarius urbis Romae

phases.t: Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and Raetia, provincialised under Diocletian
civil administration maintained under Odoacer, the Ostrogoths and Justinian

provinces.summary: Diocletian ended Italy's exemption from provincial government and taxation, dividing it into provinces under correctores. The north paid the annona to the court and army; the south, under the vicar of Rome, supplied the city.

provinces.name: Italia Annonaria (vicariate of Italy)
provinces.endedNote: Lombard invasion, 568

phases.t: northern Italy and Raetia, paying the annona in kind to court and army

provinces.summary: Northern Italy, so called because its provinces paid the annona in kind to support the court at Milan and the army; seven provinces in the Notitia.

provinces.name: Italia Suburbicaria (vicariate of Rome)
provinces.endedNote: Lombard invasion, 568

phases.t: central and southern Italy with the islands, supplying the city of Rome

provinces.summary: The 'suburbicarian' regions under the vicar of Rome, whose produce (pork, wine, grain) fed the city's dole. The term later defined the area of the pope's metropolitan authority.

provinces.name: Diocese of Africa
provinces.endedNote: Carthage fell in 439; replaced by Justinian's prefecture in 534
provinces.governor: vicarius Africae (the proconsul of Africa outside his authority)

phases.t: six provinces from Tripolitania to Mauretania Caesariensis
Vandal conquest

provinces.summary: The richest diocese of the West, whose grain fed Rome. Its counts Gildo (397-398) and Boniface (427-429) showed how a rebel in Africa could starve Italy.

provinces.name: Diocese of Hispaniae
provinces.endedNote: last Roman territory lost 472-475

phases.t: seven provinces including Tingitana
barbarian invasions; Roman control shrinks to Tarraconensis

provinces.summary: The Iberian peninsula and Tingitana, a lightly garrisoned diocese that fell apart after the Vandals, Alans and Sueves crossed the Pyrenees in autumn 409.

provinces.name: Diocese of Galliae
provinces.endedNote: Clovis defeated Syagrius in 486
provinces.governor: no vicar in the Notitia; governed directly by the praetorian prefect of the Gauls

phases.t: northern Gaul and the Rhine frontier
Rhine crossing; Franks, Burgundians and Alamanni; Roman enclave of Aegidius and Syagrius

provinces.summary: Northern Gaul and the Rhine, the most militarised region of the West. Its Roman government ended piecemeal; the last fragment, Syagrius' realm at Soissons, fell to Clovis in 486.

provinces.name: Diocese of Viennensis (Septem Provinciae)
provinces.endedNote: Provence ceded to Euric, 476

phases.t: southern Gaul
Arles the centre of Roman Gaul; annual council of the Seven Provinces (418)

provinces.summary: Southern Gaul, originally called Viennensis and later the Seven Provinces. Honorius' edict of 418 established a yearly assembly of its notables at Arles, the nearest thing to a representative body in late Roman government.

provinces.name: Diocese of Britanniae
provinces.endedNote: Roman government ended 409-410

phases.t: four provinces after Constantius I's recovery of Britain
barbarian conspiracy (367); Valentia added (369); usurpers Magnus Maximus (383) and Constantine III (407)

provinces.summary: Britain under a vicar in London. The vicar Martinus killed himself in 353 rather than submit to the purge of Constantius II's notary Paul 'the Chain' (Ammianus 14.5). Zosimus says the Britons expelled the Roman officials in 409; the rescript of Honorius in 410 telling the cities to look to their own defence may in fact refer to Bruttium.

provinces.name: Exarchate of Ravenna
provinces.createdNote: exarch first attested in a letter of Pope Pelagius II (584)
provinces.endedNote: Ravenna fell to the Lombard king Aistulf in 751
provinces.governor: exarch (patricius et exarchus), combining supreme civil and military authority

phases.t: first exarch attested 584 (Decius), then Smaragdus (585-589); duchies of Rome, Naples, Venetia, the Pentapolis and Perusia
exarch Eleutherius proclaims himself emperor and is killed (619)
exarch Isaac (625-643) plunders the Lateran treasury (640)

provinces.summary: Maurice's answer to the Lombard invasion: a single governor in Ravenna with full civil and military powers over the scattered Byzantine territories of Italy. Exarchs quarrelled constantly with the popes; Isaac seized the Lateran treasury in 640, and his tomb survives in San Vitale.

provinces.name: Exarchate of Carthage (Africa)
provinces.createdNote: exarch Gennadius attested in letters of Gregory the Great (591)
provinces.endedNote: Carthage fell in 698
provinces.governor: exarch, combining civil and military authority

phases.t: exarch Gennadius first attested (591)
the exarch Heraclius the Elder launches the revolt that makes his son emperor
exarchate under the Heraclian dynasty; Gregory's revolt (646) and death at Sufetula (647)

provinces.summary: The African counterpart of Ravenna, created amid Moorish wars. Its exarch Heraclius sent his son by sea and his nephew Nicetas overland against Phocas in 608-610, and the son entered Constantinople as emperor in October 610.

provinces.name: Quaestura exercitus
provinces.endedNote: attested into the later 6th century; fate obscure
provinces.governor: quaestor Iustinianus exercitus (first holder Bonus), with the rank of a praetorian prefect for his provinces

phases.t: Moesia II and Scythia on the Danube joined with Caria, the Islands and Cyprus (Novel 41, 18 May 536); appeals from the Aegean provinces later heard at Constantinople (Novel 50)

provinces.summary: A strikingly unconventional unit: two impoverished Danube provinces yoked to three rich Aegean ones under a single quaestor, so that the islands' revenues and shipping could supply the Danube armies directly by sea. Lydus complained that it ruined the provincials. It is often seen as the ancestor of the later Karabisianoi naval command.

provinces.name: Spania
provinces.endedNote: last towns taken by Suinthila c. 624-625 (Isidore, Historia Gothorum 62)

phases.t: Liberius' expedition intervenes in the Visigothic civil war for Athanagild against Agila; coast from Carthago Nova to Malaca and beyond
Leovigild's offensives (Baza, Medina Sidonia, Cordoba)
Sisebut and Suinthila conquer the remainder

provinces.summary: Justinian's toe-hold in Spain, won when the aged Liberius was sent to support the rebel Athanagild in 552. An inscription of 589 at Cartagena records the gate built by the patricius Comenciolus 'against the barbarian enemy'. Isidore of Seville credits king Suinthila with expelling the last Romans around 624; the Balearics and Septem stayed Byzantine.

mints.name: Amphipolis: Macedonian merides and Roman Macedonia
mints.notes: After Pydna (168) Aemilius Paullus divided Macedon into four republics (merides) and closed the royal mines; when they reopened (158) the First Meris, with its capital at Amphipolis, struck abundant tetradrachms with the bust of Artemis Tauropolos on a Macedonian shield and a club within an oak wreath. After the province was created (146) Roman officials struck tetradrachms with an Alexander-head obverse and the names of a quaestor, most famously AESILLAS Q (c. 90-70), whose mint may be Thessalonica rather than Amphipolis. These Hellenistic-looking pieces paid Roman armies in the Mithridatic and Thracian wars and travelled north to the Danube, where they were imitated.

mints.name: Dyrrhachium and Apollonia (Illyrian drachms)
mints.notes: The two Greek cities on the Adriatic, under Roman protection from 229, struck light drachms (c. 3.4 g) with a cow suckling a calf and a 'double stellate' square pattern, signed by two magistrates (a monetary magistrate and an eponymous one). Produced in huge numbers in the 2nd-1st centuries, they became a principal currency of the central Balkans and are found in Dacian hoards in thousands, alongside Roman Republican denarii. Pompey based himself here in 48 BC, and the series ends around the civil war. Common, varied and collectable by magistrate pairs.

mints.name: Athens (New Style coinage under Rome)
mints.notes: Athens' 'New Style' tetradrachms (Athena Parthenos in Attic helmet / owl on an amphora within an olive wreath) were struck in vast numbers in the 2nd-1st centuries BC, the main silver of the Aegean in Rome's age of hegemony, with annual magistrates, a symbol, and on the amphora a letter for the month of issue. The series has a crisis around Athens' alliance with Mithridates (88-86): issues with Aristion and the King, followed by Sulla's sack of the city (86). Sulla himself struck tetradrachms of Athenian type and his own denarii and aurei in the Greek East with an itinerant military mint. Dating the New Style series (the 'high' Thompson chronology against the 'low' Lewis/Mattingly one) is a classic numismatic dispute.

mints.name: Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis (Corinth)
mints.notes: Caesar's colony of 44 BC, settled largely with freedmen, struck bronze under its duoviri with Bellerophon and Pegasus, Poseidon, the Isthmus, the Acrocorinth temple and portraits of the imperial family. A break followed Galba; the colony struck again under Hadrian and later, with views of buildings (the Peirene fountain, temples on the Acrocorinth) that are used by archaeologists. Most Corinthian bronzes are of modest preservation; examples with clear architecture are prized.

mints.name: Patrae (Patras): Antony's military mint
marks: ANT AVG III VIR R P C
mints.notes: Antony wintered at Patrae in 32/31 before Actium and paid his army with the 'legionary denarii': a galley with ANT AVG III VIR R P C, and an aquila between two standards naming each legion from LEG PRI (I) to LEG XXX, plus the praetorian cohorts, the speculatores, and special legions (XVII Classica, XVIII Libyca). Their silver was deliberately lowered (to perhaps c. 92%), so Gresham's law kept them circulating for two centuries: worn legionary denarii are a regular component of hoards into the 3rd century, and Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus restored the LEG VI type. Attribution to Patrae rests on Antony's movements and is usually accepted. Common in low grade; high-grade pieces of rare legions (LEG XXIII, the cohorts, XVII CLASSICAE) bring large sums and are counterfeited.

mints.name: Colonia Augusta Iulia Philippensis (Philippi)
mints.notes: Colony settled after the battle of 42 BC and refounded after Actium with veterans including praetorians. Its most common bronze, VIC AVG (Victory) / COHOR PRAE PHIL (three standards), honours the praetorian veterans; its date is debated between Augustus and Claudius. Later colonial issues run to Gallienus. Philippi's coins are the commonest Latin-legend colonial bronzes of the Greek world and a useful introduction to Roman colonial coinage, in which Latin legends mark a colonia among Greek-speaking cities.

mints.name: Ephesus
mints.notes: The Attalid cistophorus (c. 12.6 g, valued at 3 denarii) survived the Roman takeover of Asia (133) and was struck at Ephesus and other cities into the 1st c. BC, with proconsuls' names in Latin from the 50s. Antony struck cistophori with Octavia (39 BC) here, and Octavian's AEGVPTO CAPTA and PAX cistophori (28 BC) are attributed to Ephesus, as is a series of Augustan aurei and denarii. Claudius and Hadrian struck cistophori: Hadrian's great series of c. 128 often overstruck older cistophori, including those of Mark Antony and Augustus, and names many Asian cities and cult statues (Artemis of Ephesus). In 69-71 Vespasian's eastern aurei and denarii were struck at Ephesus and carry a small EPHE or ΕΦΕ monogram below the reverse type: a rare explicit mint mark in the 1st century.

mints.name: Pergamum
mints.notes: Birthplace of the cistophorus under the Attalids (c. 166 BC); it continued to strike cistophori after 133. RIC attributes to Pergamum a famous group of Augustan cistophori of c. 19-18 BC: the hexastyle temple of Roma and Augustus with COM ASIAE (Commune Asiae), six grain ears (AVGVSTVS), and the triumphal arch with SIGNIS RECEPTIS. Claudius' cistophori with the same temple (with ROM ET AVG) belong to the same tradition. Separating Ephesus, Pergamum and other Asian mints for these silver pieces is done by style and is not always secure.

mints.name: Nicaea (Iznik)
mints.notes: One of the most prolific civic bronze mints of Roman Asia Minor, striking from Octavian to Gallienus. Nicaea's coins carry its long-running rivalry with Nicomedia over the title 'first city' of Bithynia, and show city walls, gates, temples, Dionysus (claimed as founder) and agonistic crowns. Under the Severans and Gallienus it struck abundant small bronzes with three or four letters of the legend, often confused by beginners with Alexandrian or Moesian issues. Its later fame as the site of the Council of 325 has nothing to do with the coinage, which had ended.

mints.name: Cyzicus
mints.officinae: up to 6 in the 4th c.; 2 (A, B) in the Byzantine period.
mints.notes: Already a great Greek electrum mint in the archaic and classical periods, Cyzicus became an imperial mint c. 266/7, late in Gallienus' reign or under Claudius II. It remained active through the Tetrarchy and the 4th century (SMK with Greek officina letters) and was one of the main eastern bronze mints of the Byzantine period: large folles of Justinian and later emperors marked KYZ with officina A or B, dated by regnal year from 538/9. Its Heraclian folles are frequently overstruck and roughly made. The mint closed c. 629. Do not confuse late Roman K marks (Cyzicus) with PK (Carthage) or the K of Constantinopolitan officina numbering.

mints.name: Nicomedia (Izmit)
mints.notes: Diocletian's capital and, from c. 294, a major mint. Nicomedia struck heavily for the Tetrarchs, Galerius, Maximinus Daia and Licinius (whose IOVI CONSERVATORI types dominate eastern hoards of 313-324), and for Constantine, whose Nicomedian solidi and medallions are fine. In the 4th-5th century it remained a principal bronze mint (SMN with Greek officina letters, up to five or more). In the Byzantine period Nicomedia was the third bronze mint of the empire after Constantinople and Antioch, marked NIKO with officinae A and B, struck large dated folles from 538/9 and closed under Heraclius. Identification: SMN with a Greek letter is Nicomedia; SM followed by H is Heraclea.

mints.name: Constantinopolis (Constantinople)
mints.officinae: up to 11 in the late 4th c. (A to IA); 10 on Byzantine solidi (A to I); 5 on folles (A to Є).
mints.notes: Opened in 326, before the city's dedication (11 May 330), it became the leading mint of the eastern empire for over a millennium. In the 4th c. the mark is CONS plus a Greek officina numeral, with CONSIA for the 11th; never confuse it with the Arles marks PCON, SCON, TCON (Latin officina first). Gold from c. 368 carries CONOB (CONstantinopolis + OB, for obryzum, 'refined', and the Greek numeral 72, the solidi to the pound): a convention so authoritative that CONOB was used on gold of other mints and of barbarian imitators. Light-weight solidi of the 6th-7th c. (20, 22 or 23 siliquae) are marked OB XX, OB+*, etc. Byzantine bronze reads CON with officinae A-Є; from Justinian's 12th regnal year (538/9) folles carry ANNO and the regnal year, which lets collectors date precisely. Heraclian solidi with two and three figures, and the silver hexagram (615), are Constantinopolitan.

mints.name: Heraclea Thraciae (Perinthus, Marmara Ereğlisi)
mints.notes: The old city of Perinthus, renamed Heraclea, received a mint in the Diocletianic system (c. 292/4) and struck abundantly through the 4th century: Tetrarchic folles, Licinian IOVI CONSERVATORI, and the full Constantinian range. Marks begin HT (Heraclea Thraciae) with officina letters, later SMH plus letter. Production tapered off in the 5th century and the mint did not continue into the Byzantine system, which concentrated eastern Thrace on Constantinople. SMH must be read carefully: SMHA is Heraclea, officina A; SMN with H is Nicomedia, officina 8.

mints.name: Thessalonica
marks: IS / H / Δ value marks (6th c.)
mints.notes: Galerius opened the mint c. 298 when he made Thessalonica his residence. In the 4th c. marks are TS with officina letters (often punctuated .TS.Γ.) and SMTS; gold TESOB. Constantine struck here in preparation for the Licinian war and Vetranio in 350. Thessalonica stayed a regular eastern mint into the Byzantine period with its own denominations: in the early 6th century it struck pieces of 16 nummi (IS) and 8 nummi (H) and 4 nummi (Δ), outside the 40-20-10-5 scheme used elsewhere, which numismatists explain by a local monetary tradition or tariffing. Thessalonican solidi of Justinian and his successors are of distinctive style. The mint closed in Heraclius' reign (c. 630).

mints.name: Serdica (Sofia)
mints.notes: Aurelian opened Serdica c. 271/2, his native region. It struck some of his most remarkable coins: the RESTITVTOR ORBIS and ORIENS AVG series, the rare SOLI INVICTO bronze with radiate Sol, and the obverse SOL DOMINVS IMPERI ROMANI on a coin of Sol, plus coins with DEO ET DOMINO NATO AVRELIANO AVG, titulature that announced an emperor 'born lord and god'. Probus struck an enormous series here with ornate busts. The mint closed in the 280s, reopened under Galerius (303-308) for folles marked SMSD, and once more briefly under Licinius in 313-314. Serdica folles of the Tetrarchy are scarce.

mints.name: Viminacium (Kostolac)
mints.notes: Made a colony under Gordian III, Viminacium struck large provincial bronzes for the province of Moesia Superior with the legend P M S COL VIM and Moesia standing between a bull (VII Claudia) and a lion (IV Flavia), dated by the era of the colony from AN I (239/40) to AN XVI (254/5). They are the common provincial coin of the region. In 253-256, a short-lived imperial mint here struck antoniniani and gold for Valerian and Gallienus (and perhaps Aemilianus), attributed by style and find concentration. The parallel 'PROVINCIA DACIA' bronzes, dated AN I-XI (246/7-256/7), belong to a different, unlocated Dacian mint.

mints.name: Nicopolis ad Istrum
mints.notes: Trajan's foundation (after the Dacian wars) in Moesia Inferior struck one of the most varied of all provincial bronze coinages, especially under Septimius Severus, Caracalla, Geta and Macrinus: hundreds of reverse types (deities, city gates, Hercules' labours, local river gods) with the name of the provincial governor (ΥΠ = under, for example ΥΠ ΑΥΡ ΓΑΛΛΟΥ). Governors' names date issues closely and supply prosopography otherwise lost. Common and affordable, they make a classic specialist collection.

mints.name: Marcianopolis (Devnya)
mints.notes: Trajan's city named for his sister Marciana; the great Réka Devnia hoard was found here. Its provincial bronzes under the Severans, Gordian III and Philip carry value marks: Є for 5 assaria (the pentassarion), Δ for 4, Γ for 3, B for 2, part of a regional denominational system in Moesia Inferior. Characteristic types show confronted busts of two rulers, for example Gordian III facing Serapis or Tranquillina, Philip I with Otacilia, or Macrinus with Diadumenian. Governors' names date them.

mints.name: Cherson (Chersonesos, Crimea)
mints.notes: The Byzantine outpost in the Crimea struck its own bronze on a local system with unusual value letters (H, Π, Δ and others whose meaning is debated). The best known issues, of Maurice, show emperor and empress (Constantina) standing on one side and their son Theodosius on the other, a rare depiction of a junior co-ruler with the empress. Cherson continued to strike in the later Byzantine period, but its 6th-7th century bronzes are scarce, often crude, and found mainly in the region.

mints.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia (Kayseri)
mints.notes: After Cappadocia was annexed in AD 17, Caesarea struck provincial silver on a standard linked to the denarius: drachms, didrachms and from Trajan tridrachms and hemidrachms, often with Latin-style imperial portraits and Greek legends. The signature reverse is Mount Argaeus, the volcano behind the city, sometimes with a figure or star on its summit, or set on an altar. Regnal-year dates (ET followed by a number) date many issues. Some imperial denarii and aurei were struck at Caesarea under Trajan and Hadrian and in the civil war of 193-194 (for Pescennius Niger and Septimius Severus); these are distinguished from Rome by style. The mint stopped under Gordian III.

mints.name: Tarsus
mints.notes: Capital of Cilicia, home of Paul, struck abundant civic bronze. Its 3rd-century coins are among the largest of all provincial issues, with the city's many titles abbreviated (AMK: first, greatest, most beautiful; ΓB: twice neocorate), the Perseus and Sandan cults, the pyre of Sandan, agonistic prizes, and portraits of Severan and later emperors in elaborate dress (Caracalla wearing a demiurgic crown). Tarsus also struck silver tetradrachms and civil-war pieces. Coins of Tarsus document the competitive titulature of Greek cities under Rome.

mints.name: Antiochia (Antioch on the Orontes), later Theoupolis
mints.officinae: up to 15 under Constantius II (A to IE); 5 under Justinian.
mints.notes: The capital of Roman Syria struck for six and a half centuries. Under the Republic and Augustus it issued 'posthumous' tetradrachms in the name of the Seleucid Philip Philadelphus and then imperial tetradrachms (eagle reverse) and the SC bronzes issued for the governor of Syria. Imperial denarii were struck here at intervals (for Vespasian in 69-72, Pescennius Niger in 193-194, Severus, Macrinus, Elagabalus) and antoniniani in the 3rd century, often with a distinctive eastern portrait; Antioch's tetradrachms of the 3rd century are billon. From 294 it was a regular mint with marks ANT, SMANT and Greek officina letters, and it reached up to 15 officinae under Constantius II, a measure of eastern military spending. After the earthquakes of 526 and 528 Justinian renamed the city Theoupolis ('city of God'), and the mint mark changed from ANTX to THEUP and variants. Captured and burned by Khosrow I in 540, the mint resumed; it closed when the Persians took Antioch in 610/611.

mints.name: Laodicea ad Mare (Latakia)
mints.notes: Septimius Severus rewarded Laodicea, which had backed him against Niger, by making it metropolis of Syria at Antioch's expense and opening an imperial mint there. RIC assigns to Laodicea a large group of denarii of c. 196-202 for Severus, Julia Domna, Caracalla and Geta, recognisable by a fuller, softer portrait style and by particular reverse types (for example AETERNIT IMPERI with busts of Severus and Caracalla, and RESTITVTOR VRBIS). Separating 'Laodicea' from 'Emesa' and Rome is a matter of style; specialists disagree on some groups. Laodicea also struck civic bronze and tetradrachms.

mints.name: Emesa (Homs)
mints.notes: Home of Julia Domna's family and the sun god Elagabal, worshipped as a black stone (baetyl). A Severan mint of 193-196 is attributed here, with crude early denarii of Severus and Domna (provincial lettering, misspellings) and coins of Pescennius Niger. Elagabalus struck in Syria on his way to Rome. The usurper Uranius Antoninus (253-254), apparently a priest of Elagabal who defended Emesa against Shapur I, struck aurei and billon tetradrachms here: the aurei show the conical stone of Elagabal on a cart and the legend CONSERVATOR AVG, among the great rarities of the 3rd century. Emesa's civic bronzes show the temple with the baetyl.

mints.name: Samosata (eastern mint of Valerian and Gallienus)
mints.notes: A second eastern mint operating for Valerian, Gallienus, Salonina and the Caesars in the late 250s is attributed by some to Samosata on the Euphrates and by others to Antioch or an itinerant field mint. Its antoniniani have a distinctive, often stylised portrait and reverse types tied to the Persian war (RESTITVT ORIENTIS, VICTORIA PART). Valerian's capture at Edessa in 260 ended it. Its existence is a reminder of how mints followed armies in the crisis decades.

mints.name: Tripolis (Phoenicia)
marks: XXI with officina letters and dots
mints.notes: A Syrian mint opened by Aurelian after the reconquest of the East (272-273) and active under Tacitus, Probus and Carus. It is identified by style and find spots rather than by an explicit mark; the Tripolis attribution, argued since the early 20th century, is generally accepted. Its products include reformed aureliani with XXI and Greek or Latin numerals, and they circulate with Antioch's coins, from which they must be separated by portrait style and mark punctuation. A good test case of how attributions are built from die studies and hoards.

mints.name: Tyre
mints.notes: After freeing itself from the Seleucids (126/5 BC), Tyre struck high-quality silver shekels and half-shekels with Melqart-Heracles laureate and an eagle on a prow, dated by the city's era. Because of their consistent fineness they were the coin prescribed for the Jerusalem Temple tax (Mishnah, Tosefta Ketubot 13.20), and they are the likeliest candidates for the 'thirty pieces of silver'. The latest Tyrian shekels (c. 18/19 BC to AD 65/6), cruder and marked KP or KAP, have been argued (Meshorer) to be struck at Jerusalem under Herod, a hypothesis still debated. Under the Severans Tyre struck billon tetradrachms (with a small murex shell or Melqart's club) and colonial bronzes with the legend of Dido and the founding of Carthage.

mints.name: Caesarea Maritima
mints.notes: Seat of the Roman governor of Judaea. After the fall of Jerusalem, a series of 'Judaea Capta' bronzes with Greek legends (IOYΔAIAΣ EAΛΩKYIAΣ, 'Judaea captured') for Vespasian, Titus and Domitian was struck at Caesarea, with Victory writing on a shield and Nike types, distinct from the famous Latin IVDAEA CAPTA sestertii, denarii and aurei struck at Rome and elsewhere (Judaea seated mourning under a palm, a captive Jew with hands tied). Colonial bronzes of Caesarea continue under later emperors. The Roman procuratorial prutot of Pontius Pilate (with lituus or simpulum, AD 29-31) were struck in Judaea, probably at Jerusalem.

mints.name: Jerusalem: mint of the First Revolt
mints.notes: The rebels of 66 struck silver shekels and half-shekels (and rare quarters) of excellent silver (c. 14 g), with a chalice and three pomegranates and Paleo-Hebrew legends, dated Year 1 to Year 5 (the Year 5 shekels of spring 70, when the city was under siege, are very rare). The Jewish authorities clearly chose to replace the Tyrian shekel for Temple dues. Bronze prutot read 'Freedom of Zion' and later 'For the Redemption of Zion'. The Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135) produced a second rebel coinage, overstruck on Roman denarii, drachms and tetradrachms (Temple facade with the Ark, lulav and etrog, 'For the freedom of Jerusalem'); its mint is not located (Jerusalem was not in rebel hands on most views). Both series are heavily counterfeited; die-matching and identification of undertypes are standard tests.

mints.name: Alexandria
mints.notes: Roman Egypt kept a closed currency: billon tetradrachms (nominally equal to a denarius) and bronze drachms, valid only in the province. Augustus struck only bronze; Tiberius resumed tetradrachms in AD 19/20 and they continue to Diocletian, dated by regnal year (L for 'year' plus a Greek numeral, so L IB = year 12). Their silver content sank from c. 25% in the 1st century to almost nothing by the 260s, and their huge volume makes them a key source for Egyptian price history alongside papyri. Big bronze drachms of Antoninus Pius with zodiac and Nile types are a celebrated series. Diocletian abolished the provincial coinage in 296/7 and made Alexandria an imperial mint (ALE, SMAL; gold ALE). It struck folles for Domitius Domitianus and Achilleus during their revolt (297-298). In the Byzantine period Alexandria had its own bronze: the 12-nummi (IB) and 6-nummi (S) pieces between Anastasius' reform and the Arab conquest, and briefly the 33-nummi (ΛΓ) under Justinian. Heraclius' revolt against Phocas struck consular-bust solidi here (608-610). Production ended with the Arab conquest (641-646).

mints.name: Alexandretta (Iskenderun): Heraclian revolt mint
mints.notes: During the revolt of the elder Heraclius (exarch of Africa) and his son against Phocas (608-610), coins were struck at several eastern sites under rebel control, with the two Heraclii shown as consuls (busts in consular robes, no imperial titles). Some bronze is attributed to Alexandretta in Cilicia by reading of the mint signature, though Alexandria in Egypt is sometimes preferred for parts of the group. Rare.

mints.name: Constantia (Salamis), Cyprus
mints.notes: Cyprus struck coins first for the Heraclian revolt against Phocas (608-610: consular busts of the two Heraclii, KYΠP), and again late in Heraclius' reign (626-629) when it produced folles and some gold with the emperor and his sons; the mint is placed at the island's capital Constantia. Cyprus later yielded major Byzantine treasures (the Lambousa or 'First and Second Cyprus Treasures', including the David Plates), deposited in the 650s during the Arab raids.

mints.name: Seleucia Isauriae (Silifke)
mints.notes: A temporary mint opened by Heraclius during the Persian war, when Antioch, Alexandria and much of the eastern mint network had been lost. It struck folles and half-folles with Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine, marked SELIS (Seleucia Isauriae) and dated by regnal year (years 5-8, 614/5-617/8). Its coins illustrate the emergency relocation of production behind the front, alongside the short-lived Isaura mint.

mints.name: Isaura
mints.notes: Successor to Seleucia as Heraclius' emergency eastern bronze mint for a single year or so (regnal years 8-9). Its folles, marked ISAYP or similar, are rare and usually overstruck and crude. With Seleucia, it fills the gap left by the closure of Antioch (610) during the Persian advance into Anatolia.

mints.name: Gades (Cádiz)
mints.notes: The Phoenician city struck bronze and some silver for centuries with Melqart (Herakles) in lion-skin and tunny fish, with Neo-Punic legends; under Roman rule it continued into the reign of Augustus, adding Latin legends that honour the Balbi (Gades' famous family, L. Cornelius Balbus the Younger was pontifex there), Agrippa, Gaius and Lucius. The tunny types are a favourite of collectors and a reminder of the city's salt-fish trade. Gades' series ends with the early Principate, like almost all Spanish civic coinage by Caligula.

mints.name: Roma (Rome): Moneta
mints.locNote: Republican mint traditionally by the temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx [12.4829, 41.8937]; the imperial mint lay in Regio III near San Clemente, where dedications by the officinatores of Trajan's mint (CIL VI 42-44) were found.
marks: (none: moneyer names and control marks, Republic)
officina numerals P S T Q V VI ... XII in field (3rd c.)
mints.officinae: Republic: unknown number of workshops under the tresviri monetales. Up to 12 officinae under Gallienus; 6-7 after 274; usually 4 (P, S, T, Q) in the 4th c., sometimes more; one or two in the Byzantine period.
mints.notes: The longest-lived mint of antiquity, striking from the aes grave of the early 3rd c. BC to the papal and Byzantine coinage of the 7th-8th centuries. Republican coins carry no mint mark: they are signed by the moneyers (IIIviri aere argento auro flando feriundo) and from c. 140 BC increasingly advertise their families, which is why the Republican series is studied by moneyer and dated by Crawford's die-link and hoard sequence (RRC). Many late Republican issues carry control marks (letters, numerals, symbols) marking individual dies: Piso Frugi (RRC 340) and the moneyers of the 80s used hundreds. Under Augustus gold and silver moved to Lugdunum c. 15-12 BC, while Rome struck the moneyers' aes (signed IIIVIR AAAFF until c. 4 BC); Nero restored precious-metal production at Rome by 64. In 271 the mint workers under the rationalis Felicissimus rebelled against Aurelian and were crushed with heavy loss (Aurelius Victor gives 7,000 soldiers killed); the mint was cut down and reorganised. From 294 Rome uses R plus officina letter; Maxentius (306-312) made it a showcase (Romulus and Remus, temple of Roma AETERNAE). In the 4th c. look for RP, RS, RT, RQ, often with a wreath or star; from the 370s SMROM and RMPS (silver). Late gold reads COMOB with R M flanking.
