scholarship: Guest, The Late Roman Gold and Silver Coins from the Hoxne Treasure (2005)

coinage.t: VRBS ROMA, CONSTANTINOPOLIS and GLORIA EXERCITVS (330-341)
coinage.text: To mark the dedication of Constantinople (11 May 330) every mint struck two 'city commemoratives' in parallel: VRBS ROMA (helmeted Roma / she-wolf and twins) and CONSTANTINOPOLIS (Constantinopolis helmeted with sceptre / Victory on a prow), in vast numbers until 337 and beyond. Alongside, the standard type was GLORIA EXERCITVS with two soldiers and two standards (330-335), then with one standard (335-341), a reduction marked by a lighter coin. Small symbols in the standard (chi-rho, wreath, letters) distinguish issues. Collectors use these common coins to learn the late Roman mint system, since nearly every mint and officina can be collected.

coinage.t: How to read a late Roman mint mark
coinage.text: From 294 almost every coin carries in the exergue a mark built from (1) an optional prefix: SM (sacra moneta, sacred mint), P (pecunia) or M (moneta); (2) the mint abbreviation (TR Trier, LVG Lyon, ARL or CON Arles, R or RM Rome, AQ Aquileia, SIS Siscia, SIRM Sirmium, TS or TES Thessalonica, H or HT Heraclea, CONS Constantinople, N or NIC Nicomedia, K Cyzicus, ANT Antioch, ALE Alexandria, K or PK Carthage, T Ticinum, OST Ostia, LON or PLN London, AMB Amiens, MD Milan, RV Ravenna); (3) an officina mark, Latin in the West (P, S, T, Q) and Greek in the East (A, B, Γ, Δ, Є, S, Z, H, Θ, I, IA); and (4) field symbols or letters marking sub-issues. Precious-metal marks add OB (gold, obryzum, and the Greek numeral 72) or PS (silver, pusulatum). Traps: CON with a Latin letter in front is Arles; CONS with a Greek letter after is Constantinople; SMH is Heraclea, SMN is Nicomedia; COMOB on gold is used by many mints. RIC VI-X tabulate every mark.
scholarship: Sear, Roman Coins and their Values IV-V

coinage.text: Emperors took public vows (vota) for their own welfare at fixed intervals, discharged at quinquennalia, decennalia and vicennalia. Coins record them: VOT V (vows for five years taken), VOT X MVLT XX (ten-year vows fulfilled, twenty undertaken), VOT XXX MVLT XXXX. Because the vows were taken at anniversaries, often in advance, the numbers date coins to within a few years: Constantine's VOT XX coins of 315-320, Theodosius II's VOT XX MVLT XXX solidi with a long cross (c. 420-422), the VOT X MVLT XV of Arcadius and Honorius. Caveat: vows could be anticipated by a year or two, and junior emperors' vows ran from their own accession, which can mislead.
scholarship: Chastagnol, 'Les années régnales de Maximien Hercule', RN 1967

coinage.text: The coinage turned Christian slowly. Sol Invictus remained on Constantine's coins until c. 318-320; the chi-rho first appears as a small mark on the helmet of the Ticinum silver medallion of 315 and as a field mark in the 320s, and on the labarum piercing a serpent (SPES PVBLIC, Constantinople, c. 327). Constantine's posthumous coins (337) show him veiled and ascending in a quadriga with the hand of God reaching down: a hybrid of pagan consecration and Christian heaven. Magnentius made the chi-rho the whole reverse (353). Theodosius II's solidi with Victory holding a long jewelled cross (c. 420) put the cross at the centre; Tiberius II replaced Victory with the cross on steps (578); Justinian II's Christ portrait (692) falls after 641. The pace of change is a gauge of how cautiously emperors moved in public religion.
scholarship: Bruun, 'The Christian signs on the coins of Constantine', Arctos 1962

coinage.t: FEL TEMP REPARATIO (348) and the bronze reforms of the 350s
coinage.standard: large coin c. 5.3 g with a small silver content; reduced in 352/3 and again c. 355
coinage.text: For the 1,100th anniversary of Rome (348) Constans and Constantius II issued new bronze with the slogan FEL TEMP REPARATIO ('the restoration of happy times'), each denomination with its own type: the emperor dragging a barbarian from a hut, a phoenix on a globe or pyre, the emperor on a galley steered by Victory, and above all a soldier spearing a fallen horseman. Names such as maiorina and centenionalis come from laws in the Theodosian Code (title 9.23, on transport of money), and matching them to coins is uncertain. The falling horseman type became the standard eastern coin of the 350s, shrinking steadily, and it was copied massively in Britain and Gaul. Gallus Caesar's portraits and Julian's early Caesar coins belong to this series.
scholarship: Carson, 'The reform of the bronze coinage under Constans and Constantius II'

coinage.t: The Valentinianic reform of gold and silver (c. 366-368)
coinage.text: After Procopius' revolt (365-366), during which coins of doubtful purity were struck, Valentinian I and Valens tightened control of precious metals. Gold received in taxes was to be melted into bullion before reuse, refined gold was struck at mints that followed the court (the comitatus), and coins carried OB (obryzum, refined gold) and PS (refined silver). COMOB became the standard gold mark (COM for comitatus or the comes sacrarum largitionum, plus OB), and later CONOB for Constantinople. The reform helps explain why later 4th-century gold is so pure and why gold minting shifted with the emperors' movements between Trier, Milan, Sirmium and Antioch.
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985) 386-394

coinage.standard: c. 1.5 g (8 siliquae)
coinage.text: Introduced under Theodosius I (from c. 383), the tremissis replaced the 1.5-scripulum piece as the small gold denomination and became the dominant gold coin of the Germanic successor kingdoms of the West, where Merovingian, Visigothic and Lombard rulers copied it for centuries. Typical late Roman reverse: Victory advancing with wreath and globus cruciger, VICTORIA AVGVSTORVM; Byzantine tremisses show a cross. The 37 Merovingian tremisses of Sutton Hoo show the coin's long afterlife.
scholarship: Grierson and Blackburn, Medieval European Coinage I (1986)

coinage.t: The late Roman AE4 and the collapse of the bronze
coinage.standard: AE4 c. 1-1.5 g, 11-13 mm, falling below 1 g in the 5th century
coinage.text: From the 380s the main bronze became a tiny coin, SALVS REIPVBLICAE (Victory dragging a captive) and VICTORIA AVGGG, and after 395 the larger AE2 was abolished. The West stopped sending fresh bronze to Britain after c. 402, which is why Romano-British site finds end abruptly. In the 5th century, minimi of Leo I, Zeno and the Vandals, with monograms or a cross in a wreath, sank below a gram; one solidus was worth some 7,000 nummi by the end of the century. The reform of Anastasius (498) finally created multiple-nummus coins to make the small change usable again.
scholarship: Reece, The Coinage of Roman Britain (2002)

coinage.t: Clipped siliquae in late Roman Britain
coinage.text: Most siliquae found in Britain from the late 4th and early 5th centuries have had their edges clipped, sometimes so severely that the legend vanishes and the portrait is cut. Clipping went on after the flow of new coin stopped (c. 402-410) and seems to have been tolerated, perhaps systematic: it produced silver for imitations or for bullion while keeping the clipped coins in circulation. The Hoxne hoard, with over 14,000 siliquae nearly all clipped, is the main evidence, and the degree of clipping helps date hoards. Clipping was almost unknown on the Continent, which marks Britain's isolation in the last Roman decades.
scholarship: Guest, The Late Roman Gold and Silver Coins from the Hoxne Treasure (2005)
Abdy, 'After Patching', in Hunter and Painter (eds.) 2013

coinage.text: Large bronze medallions with a raised rim and a deep groove (contorno) around the edge, made in Rome in the later 4th and 5th centuries, perhaps as New Year's gifts or tokens connected with the circus games. They show emperors of the distant past (Nero, Trajan), Alexander the Great, Homer, Apuleius and charioteers, with pagan myths, circus scenes and the palm monogram (PE). Often linked with the pagan senatorial aristocracy of Rome (the circle of Symmachus), though the connection is debated. They are not coins. Rare, and copied in modern times.
scholarship: Mittag, Alte Köpfe in neuen Händen (1999)

coinage.text: Medallions were special issues outside the circulating system, struck from the 2nd century (Hadrian and the Antonines produced large bronze medallions, sometimes bimetallic with an orichalcum centre and copper ring) to the Byzantine period. Late Roman gold multiples (from 1.5 to 9 solidi and larger) were imperial gifts to officers and allied kings: the Beaurains (Arras) medallion of Constantius I, the Szilágysomlyó medallions of Valens, the 36-solidus medallion of Justinian (stolen from the Cabinet des Médailles in 1831 and melted; electrotypes survive). They carry ambitious iconography (imperial adventus, largitio scenes, triumphs) and are documents of court art and diplomacy.

Imperial women appear on coins in a sequence that tracks their public status. Livia appears anonymously (as Pax or Salus) and then named under Tiberius and as DIVA AVGVSTA under Claudius; Agrippina the Younger shares the obverse with Nero in 54; the Flavian and Trajanic women (Domitia, Plotina, Marciana) begin regular series. The Faustinas, Lucilla, Crispina, Julia Domna (with MATER CASTRORVM), Julia Maesa, Julia Mamaea, Otacilia Severa, Salonina and Severina carry dynastic and religious messages. In the 4th century Helena and Fausta (324-326) and later Flaccilla, Eudoxia, Pulcheria, Galla Placidia, Licinia Eudoxia, Ariadne and Sophia appear, often with the hand of God crowning them. The empress's crescent under the bust marks a double denomination in the 3rd century. Coins of empresses are a principal source for women's honorific titles (Augusta, Mater castrorum, Diva).
scholarship: Kleiner, 'Women and family life on Roman imperial coinage'
Brubaker and Tobler, 'The gender of money', Gender and History 12 (2000)

coinage.text: When an emperor or member of his family was deified, the mint issued commemoratives with DIVO or DIVVS and the symbols of apotheosis: an eagle (for an emperor) or peacock (for an empress) carrying the soul aloft, a multi-storey funeral pyre (rogus), an altar, a carpentum (ceremonial carriage) drawn by mules or elephants, the deified figure on a flying eagle. Decius' series of c. 250-251 restoring coins of eleven deified emperors (DIVO AVGVSTO to DIVO ALEXANDRO) and Claudius II's DIVO CLAVDIO coins (the most copied coins in Britain) are celebrated groups. The last pagan-style consecration issue is Constantine's (337), already infused with Christian imagery. Consecration coins are a primary source for the imperial cult.
scholarship: Gesche, 'Die Divinisierung der römischen Kaiser in ihrer Funktion als Herrschaftslegitimation'
Price, 'From noble funerals to divine cult', in Cannadine and Price (eds.) Rituals of Royalty (1987)

coinage.text: The successor kingdoms kept the Roman system. The Vandals at Carthage left gold to the emperor but struck silver and bronze with royal names and value marks (N XLII, N XXI, N XII). In Italy Odoacer and the Ostrogoths struck gold in the name of the eastern emperor, adding their own monograms on silver and bronze, and revived large bronze at Rome: 40-nummi pieces with INVICTA ROMA and the she-wolf, or an eagle, deliberately evoking the old sestertius. Theodahad's bronze with his own moustached portrait wearing a closed crown and Baduila (Totila)'s coins with his bust are rare exceptions to the convention of not portraying the king. These coinages are vital evidence for the political relationship with Constantinople.
scholarship: Grierson and Blackburn, Medieval European Coinage I (1986)
Metlich, The Coinage of Ostrogothic Italy (2004)

coinage.standard: first series follis c. 8-9 g (498); doubled to c. 17-18 g in c. 512
coinage.text: Marcellinus Comes records under 498 that Anastasius issued coins 'which the Romans call terunciani and the Greeks follares' and so made an exchange that pleased the people. He replaced the worthless nummus with multiples marked by large Greek numerals: M (40), K (20), I (10) and later Є (5), with the mint and officina below. After a first light series, the coins were doubled in weight around 512. The reform, partly anticipated by the Vandal and Ostrogothic coins of value, created the standard Byzantine bronze system and, by fixing the follis to the solidus, eased small transactions in the cities. Collectors date Anastasian folles to the light or heavy series by size and officina marks. It was part of a broader fiscal programme: the same year Anastasius abolished the hated chrysargyron.
scholarship: Metcalf, The Origins of the Anastasian Currency Reform (1969)

coinage.t: Justinian's dated folles and facing busts (538/9)
coinage.standard: follis increased to c. 22-25 g (538/9), reduced from c. 542
coinage.text: In Justinian's 12th regnal year (538/9) the follis became heavier and changed design: a facing bust of the emperor in helmet and cuirass holding a cross on globe, and on the reverse the value letter M with ANNO and the regnal year (XII, XIII...). Byzantine bronze is therefore dated by year from 538 to the 7th century. These massive folles, the largest Roman bronze since the 3rd-century sestertius, were reduced in weight from c. 542, probably owing to the fiscal shock of the Justinianic plague, and the reduction itself is visible year by year. The solidus also changed to a facing bust in the 530s-540s. Dated folles let collectors follow mint output year by year, a rare quantitative window on the 6th-century state.

From Justinian to the 7th century the Constantinople mint struck small numbers of solidi below the standard of 24 siliquae, marked in the exergue OB XX (20 siliquae), OB*+ (22) or with other signs (23). They are found mostly outside the empire, in Gaul, the Rhineland and Scandinavia, and their purpose is debated: trade with Frankish markets where gold was valued differently, diplomatic payments, or wages. Collectors should not confuse them with clipped coins or with Merovingian imitations.
scholarship: Adelson, Light Weight Solidi and Byzantine Trade in the Sixth and Seventh Centuries (1957)

coinage.text: Tiberius II replaced the Victory, or the angel holding a cross that had stood on the solidus since Justin I, with a cross potent set on four steps, often taken to represent the cross erected on Golgotha. It became the standard Byzantine gold reverse for over a century. Tiberius also restored more classical portraits and was later remembered for his generosity: chroniclers say he distributed vast sums and found treasure in the palace. The cross on steps lets a collector tell his solidi from those of Justin II at a glance.

In 615, with the Persians at Chalcedon, Heraclius introduced a large silver coin of 6 grammata (hence hexagram), with the legend DEVS ADIVTA ROMANIS ('God help the Romans') around a cross on a globe set on steps, and on the obverse the emperor with his son Heraclius Constantine. The Chronicon Paschale records that it was introduced in that year and that imperial salaries were thereafter paid at half their former rate in the new coin. In 622 Heraclius melted church plate to coin (Theophanes AM 6113), feeding the hexagram's production. It was struck in large numbers through the Persian war and into the reign of Constans II, then declined; it is the main Byzantine silver coin of the 7th century and a direct witness to the crisis that nearly destroyed the empire.

The war with Persia (602-628) and the loss of Syria and Egypt reduced the follis to a light, carelessly struck coin, very often overstruck on earlier folles (especially Phocas', whose memory Heraclius condemned) without removing the old design. Antioch closed in 610, Alexandria passed to the Persians (618/19-629), Thessalonica, Nicomedia and Cyzicus closed by c. 630, leaving Constantinople, Carthage, Ravenna, Sicily and Alexandria (after 629) as the working mints. Emergency mints at Seleucia and Isaura (615-618) show the front line. A typical Heraclian follis shows three standing figures (Heraclius, Heraclius Constantine, Heraclonas) with M and ANNO on the reverse; regnal dates continue but are frequently illegible.
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)

coinage.t: Forgeries and how collectors detect them
coinage.text: Ancient coins have been faked since the Renaissance: Paduan 'Paduans' by Giovanni Cavino (16th c.) imitated sestertii and are now collected themselves; Carl Wilhelm Becker (1772-1830) cut hundreds of dies of rarities; 20th-century 'Slavey' and other Bulgarian workshops, Lebanese and Chinese factories produce struck and cast fakes of high quality today. Cast copies show soft details, pitting, a seam on the edge and low weight; transfer-die and struck fakes can be detected by die studies, by comparing with published die pairs (Crawford, RIC and specialist corpora), by fabric and flan shape, and increasingly by metallurgical analysis. Tooling (re-engraving a worn coin) and smoothing are more insidious frauds. Classic fake targets: EID MAR, Social War denarii, Caesar portraits, Judaea Capta sestertii, Otho sestertii (none genuine exist), Pertinax and Didius Julianus aurei, Uranius Antoninus, the Tetrici gold, Magnus Maximus solidi. Provenance and good references are the best defences.
scholarship: Klawans, An Introduction to Ancient and Medieval Counterfeit Coins (1977)

coinage.issuerName: Pompey the Great (and the Pompeian coinages)
coinage.t: Coinage of Pompey and the Pompeians
coinage.text: Pompey never put his own living portrait on a coin. His one personal issue in Rome is a gold aureus (RRC 402) with the head of Africa and MAGNVS, and on the reverse Pompey in a triumphal quadriga, PROCOS, struck for one of his triumphs (71 or 61). In 49 the Pompeian consuls and his proquaestors (Lentulus, Marcellus, Cn. Piso, Varro) struck denarii in the East naming him MAGN PRO COS with Jupiter, Terminus or a dolphin and eagle-tipped sceptre. His portrait appears only posthumously, on the coins of his sons: Gnaeus the younger in Spain (46-45) and Sextus in Sicily (c. 42-36), who showed Magnus as Neptune's favourite with trident and dolphin. The Pompeian African issues of Metellus Scipio and Cato (47-46) belong to the same cause.
keyTypes: posthumous portraits on coins of Sextus
coinage.rarity: Aureus extremely rare; Pompeian denarii of 49 scarce; posthumous portrait denarii of Sextus rare.
coinage.confusions: The Neptune portrait on Sextus' coins is Pompey, not Sextus; Gnaeus the younger's portrait coins are rare and much faked.
coinage.dating: The 49 issues name the consuls of 49 (L. Lentulus, C. Marcellus); Sextus' coins carry PRAEF CLAS ET ORAE MARIT EX S C (from 43).

coinage.text: Caesar's coins tell the story of the civil war. In 49-48 the elephant denarius (CAESAR) was struck in tens of millions from the treasury seized in Rome. Travelling mints followed him: Venus / Aeneas carrying Anchises and the Palladium (Africa, 47-46), recalling his descent from Venus through Iulus; Venus / trophy with seated Gallic captives (Spain, 46-45). For his quadruple triumph of 46 the praetor A. Hirtius struck the largest Republican gold issue (veiled female head / lituus, jug and axe, C CAESAR COS TER), the most common Republican aureus. In 44 his living portrait appeared on the denarii of the Rome moneyers, a decisive break with Republican custom. After his death Octavian and the triumvirs placed DIVOS IVLIVS and the comet (sidus Iulium) on their coins.
coinage.rarity: Elephant and Aeneas denarii common; Gallic trophy scarce; portrait denarii scarce to rare and very expensive in good style; Hirtius aureus the most available gold of the period.
coinage.confusions: Posthumous portraits on Octavian's and Antony's coins (with DIVI IVLI or the star) are not lifetime issues; ancient plated copies of the elephant denarius are common.
coinage.dating: Portrait denarii are sequenced by Caesar's titles (DICT QVART January-February 44, DICT PERPETVO from mid-February 44) and moneyers' names.

coinage.text: After leaving Italy in 44 Brutus took over the Balkans and Asia and struck gold and silver with military mints that moved with him and his legates (Costa, Casca, Plaetorius Cestianus, Servilius). Types: Libertas, Apollo, a trophy, Victory breaking a diadem (Casca), the consul Brutus between lictors, and finally his own bare portrait on the EID MAR denarius and on aurei. The gold staters inscribed KOΣΩN, showing a Roman consul between lictors and an eagle, with a BR monogram on some, are linked with Brutus' dealings with a Thracian or Dacian king (Koson) and are found in quantity in Transylvania; they are also heavily faked. The issue sequence reflects the frantic fund-raising before Philippi.
coinage.rarity: All Brutus imperatorial denarii are scarce; portrait coins very rare; KOΣΩN staters not rare, but many on the market are modern.
coinage.confusions: Do not confuse with his moneyer issue of 54 (Brutus/Ahala, Libertas) or with coins of Decimus Brutus.
coinage.dating: Struck 43-42, ending at Philippi (October-November 42).

coinage.text: Cassius' coins come from his campaigns in Asia and Syria in 43-42, when he extorted huge sums from the province and sacked Rhodes. Types include Libertas veiled and diademed / jug and lituus (Cassius was augur), a tripod with the head of Apollo, and, after the fall of Rhodes, a crab holding an aplustre with a rose, the Rhodian emblem, and a diademed head of Rhodes' god Helios. His legate P. Lentulus Spinther struck alongside him. Unlike Brutus, Cassius never put his own portrait on his coins.
coinage.rarity: Scarce to rare; aurei very rare.
coinage.confusions: Earlier moneyer coins of the Cassii (Q. Cassius, L. Cassius Longinus) are different people; Lentulus Spinther's coins name him, not Cassius, on the obverse.
coinage.dating: 43-42, ended by his suicide at the first battle of Philippi.

legends: M ANT IMP AVG III VIR R P C
ANT AVG III VIR R P C
coinage.text: Antony's coinage is the most varied of the triumviral period. Portrait coins with Caesar (43) and with Octavian (41-40) proclaim the triumvirate; cistophori of 39 show Antony with ivy wreath as the New Dionysus and Octavia on a cista. The 'fleet coinage' of his admirals (c. 38-37) introduced bronze denominations with value marks that anticipate Augustus' system. The famous denarius of 32 pairs Antony (ANTONI ARMENIA DEVICTA) with Cleopatra (CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM), the only Roman denarius showing a foreign queen. Finally the vast legionary denarii of 32-31 paid his army before Actium and circulated for two centuries.
coinage.rarity: Legionary denarii common (rare legions excepted); Cleopatra denarius scarce and in demand; portrait aurei rare.
coinage.confusions: Legionary denarii restored by Marcus and Verus (LEG VI) carry their names; heavily worn legionary denarii in 2nd-century hoards are originals, not restorations.
coinage.dating: Titles: IMP, IMP III, COS DESIG ITER ET TERT; III VIR R P C (from 43); AVG (augur).

legends: LEPIDVS PONT MAX III V R P C
coinage.text: As moneyer in 61 Lepidus advertised his ancestor of the same name as guardian of Ptolemy V (TVTOR REG) and the equestrian statue of another ancestor. As triumvir (43-36) he shared portrait denarii and aurei with Antony and Octavian, often styled PONT MAX after he succeeded Caesar as pontifex maximus. His share of the triumviral coinage is smaller than his colleagues', mirroring his political weight, and his coins stop with his removal by Octavian in 36.
coinage.rarity: Triumviral portrait denarii rare; aurei very rare.
coinage.confusions: Other Aemilii Lepidi struck moneyer coins (the Basilica Aemilia type is by another Lepidus).
coinage.dating: III V R P C coins 43-36.

legends: PRAEF CLAS ET ORAE MARIT EX S C
coinage.text: Sextus struck first in Spain (45-44) with Pietas types honouring his father and brother, then in Sicily as commander of the fleet and coasts, a title voted by the Senate in 43. His Sicilian coinage celebrates Neptune and his naval victories over Octavian: the head of Pompey with trident and dolphin, Neptune with foot on a prow, the Pharos of Messina with Scylla, the Catanaean brothers carrying their parents, and a naval trophy. Aurei carry portraits of Sextus with those of his father and brother. The coins are a rare document of the 'sea-king' who starved Rome until Naulochus (36).
coinage.rarity: Rare; aurei very rare.
coinage.confusions: The bearded portrait is Pompey Magnus; Sextus himself appears on gold.
coinage.dating: MAG PIVS IMP ITER and the naval titles date issues to 42-36.

coinage.text: In Egypt Cleopatra struck debased silver tetradrachms in the Ptolemaic tradition and large bronzes marked Π (80) and M (40) drachmai, with a portrait showing a strong hooked nose and melon coiffure that is very different from Hollywood. In the East (Ascalon, Chalcis, Damascus, Orthosia) and in the territories Antony granted her, coins show her with Antony. The Roman denarius of 32 with Antony on the other side is the best known. Her portraits are the main evidence for her real appearance and are much studied.
coinage.rarity: Bronzes scarce; tetradrachms rare; denarius scarce.
coinage.confusions: Many 'Cleopatra' coins sold are of earlier Ptolemaic queens or are modern fakes.
coinage.dating: Regnal years (L + numeral) on Egyptian issues.

coinage.text: Son of Caesar's lieutenant turned enemy, Labienus fled to Parthia after Philippi and led a Parthian army into Syria and Asia in 40. His coins show his own bare head and, on the reverse, a saddled Parthian horse with bow case and quiver. The title Parthicus was ironic by Roman convention: it normally meant 'conqueror of the Parthians', but Labienus took it as their ally. Ventidius Bassus defeated and killed him in 39. Extremely rare.
coinage.rarity: Very rare; aurei unique or nearly so.
coinage.confusions: None among genuine coins, but fakes exist.

legends: CAESAR AVGVSTVS DIVI F PATER PATRIAE
coinage.text: Octavian's coinage before 27 is propaganda for a civil war: CAESAR DIVI F with Venus, Pax, Victory on a globe, Octavian as Neptune, the Actian Apollo, AEGYPTO CAPTA with a crocodile, IMP CAESAR with the Curia Julia. After 27 his coins proclaim the new order: the civic oak wreath (OB CIVIS SERVATOS), the clipeus virtutis, SIGNIS RECEPTIS with Parthian standards (20-19), the comet of Divus Iulius, his Capricorn birth sign, Mars Ultor. The moneyers' aes of Rome and the Altar of Lugdunum series made bronze common again. The commonest type of all, the denarius with Gaius and Lucius Caesares as principes iuventutis (2 BC-AD 4), was struck at Lugdunum in millions. His portrait stays youthful for 45 years.
coinage.rarity: Gaius-Lucius denarii and Altar asses common; pre-27 and Spanish denarii scarce; most aurei rare.
coinage.confusions: Posthumous DIVVS AVGVSTVS PATER coins of Tiberius (radiate head, altar, eagle, thunderbolt) are very common and not lifetime pieces; colonial bronzes with his portrait are provincial, not imperial.
coinage.dating: IMP numerals (IMP X etc.), TR POT, COS numerals, and PATER PATRIAE (from 2 BC) date issues; moneyers' names date the Rome aes (c. 19-4 BC).

legends: TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS
coinage.text: Tiberius' gold and silver were struck almost entirely at Lugdunum and dominated by one type, the seated female figure with PONTIF MAXIM, the 'tribute penny'. The bronze from Rome is more varied: the CIVITATIBVS ASIAE RESTITVTIS sestertius (Tiberius seated) for his relief of the Asian cities after the earthquake of 17, the shields of CLEMENTIAE and MODERATIONI (c. 16-22), Livia as SALVS AVGVSTA, IVSTITIA and PIETAS on dupondii (22-23), the asses of his son Drusus, and the enormous series of DIVVS AVGVSTVS PATER asses with an altar (PROVIDENT) and other types honouring his adoptive father. His portrait is idealised and changes little.
keyTypes: PROVIDENT altar as of Divus Augustus
coinage.rarity: Denarii common; aurei available; Asian cities sestertius scarce.
coinage.confusions: Coins of Tiberius as Caesar under Augustus (TI CAESAR AVG F TR POT XV, 13-14) carry Augustus on the obverse; the Divus Augustus asses are frequently attributed to Caligula or Claudius by beginners.
coinage.dating: Aes dated by TR POT numbers (TR POT XXIIII = 22/23 etc.); denarii undated.

legends: C CAESAR AVG GERM P M TR POT
coinage.text: A short reign with a dynastic coinage. Gaius honoured his murdered family: aurei and denarii for his mother Agrippina the Elder and father Germanicus, a sestertius with MEMORIAE AGRIPPINAE and a carpentum, asses of Germanicus. The sestertius of the three sisters (Agrippina, Drusilla and Julia as Securitas, Concordia and Fortuna) is a unique honour for living women. ADLOCVT COH shows him addressing the praetorians; quadrantes marked RCC record the remission of the half-percent sales tax (37-38). After his murder his bronze was recalled and melted by senatorial decree (Dio), and many surviving coins had his name erased or countermarked. Gold and silver moved from Lugdunum to Rome during his reign.
coinage.rarity: Vesta as and quadrantes common; denarii rare; three sisters sestertius scarce and heavily tooled or faked.
coinage.confusions: Germanicus asses were struck by Gaius (and later Claudius), not Germanicus; C CAESAR on quadrantes of Augustus' grandsons is different.
coinage.dating: TR POT and COS numerals (COS II 39, COS III 40, COS IIII 41).

legends: TI CLAVD CAESAR AVG P M TR P
NERO CLAVD CAES DRVSVS GERM PRINC IVVENT
coinage.text: Claudius' gold and silver open with the frankest admission of how he came to power: the praetorian camp (IMPER RECEPT) and a soldier clasping hands with him (PRAETOR RECEPT), donative coins for the guard who made him emperor. DE BRITANN and a triumphal arch celebrate the conquest of 43. Later coins honour Agrippina the Younger and her son Nero as heir. The bronze includes the very common Minerva and Constantia asses, the SPES AVGVSTA sestertius and the dupondius of his mother Antonia. In Britain Claudian asses were copied on a vast scale (the 'Claudian copies') to supply the army and new province before 64.
coinage.rarity: Minerva asses common; denarii scarce; aurei moderately available; DE BRITANN gold rare.
coinage.confusions: Claudian copies are lighter and cruder; coins of Nero Claudius Drusus (Claudius' father) and Antonia were struck by Claudius; PRAETOR RECEPT is not a coin of the praetorians.
coinage.dating: TR P numbers (I-XIV), IMP numerals, P P from 42.

legends: NERO CLAVD DIVI F CAES AVG GERM IMP TR P
PACE P R TERRA MARIQ PARTA IANVM CLVSIT
coinage.text: Early coins (54-60) show the young Nero with his mother Agrippina face to face (54) and jugate (55), and reverses with EX S C in an oak wreath, signalling deference to the Senate. After 64 the reformed coinage shows a heavy, jowly emperor with stepped hair (coma in gradus) and later a neck beard. Gold and silver types are few (IVPPITER CVSTOS, SALVS, ROMA, VESTA, AVGVSTVS AVGVSTA), but the bronze is the finest of the 1st century: the harbour of Ostia, the closed Temple of Janus, the Macellum, the Congiarium, Nero as Apollo Citharoedus, and Decursio horseman types. Lugdunum aes is marked by a globe at the bust point.
coinage.rarity: Post-64 denarii common; aurei available; Agrippina gold rare; port sestertius scarce and expensive.
coinage.confusions: Pre-64 aurei and denarii are heavier and finer; Nero as Caesar under Claudius appears with Claudius' legends; Alexandrian tetradrachms of Nero are billon and very common.
coinage.dating: Early coins dated by TR P; post-64 by legend forms and portrait (beard from 64).

coinage.text: The legate of Africa revolted against Nero in 68, raised a new legion (I Macriana Liberatrix) and blocked the grain supply to Rome before Galba had him killed. His denarii, struck at an African mint (probably Carthage), avoid the imperial title: they show his bare head or Africa / Libertas, with legionary eagles and his title propraetor, and celebrate LEG III AVG LIB. They are a good example of a Republican-style coinage in the civil war of 68.
coinage.rarity: Very rare; prime targets for forgers.
coinage.confusions: Civil war 'autonomous' issues share types but lack his name.
coinage.dating: Spring-autumn 68.

legends: SER GALBA IMP CAESAR AVG TR P
IMP SER SVLP GALBA CAES AVG
coinage.text: Galba struck first in Spain as legatus of the Senate and People and then as emperor, before entering Rome in the autumn of 68. Spanish issues include HISPANIA, CONCORDIA PROVINCIARVM and a bust of Galba on horseback. At Rome his denarii and aurei carry SPQR OB C S (for saving citizens) in an oak wreath and LIBERTAS PVBLICA; his sestertii are large, carefully engraved, showing a bald old man with a hooked nose. The portrait changes from a heavier Spanish style to a gaunt, realistic Roman one.
coinage.rarity: Denarii scarce; sestertii scarce; aurei rare.
coinage.confusions: Civil war anonymous issues of 68-69; posthumous restorations under Titus (rare).
coinage.dating: 68-69; mint by style and legend forms.

legends: IMP M OTHO CAESAR AVG TR P
IMP OTHO CAESAR AVG TR P
coinage.text: Otho reigned three months (January-April 69) and the Rome mint struck only gold and silver for him; no sestertii, dupondii or asses. His portrait shows the heavy stepped wig mentioned by Suetonius. The handful of reverse types (Securitas, Pax, Aequitas, Ceres, Victory) were struck in quantity, so his denarii are scarce rather than rare. Antioch struck bronze and Alexandria tetradrachms for him.
coinage.rarity: Denarii scarce; aurei rare; any 'Otho sestertius' is a Paduan or forgery.
coinage.confusions: Legend variants with and without M (Marcus); provincial Otho bronzes are not imperial aes.
coinage.dating: January-April 69.

legends: A VITELLIVS GERMANICVS IMP AVG P M TR P
A VITELLIVS GERMAN IMP TR P
coinage.text: Vitellius, proclaimed by the Rhine legions, struck first in Spain and Gaul and then at Rome (summer to December 69). His denarii show a heavy-jowled portrait and types honouring his family: his children (LIBERIS IMP GERMANICI), his father Lucius Vitellius, three times consul and censor under Claudius, and his own priesthood as a quindecimvir (tripod with dolphin and raven). His sestertii are rare. He rejected the name Caesar at first, hence legends with GERMANICVS only.
coinage.rarity: Denarii scarce; aes rare; aurei rare.
coinage.confusions: Early coins lack CAESAR; Spanish and Gallic styles differ markedly from Rome.
coinage.dating: April-December 69.

coinage.text: Vespasian's huge coinage rebuilt a treasury emptied by civil war. Its realism shows a square-headed, furrowed old soldier. Key themes: the Jewish victory (IVDAEA CAPTA, Judaea seated under a palm), ROMA RESVRGES (the emperor raising Roma), Pax and the dedication of the Temple of Peace (75), the cow of Myron's famous statue, the Capitol restored after 69, and the presentation of Titus and Domitian as heirs (Caesars on horseback). Many types copy Augustan and Republican originals deliberately, aligning the new dynasty with Augustus. His eastern denarii of 69-71 struck at Ephesus carry an EPHE monogram.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; aurei available; Judaea Capta sestertii scarce and expensive.
coinage.confusions: Coins naming Titus and Domitian as Caesars struck under Vespasian; posthumous DIVVS AVGVSTVS VESPASIANVS coins of Titus (EX SC on shield, quadriga) are not lifetime issues.
coinage.dating: COS numerals (COS II 70 to COS VIIII 79) and TR POT on many coins.

legends: IMP TITVS CAES VESPASIAN AVG P M
TR P VIIII IMP XV COS VIII P P
coinage.text: As Caesar under his father Titus struck in his own name at Rome and Lugdunum; as Augustus (June 79-September 81) his types include the elephant, the pulvinaria (draped chairs with wreaths or thunderbolts, for the gods) issued for the inauguration of the Colosseum in 80, Divus Vespasian, Julia Titi, the famous Colosseum sestertius without obverse portrait, and a series of restored coins of earlier emperors. His portrait is a softer, rounder version of his father's.
coinage.rarity: Denarii fairly common; Colosseum sestertius very rare and much forged; Julia Titi scarce.
coinage.confusions: Titus as Caesar (69-79) vs Augustus (79-81) is told by legend (CAESAR vs IMP ... AVG); his coins honouring Vespasian are posthumous.
coinage.dating: TR P VIII-XI and IMP XIIII-XVII; COS VII (79), COS VIII (80-81).

legends: IMP CAES DOMITIANVS AVG GERM P M TR P
IMP CAES DOMIT AVG GERM COS XVI CENS PER P P
coinage.text: Domitian's coinage is large, carefully engraved and highly regular. His denarii from 85 onward repeat four Minerva types (standing with spear, fighting on a galley prow, standing with thunderbolt, fighting) year after year, with his titles, which makes them a perfect series for dating. GERMANIA CAPTA (84-85) celebrates the Chattan war; a magnificent series for the Secular Games of 88 shows the herald, sacrifices and the distribution of purification materials. His wife Domitia and their deified infant son (DIVVS CAESAR, a baby seated on a globe surrounded by seven stars) appear on rare gold and silver. He raised the silver standard in 82 before cutting it again.
coinage.rarity: Minerva denarii very common; Secular Games coins scarce; Domitia rare; Divus Caesar very rare.
coinage.confusions: Domitian Caesar coins under Vespasian and Titus; coins of 82-85 have higher silver; post-damnatio defacements occur.
coinage.dating: TR P (I-XVI) with IMP numbers and COS (VIII to XVII); CENS PER (perpetual censor) from late 85.

legends: IMP NERVA CAES AVG P M TR P COS II P P
coinage.text: A short reign with an unusually 'programmatic' bronze coinage: the abolition of false accusations under the Jewish tax (palm tree), a grain distribution to the urban plebs (modius), the remission of the costs of the state post in Italy (two mules grazing), and LIBERTAS PVBLICA. CONCORDIA EXERCITVVM (clasped hands over a legionary eagle) tries to secure the armies after Domitian's murder. Nerva also restored coins of Augustus. His long-nosed, thin-necked portrait is distinctive.
coinage.rarity: Denarii fairly common; FISCI IVDAICI sestertius scarce.
coinage.confusions: Posthumous DIVVS NERVA coins of Trajan; restored issues.
coinage.dating: COS II (96), COS III (97), COS IIII (98).

legends: IMP CAES NERVA TRAIAN AVG GERM
IMP TRAIANO AVG GER DAC P M TR P COS V P P
IMP CAES NER TRAIANO OPTIMO AVG GER DAC PARTHICO
coinage.text: Trajan's coinage is an atlas of his building and conquest. Dacia captive under a trophy, the Danube bridge, the Column (struck c. 112-114), the Forum and Basilica Ulpia, the Circus Maximus, the Via Traiana, the harbour at Portus, Arabia acquired with a camel, the crowning of Parthamaspates (REX PARTHIS DATVS) and PARTHIA CAPTA. The ALIM ITAL type records the alimenta, the child-welfare scheme for Italy. The reverse formula SPQR OPTIMO PRINCIPI runs from 103. Trajan also issued the restored Republican and imperial coins of c. 107 and recalled worn coinage. Coins of Plotina, Marciana and Matidia, and of Trajan's father (DIVVS PATER TRAIAN), round out the dynasty.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; architectural sestertii scarce to rare; Plotina and Marciana rare.
coinage.confusions: Restored issues (REST); coins of Divus Traianus Pater; 'OPTIMO' in the obverse from 114 and PARTHICO from 116 distinguish late coins.
coinage.dating: GERM (98), DAC (from late 102), COS V (103-111), COS VI (112-117), OPTIMO in titulature (114), PARTHICO (116).

legends: HADRIANVS AVG COS III P P
coinage.text: The first bearded emperor, Hadrian set a fashion for two centuries. His coinage reflects his travels: the 'travel series' of c. 134-138 shows each province in three ways, ADVENTVS (his arrival), RESTITVTORI (the emperor raising the kneeling province) and EXERCITVS (addressing the army), and the 'province series' presents personifications with their attributes (Aegyptos with an ibis, Africa wearing an elephant scalp, Hispania with a rabbit, Britannia seated). Others celebrate the founding of Rome (ROMVLO CONDITORI), the temple of Venus and Roma, the Tiber, Nilus reclining. His wife Sabina and his first heir Aelius Caesar are well represented.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; travel series sestertii scarce; Aelius Caesar denarii scarce.
coinage.confusions: Early coins (117-123) still use Trajanic legends with PARTH and COS; the absence of TR P numbers after 119 makes dating depend on legend forms; cistophori are provincial silver.
coinage.dating: Long Trajanic legends (117-123), HADRIANVS AVGVSTVS (c. 125-128), HADRIANVS AVG COS III P P (128-138, after he accepted P P).

legends: ANTONINVS AVG PIVS P P TR P COS III
IMP T AEL CAES HADR ANTONINVS AVG PIVS
coinage.text: Pius' long and peaceful reign produced abundant, conservative coins. Highlights: the posthumous coinage of his wife Diva Faustina (from 141), one of the largest series for any empress, with AETERNITAS and her temple in the Forum; the Britannia types of 143-144 for the Antonine Wall campaign and the crude BRITANNIA asses of 154-155, found mainly in Britain and perhaps struck for it; the legendary history of Rome for the 900th anniversary (147-148), with Aeneas carrying Anchises, the sow of Lavinium and the wolf; and client kings installed in Armenia and among the Quadi. Alexandria's zodiac drachms of year 8 (144/5) are a celebrated provincial series.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; Diva Faustina common; REX types scarce.
coinage.confusions: Marcus as Caesar shares the reign; posthumous DIVVS ANTONINVS coins (pyre, column of Antoninus) were struck by Marcus and Lucius.
coinage.dating: COS II (139), COS III (140-144), COS IIII (145-161); TR POT numbers on many.

legends: AVRELIVS CAESAR AVG PII F (as Caesar)
IMP CAES M AVREL ANTONINVS AVG
M ANTONINVS AVG ARM PARTH MAX
coinage.text: Marcus appears from 139 as a beardless Caesar and ages visibly on the coins into a heavily bearded philosopher-emperor. His joint reign with Lucius Verus (161-169) has concordia types; the Parthian war adds ARMENIACVS and PARTHICVS MAXIMVS; the Marcomannic wars (from 167) produce DE GERMANIS (172), DE SARMATIS (175), GERMANIA SVBACTA and trophies with captives. His wife Faustina the Younger has a large coinage whose hairstyles evolve and date issues; Commodus appears as Caesar (166) and co-Augustus (177). Marcus' denarii show the slow fall in fineness during the wars and plague.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; aurei available; Marcomannic sestertii common.
coinage.confusions: Marcus vs Lucius: Lucius' beard is fuller and curlier and his legends read L VERVS; Marcus as Caesar coins date from 139-161.
coinage.dating: TR P XV (161) to TR P XXXIIII (180), with IMP numbers and titles ARM (164), PARTH MAX (166), GERM (172), SARM (175).

legends: L VERVS AVG ARM PARTH MAX
coinage.text: Co-emperor with Marcus, Lucius led (nominally) the Parthian war of 162-166. His coins celebrate the installation of Sohaemus as king of Armenia (REX ARMENIIS DATVS, Lucius seated on a platform), Armenia mourning, Parthian captives, and victory titles. His portrait has thick curly hair, a full beard and bulging eyes. His wife Lucilla, daughter of Marcus, has a substantial coinage. Divus Verus consecration coins followed his death in 169.
coinage.rarity: Denarii common but less so than Marcus; REX ARMENIIS sestertius scarce.
coinage.confusions: Distinguished from Marcus by legend (L VERVS) and portrait style.
coinage.dating: TR P I-IX (161-169) and titles ARMENIACVS (164), PARTH MAX (165-166), MEDICVS (166).

legends: M COMM ANT P FEL AVG BRIT
L AEL AVREL COMM AVG P FEL
coinage.text: As Caesar (166) and co-emperor (177) Commodus shares his father's coinage; alone (180-192) he moves steadily from conventional types to a personal cult. VICT BRIT (184-185) records Ulpius Marcellus' war in Britain. From 190-191 he renamed himself Lucius Aelius Aurelius Commodus and appears in the lion-skin of Hercules, with HERCVLI ROMANO AVG and the club, and as founder of a new Rome (COL L AN COM, Colonia Lucia Annia Commodiana). Commodus' medallions are among the finest of the century. His wife Crispina has coins until her exile.
coinage.rarity: Denarii common; Hercules portrait coins scarce; medallions rare.
coinage.confusions: Early coins of 'L AVREL COMMODVS' as Caesar and with Marcus; changing names (M COMMODVS, then L AEL AVREL COMM) date issues.
coinage.dating: TR P numbers to XVIII (192), IMP up to VIII, COS up to VII; titles PIVS (183), BRIT (184), FELIX (185).

legends: IMP CAES P HELV PERTIN AVG
OPI DIVIN TR P COS II
coinage.text: Emperor for 87 days (January-March 193), Pertinax tried to restore discipline and finances after Commodus. His coins are restrained: Providentia raising her hand to a large star (PROVIDENTIAE DEORVM), Laetitia, Ops, Aequitas and Liberalitas. He raised the silver of the denarius slightly. Severus later honoured him with consecration coins (DIVVS PERT PIVS PATER) and took his name. His portrait shows a full-bearded elderly man.
coinage.rarity: Denarii rare; sestertii rare; aurei very rare; heavily faked.
coinage.confusions: Severus' consecration issues for Pertinax are posthumous; Alexandrian tetradrachms are provincial.
coinage.dating: January-March 193.

legends: IMP CAES M DID IVLIAN AVG
coinage.text: Julianus bought the empire from the praetorians at auction in March 193 and was killed 66 days later. His coins emphasise his claims: CONCORD MILIT (Concordia with standards), RECTOR ORBIS (the emperor holding a globe), Fortuna. His wife Manlia Scantilla and daughter Didia Clara received the title Augusta and rare coins of their own. The short reign makes his coins rare and sought after.
coinage.rarity: Denarii rare; sestertii rare; Didia Clara and Scantilla very rare; frequent forgeries.
coinage.confusions: Fakes and tooled sestertii are common; check style against genuine dies.
coinage.dating: March-June 193.

legends: IMP CAES C PESC NIGER IVST AVG
coinage.text: Proclaimed by the Syrian legions in 193, Niger struck denarii at eastern mints (Antioch and Caesarea, possibly others) until his defeat at Issus (194). The engraving is provincial, with spelling errors and unusual types (BONI EVENTVS with odd spelling, a trophy, Sol), and his title IVSTVS ('the Just') appears in the legend. All his coins are rare, and forgeries are abundant; an authentic piece should show the irregular eastern style and slightly crude lettering.
coinage.rarity: Rare; aurei extremely rare.
coinage.confusions: Many fakes; also confusions with early Severan eastern denarii of similar crude style.
coinage.dating: April 193 to spring 194.

legends: D CLOD SEPT ALBIN CAES (Caesar, Rome)
IMP CAES D CLO SEP ALB AVG (Augustus, Lugdunum)
coinage.text: Governor of Britain, Albinus was made Caesar by Severus in 193 to keep him quiet, and the Rome mint struck coins for him with the name Septimius. In 195 he declared himself Augustus and struck at Lugdunum: GEN LVG (the genius of Lugdunum), FIDES LEGION, and types of Minerva and Felicitas. Severus defeated him near Lyon in February 197. His portrait shows a tight curly-haired man with short beard.
coinage.rarity: Caesar denarii scarce; Augustus (Lugdunum) denarii rare.
coinage.confusions: Distinguish Caesar issues (CAES, Rome) from Augustus issues (AVG, Lugdunum style).
coinage.dating: Caesar 193-195; Augustus 195-197.

legends: IMP CAE L SEP SEV PERT AVG
L SEPT SEV PERT AVG IMP XI
coinage.text: Severus' coinage is huge and dynastic. In 193 he struck legionary denarii naming the Danubian and Rhine legions that made him emperor (LEG XIIII GEM M V and others), a deliberate echo of Antony. Eastern mints (Emesa early, Laodicea 196-202) produced characteristic styles. Later types honour Africa and Carthage (Dea Caelestis riding a lion, INDVLGENTIA AVGG IN CARTH, 203-204), the Secular Games of 204, and the British campaign (VICTORIAE BRIT, 208-211). Julia Domna, Caracalla and Geta appear constantly. His portrait develops from the 'Pertinax' beard to a Serapis type with forked beard and corkscrew curls around 200. He debased the denarius to about 50% silver.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; legionary denarii common to scarce; VICTORIAE BRIT sestertii scarce.
coinage.confusions: Eastern denarii with crude lettering are genuine Severan issues, not necessarily fakes; separate Rome, Emesa and Laodicea by style; Divus Severus (DIVO SEVERO PIO) is posthumous.
coinage.dating: PERT in titulature (193-c. 200), IMP numerals to XII, COS II (194-201), COS III (202-211); PIVS from c. 201, BRIT from 210.

legends: P M TR P XVIII COS IIII P P
coinage.text: Caracalla's coins follow him from a pudgy boy Caesar (196) to a scowling bearded soldier-emperor with brows knitted in imitation of Alexander. His titles track his campaigns: BRIT (210), GERM (213). In 215 he introduced the antoninianus with a radiate crown, and he cut the aureus to 1/50 lb. Types include Serapis, Sol, Aesculapius (whose shrines he visited for his health), the Circus Maximus, and Rome-mint largesse coins. His wife Plautilla (202-205) has a coinage cut off by her fall. Massive eastern billon tetradrachms (Antioch, Tyre and others) bear his portrait.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; antoniniani common; aurei available.
coinage.confusions: Caracalla and Elagabalus both use ANTONINVS PIVS FEL AVG and COS IIII: check TR P numbers (Caracalla XVI-XX in 213-217; Elagabalus II-V) and the portrait (Elagabalus younger, sometimes with the 'horn').
coinage.dating: TR P numbers (I-XX), COS (II 205, III 208, IIII 213), BRIT 210, GERM 213; antoniniani only from 215.

legends: P SEPTIMIVS GETA PIVS AVG BRIT
coinage.text: Caesar from 198, Augustus from 209, Geta was murdered by Caracalla in December 211. Coins show a chubby boy and then a young bearded man, often with PRINC IVVENT and Castor types. After his death Caracalla imposed a damnatio memoriae: Geta's name was erased from inscriptions and provincial coins were countermarked or defaced, and many of his supporters (Dio says 20,000 people) were killed. His Augustus coins (209-211) are much rarer than his Caesar issues.
coinage.rarity: Caesar denarii common; Augustus denarii scarce.
coinage.confusions: Early Caracalla Caesar coins look similar; check names (Geta's praenomen changes from L to P around 205).
coinage.dating: Caesar 198-209 (CAES), Augustus 209-211 (AVG, BRIT from 210).

legends: IMP C M OPEL SEV MACRINVS AVG
PONTIF MAX TR P COS P P
coinage.text: The praetorian prefect who arranged Caracalla's murder became the first equestrian emperor (April 217-June 218). His son Diadumenian was Caesar and briefly Augustus. Macrinus' portraits come in two styles: a short beard at first and a long, philosophical beard later, the latter possibly evoking Marcus Aurelius. Types stress the soldiers' loyalty (FIDES MILITVM) and Jupiter as guardian. Both struck antoniniani as well as denarii, and they appear together on facing-bust provincial bronzes at Marcianopolis.
coinage.rarity: Macrinus denarii scarce; Diadumenian scarce to rare; antoniniani of both rare.
coinage.confusions: Diadumenian as Caesar vs Augustus (rare); provincial joint issues are common in the Balkans.

legends: IMP CAES M AVR ANTONINVS AVG
coinage.text: The teenage priest of the Emesene sun god brought his god to Rome. Coins show the sacred conical stone of Elagabal on a quadriga, the emperor in Syrian priestly dress sacrificing (INVICTVS SACERDOS AVG), and a curious 'horn' projecting from the front of the laurel wreath on some portraits, interpreted variously as a bull's horn connected with his priesthood or a cult object. Rapid marriages are recorded by coins of Julia Paula, the Vestal Aquilia Severa and Annia Faustina; his grandmother Julia Maesa and mother Julia Soaemias also issue coins. He abandoned the antoninianus c. 219.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; antoniniani scarce; Aquilia Severa and Annia Faustina rare.
coinage.confusions: Confused with Caracalla by legend; the young, thinly bearded portrait and TR P II-V identify Elagabalus.
coinage.dating: TR P I-V (218-222), COS II (219), COS III (220), COS IIII (222).

legends: IMP C M AVR SEV ALEXAND AVG
P M TR P COS P P
coinage.text: Alexander struck no antoniniani: the denarius was again the only silver coin, and his denarii survive in very large numbers. Types are conventional but include the restored Colosseum (223) and the Nymphaeum Alexandri on the Esquiline, the Persian war (VIRTVS AVG, Alexander crowned by Victory, 231-233), and his mother Julia Mamaea, who dominated the regime, as well as his wife Orbiana, sent away by Mamaea. The portrait matures from a beardless boy to a lightly bearded young man.
coinage.rarity: Denarii very common; Orbiana scarce; Colosseum sestertius rare.
coinage.confusions: None serious; Alexandrian tetradrachms are provincial billon.
coinage.dating: P M TR P numbers (I-XIV) annually; COS II (226), COS III (229); legend changes to IMP ALEXANDER PIVS AVG c. 228.

coinage.issuerName: Maximinus I Thrax (with Maximus Caesar and Diva Paulina)
coinage.text: The first soldier-emperor never visited Rome, but its mint struck abundant denarii and sestertii for him. His first portraits borrow Severus Alexander's features; within a year the mint adopted a realistic image of his massive jaw and heavy brow, which matches the sources' description of a giant. VICTORIA GERM and GERMANICVS celebrate his campaign of 235-236 beyond the Rhine. His son Maximus appears as Caesar (PRINC IVVENTVTIS, PIETAS AVG with priestly implements); his dead wife Paulina receives consecration coins (peacock carrying her to heaven). He struck no antoniniani.
coinage.rarity: Denarii common; Maximus scarce; Paulina rare.
coinage.confusions: Early 'idealised' portraits can be mistaken for Severus Alexander; legends settle it.
coinage.dating: P M TR P I-IIII; GERM from late 236; COS (236).

legends: IMP M ANT GORDIANVS AFR AVG
P M TR P COS P P
coinage.text: The elderly proconsul of Africa, proclaimed at Thysdrus in March 238 and recognised by the Senate, reigned about three weeks before his son fell in battle at Carthage and he hanged himself. The Rome mint struck denarii and sestertii for him and his son with the cognomen AFR (Africanus). His portrait shows a long, lined face with a receding hairline and short beard.
coinage.rarity: Rare; sestertii rare; intensely forged.
coinage.confusions: Gordian II has a younger, fuller face; both read GORDIANVS AFR AVG. Judge by portrait and published dies.
coinage.dating: March-April 238.

legends: IMP M ANT GORDIANVS AFR AVG
coinage.text: Co-emperor with his father in 238, killed fighting Capelianus, governor of Numidia, outside Carthage. His coins share types with his father's but show a younger man with a stockier face and slightly fuller hair. The two Gordians are one of the classic attribution problems of Roman coinage.
coinage.rarity: Rare to very rare; forged.
coinage.confusions: Gordian I (older portrait); posthumous DIVO GORDIANO issues are uncertain.
coinage.dating: March-April 238.

legends: IMP C M CLOD PVPIENVS AVG
coinage.text: The Senate's two emperors of 238 (April-July), Pupienus and Balbinus, revived the antoninianus, with reverses of clasped hands proclaiming their mutual love and loyalty (which did not last: the praetorians killed both). Pupienus is shown as a long-bearded, severe old soldier. PATRES SENATVS emphasises their senatorial legitimacy. Gordian III appears as Caesar on rare coins of the same months.
coinage.rarity: Denarii and antoniniani scarce; sestertii scarce; aurei very rare.
coinage.confusions: Balbinus has a rounder face and shorter beard; legends identify.
coinage.dating: April-July 238.

legends: IMP C D CAEL BALBINVS AVG
coinage.text: Pupienus' colleague, a wealthy aristocrat with a reputation for luxury, is shown round-faced with a short beard. His antoniniani with clasped hands mirror Pupienus'. The coins of the 98-day joint reign are a compact and attractive collecting group, with the revived antoninianus as its key innovation.
coinage.rarity: Scarce.
coinage.confusions: Pupienus (long beard).
coinage.dating: April-July 238.

legends: IMP CAES M ANT GORDIANVS AVG
P M TR P II COS P P
coinage.text: The boy emperor's coins are among the most abundant of the 3rd century. The antoninianus became the principal silver coin and the denarius was struck only until c. 241. Early portraits are childlike, later ones show a plump youth. Types include Sol (AETERNITATI AVG), Laetitia, Virtus and the annual P M TR P series, and, for the Persian expedition of 242-244, PROFECTIO AVG and MARS PROPVG. Antioch's antoniniani of this reign have a distinctive style. His wife Tranquillina (241) has scarce coins. Provincial bronzes with Gordian facing Tranquillina or Serapis are common in the Balkans.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani very common; denarii common; Tranquillina scarce to rare; medallions rare.
coinage.confusions: Gordian III as Caesar (238) is rare; Antioch issues vs Rome by style and legend punctuation.
coinage.dating: P M TR P I-VII; COS II (241); PIVS FEL in obverse from c. 240.

coinage.issuerName: Philip I (with Philip II and Otacilia Severa)
coinage.text: Philip's coinage culminates in the celebration of Rome's 1,000th birthday (April 248): antoniniani with SAECVLARES AVGG and the animals shown in the arena (lion, she-wolf with twins, stag, antelope, elk or deer, goat, hippopotamus), each struck by one officina (marked I-VI), plus SAECVLVM NOVVM (temple) and MILIARIVM SAECVLVM (column). Philip II appears as a boy Caesar (244) and Augustus (247), and the empress Otacilia Severa has a large coinage. Antioch antoniniani of this reign are common and stylistically distinct. Philip was the first emperor of Arab origin, from Shahba in Trachonitis.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani very common; the hippopotamus and elk types scarcer; aurei rare.
coinage.confusions: Philip II is beardless; legends M IVL PHILIPPVS CAES (Caesar) or IMP PHILIPPVS AVG (both men as Augustus): judge by portrait.
coinage.dating: P M TR P I-VI; COS III (248); Saecular types 248.

legends: IMP TI CL MAR PACATIANVS P F AVG
ROMAE AETERN AN MILL ET PRIMO
coinage.text: A short-lived usurper among the Danube legions in 248-249, Pacatian is known from a handful of literary mentions and from antoniniani struck at a Moesian mint (probably Viminacium). The most famous type, ROMAE AETERN AN MILL ET PRIMO, dates itself to Rome's 1,001st year, just after Philip's millennial games. Decius was sent to deal with the revolt and ended by usurping himself.
keyTypes: ROMAE AETERN AN MILL ET PRIMO
coinage.rarity: Very rare; forged.
coinage.confusions: None among genuine coins.

legends: IMP M F RV IOTAPIANVS AVG
coinage.text: Proclaimed in Syria or Cappadocia under Philip, Jotapian claimed descent from Alexander Severus (and perhaps the royal house of Commagene, where Iotape was a dynastic name). His antoniniani are crudely engraved at an eastern mint with a heavy-featured radiate bust and Victory. He was killed by his own troops.
coinage.rarity: Extremely rare.
coinage.confusions: Modern fakes.

coinage.text: Two 'emperors' known only from coins. Silbannacus is attested by one antoninianus in the British Museum (with MERCVRIO VICTORI) and a second found in France in 1996 (VICTORIA AVG), apparently struck at Rome or in Gaul in the late 240s or c. 253: an otherwise unknown pretender. Sponsian is known from a few gold pieces found in Transylvania in 1713, long dismissed as 18th-century fakes because of their odd design (a Republican reverse copied from a denarius of 135 BC); scientific analysis published in 2022 (Pearson and others) argued that wear and soil deposits show genuine ancient circulation, reviving the idea of a local commander in isolated Dacia in the 260s. The debate continues; most specialists remain cautious.
coinage.rarity: Unique to a handful of specimens.
coinage.confusions: Sponsian's authenticity is disputed.
coinage.dating: Silbannacus late 240s or c. 253; Sponsian probably 260s if genuine.

coinage.issuerName: Trajan Decius (with Herennius Etruscus, Hostilian and Herennia Etruscilla)
legends: IMP C M Q TRAIANVS DECIVS AVG
Q HER ETR MES DECIVS NOB C
C VALENS HOSTIL MES QVINTVS N C
coinage.text: Decius, from Pannonia, celebrated his Danubian roots: GENIVS EXERC ILLVRICIANI, the two Pannoniae, and Dacia holding a staff topped by a donkey's head (or a Dacian draco). He introduced the radiate double sestertius and issued a remarkable 'Divi' series of antoniniani commemorating eleven deified emperors from Augustus to Severus Alexander, interpreted as a programme of traditional religion that matches his edict of universal sacrifice (250). His sons Herennius Etruscus and Hostilian appear as Caesars; Herennius was made Augustus in 251 and died with his father at Abritus. The empress Herennia Etruscilla has abundant coins.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani common; Divi series scarce; Herennius and Hostilian moderately scarce.
coinage.confusions: Divi antoniniani show the deified emperor, not Decius; Hostilian appears both as Caesar under Decius and as Augustus under Gallus.
coinage.dating: COS II (250), COS III (251); Divi series c. 250-251.

coinage.t: Coinage of Trebonianus Gallus and Volusian
legends: IMP C C VIB TREB GALLVS AVG
IMP CAE C VIB VOLVSIANO AVG
coinage.text: Gallus took power after Abritus and made peace with the Goths. His coins carry Juno Martialis in a round temple, a rare cult, and APOLL SALVTARI, Apollo the Healer, an appeal for relief from the Plague of Cyprian that killed his colleague Hostilian in 251. His son Volusian was Caesar and Augustus. Antioch's antoniniani for the pair are plentiful. Silver content declined further.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani common; Hostilian as Augustus scarce.
coinage.confusions: Volusian is younger, short-bearded; check names.

legends: IMP CAES AEMILIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Governor of Moesia, Aemilian won a victory over the Goths, was proclaimed, defeated Gallus and reigned about 88 days before his own soldiers killed him as Valerian approached. His Rome antoniniani show a series of protective deities (Apollo, Diana, Hercules, Mars, Jupiter). His wife Cornelia Supera has very rare coins.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani scarce; sestertii rare; Supera very rare.
coinage.confusions: Short reign; some coins once attributed to other mints are disputed.
coinage.dating: Summer 253.

legends: L IVL AVR SVLP VRA ANTONINVS
coinage.text: A priest of Elagabal who led the defence of Emesa against Shapur I's invasion of 253 and claimed the purple. His aurei, very carefully made at Emesa, include CONSERVATOR AVG with the conical stone of Elagabal on a cart and copies of Roman types (including Philip's Saecular reverse). Billon tetradrachms and civic bronzes were also struck. His story is almost entirely recovered from coins and a few late sources (Malalas, the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle).
coinage.rarity: Aurei very rare; tetradrachms rare.
coinage.confusions: Heavily faked; also confused with earlier emperors called Antoninus.

coinage.issuerName: Valerian I (with Valerian II, Saloninus and Mariniana)
legends: IMP C P LIC VALERIANVS AVG
IMP C P LIC VALERIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Valerian shared power with his son Gallienus and appointed grandsons as Caesars: Valerian II (died 258, consecration coins DIVO VALERIANO CAES) and Saloninus. His wife Mariniana appears only as diva. Mints multiplied to meet military needs: a western mint (Cologne or Trier) from c. 257, Milan, Viminacium, Antioch and a second eastern mint (Samosata?). Eastern types such as RESTITVT ORIENTIS and VICTORIA PARTICA belong to the Persian war that ended with his capture by Shapur at Edessa (260), the greatest humiliation of a Roman emperor.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani common; Valerian II and Mariniana scarce.
coinage.confusions: Joint coinage with Gallienus; the two Valerians are told by legend (Valerian II is P LIC VALERIANVS CAES).
coinage.dating: 253-260; AVGG reverses are joint reign; mint by style and field marks.

legends: IMP C P LIC GALLIENVS AVG
LEG II ADI VI P VI F
coinage.text: Gallienus' coinage covers the worst years of the crisis and is the most varied of the 3rd century. During the joint reign (253-260) a western mint celebrated his German victories (VICT GERMANICA, GERMANICVS MAX V). In his sole reign (260-268) the antoninianus collapsed to a few per cent silver, but the mint produced remarkable series: the 'zoo' coins (c. 267-268) with animals sacred to protective gods (stag and doe for Diana, centaur and griffin for Apollo, Pegasus and bull for Sol, panther for Liber, hippocamp for Neptune, goat for Jupiter), the Milan legionary series naming legions with their badges, and gold with VBIQVE PAX and the enigmatic GALLIENAE AVGVSTAE (a female head crowned with grain). His Hellenising portrait with upturned gaze reflects his philhellenism. Salonina and Saloninus (killed at Cologne 260) appear widely.
coinage.rarity: Sole-reign antoniniani extremely common; legionary types scarce; gold rare; GALLIENAE AVGVSTAE rare.
coinage.confusions: Joint vs sole reign by reverse legends (AVGG vs AVG) and style; Postumus' coins of Milan under Aureolus imitate Gallienic fabric.
coinage.dating: Joint 253-260; sole 260-268; officina numerals and field marks (P, S, T, etc.) by mint.

legends: IMP C FVL MACRIANVS P F AVG
IMP C FVL QVIETVS P F AVG
coinage.text: After Valerian's capture, his finance officer Fulvius Macrianus had his two sons proclaimed in the East. Their antoniniani, struck at eastern mints, show youthful portraits and a narrow repertoire of types. The elder Macrianus marched west and was defeated by Aureolus in 261; Quietus was killed at Emesa by Odaenathus of Palmyra, acting for Gallienus.
coinage.rarity: Scarce.
coinage.confusions: The two brothers look alike; legends identify.

legends: IMP C P C REGALIANVS AVG
coinage.text: A commander in Pannonia proclaimed in 260 and soon killed. His antoniniani and those of his wife Dryantilla were overstruck on old Severan denarii, giving them a small, thick and often double-struck look with traces of the undertype. They are found mostly near Carnuntum.
coinage.rarity: Rare.
coinage.confusions: Undertypes of Severan denarii are part of the evidence for authenticity.

legends: IMP C POSTVMVS P F AVG
P M TR P COS II P P
coinage.text: Founder of the Gallic Empire after killing Saloninus at Cologne (260), Postumus struck coins of a quality unmatched elsewhere in the 260s: antoniniani with noticeably more silver than Gallienus', double sestertii (large radiate bronzes, often overstruck on old sestertii), and gold with facing and three-quarter portraits and a series of Hercules' labours. Local cults appear (Hercules Deusoniensis, Hercules Magusanus). His consulships (to COS V) date issues. In 268 Aureolus at Milan struck in his name before being besieged by Gallienus. His own troops killed him in 269 after he refused to let them sack Mainz.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani common; double sestertii common to scarce; aurei rare.
coinage.confusions: Milan issues of Aureolus for Postumus have Italian fabric; attribution of his main mint (Trier vs Cologne vs Lyon) is debated.
coinage.dating: COS I-V (260-269); TR P numbers.

legends: IMP C LAELIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: A rebel against Postumus at Mainz in 269, Laelianus held out briefly before Postumus besieged and killed him. His antoniniani, struck at a Gallic mint, show a youthful radiate bust and few reverse types, one showing a reclining Hispania with a rabbit (TEMPORVM FELICITAS), suggesting a claim on Spain.
coinage.rarity: Rare.
coinage.confusions: Fakes exist.

legends: IMP C M AVR MARIVS AVG
coinage.text: The sources make Marius a blacksmith who reigned two or three days after Postumus. His coinage, though, is too large for that: antoniniani from both Gallic mints in several types, including clasped hands (CONCORDIA MILITVM), and gold. A reign of a few weeks to three months is now assumed. A classic case where coins correct the literary tradition.
coinage.rarity: Scarce.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: IMP C VICTORINVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Postumus' praetorian prefect, Victorinus ruled Gaul and Britain (Spain went back to Claudius II) until he was murdered at Cologne for seducing an officer's wife. His antoniniani are abundant and low in silver; his gold includes a famous series of legionary aurei naming the legions that supported him with their emblems. The portrait shows a bearded man with a pointed beard; INVICTVS with Sol is a common type.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani common; legionary aurei very rare.
coinage.confusions: Barbarous copies are common in Britain.

legends: IMP C TETRICVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The last Gallic emperors: Tetricus I, governor of Aquitania, and his son Tetricus II as Caesar. Their antoniniani were struck in huge numbers with very little silver and are probably the commonest coins found in Britain and northern Gaul, together with the vast mass of 'barbarous radiates' copied from them. Tetricus II's PIETAS AVGVSTOR shows sacrificial implements. In 274 Tetricus surrendered to Aurelian at Châlons, walked in his triumph, and was given a post in Italy. Gold of the Tetrici is rare.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani extremely common; gold rare.
coinage.confusions: Barbarous radiates (lighter, crude, garbled legends) far outnumber official coins in some finds.

legends: IMP C DOMITIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Zosimus and Zonaras mention a Domitianus who rebelled under Aurelian, and a single antoninianus found at Les Cléons (France) in 1900 was long suspected. The discovery of a second specimen in the Chalgrove hoard (Oxfordshire) in 2003, die-unrelated but in the same Gallic style, confirmed that a Domitianus struck coins in the Gallic Empire around 271, probably briefly between Victorinus and Tetricus. A textbook case of a coin restoring a lost ruler.
coinage.rarity: Two known.
coinage.confusions: None.

coinage.text: Claudius' antoniniani mark the low point of silver (often 1-2%) and are extremely common. Types are conventional, with VICTORIAE GOTHIC (rare) for the great victory at Naissus (269) that earned him his surname. After his death from plague Quintillus and Aurelian issued DIVO CLAVDIO consecration coins with an altar or eagle, which became the most copied coins in late 3rd-century Britain and Gaul. Constantine later claimed descent from Claudius, and issued a commemorative coin for him in 317-318.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani very common; gold rare.
coinage.confusions: Barbarous DIVO CLAVDIO copies; Constantinian MEMORIAE DIVI CLAVDI (317-318) commemoratives are 4th-century nummi.
coinage.dating: 268-270; mint marks and officina numerals by mint.

legends: IMP C M AVR CL QVINTILLVS AVG
coinage.text: Claudius' brother reigned a few weeks or months in 270 before the army chose Aurelian. His antoniniani are plentiful given the brevity of the reign, which suggests he ruled longer than the 17 days of some sources. The portrait resembles Claudius with a longer nose.
coinage.rarity: Scarce.
coinage.confusions: Claudius II (different name).

legends: DEO ET DOMINO NATO AVRELIANO AVG
coinage.text: Aurelian's coins chart the reunification of the empire: early antoniniani of the same poor quality as Claudius', joint issues with Vaballathus at Antioch (270-272), and after 274 the reformed coin marked XXI or KA. Sol Invictus dominates (ORIENS AVG, Sol trampling captives), with RESTITVTOR ORBIS and his godlike titles at Serdica. His wife Ulpia Severina has an unusually large coinage, including issues once thought to date to an interregnum after his murder in 275. Rarer: the pre-reform denarius, the post-reform laureate 'denarius' and small sestertii.
coinage.rarity: Reformed coins common; Serdica 'deus et dominus' types rare; gold scarce.
coinage.confusions: Pre- vs post-reform coins: post-274 coins are heavier and carry XXI/KA; mint by officina marks.
coinage.dating: Reform 274; mint marks with officina letters date post-reform issues.

legends: VABALATHVS V C R IM D R
IMP C AVRELIANVS AVG (obverse of joint issues)
coinage.text: Zenobia's son, heir of Odaenathus. From 270 Antioch struck antoniniani with Aurelian on one side and Vaballathus on the other, styled VCRIMDR: v(ir) c(larissimus) r(ex) im(perator) d(ux) R(omanorum), titles that claim Roman command while acknowledging Aurelian. In 272, as Aurelian marched east, Palmyra broke away and coins call Vaballathus Augustus (rare). Alexandrian tetradrachms also pair him with Aurelian, dated by both their regnal years.
coinage.rarity: Joint coins scarce; Augustus coins rare.
coinage.confusions: The joint coin is often catalogued under Aurelian.

coinage.text: In 272 the queen of Palmyra took the title Augusta for herself, and Antioch struck a few antoniniani with her bust on a crescent and IVNO REGINA. Alexandrian tetradrachms of her year 5 also exist. These coins mark the brief moment when the Palmyrene regime claimed the empire itself, just before Aurelian's victories at Immae and Emesa.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani very rare; tetradrachms rare.
coinage.confusions: Many fakes.

legends: IMP C M CL TACITVS AVG
coinage.text: An elderly senator (or more likely a soldier) chosen after Aurelian's murder, Tacitus reigned about seven months. His reformed coins continue Aurelian's system with XXI and officina marks; his gold is relatively plentiful. The last city coinages of the Greek East (Perge, Side) bear his portrait. Florianus succeeded him.
coinage.rarity: Common to scarce.
coinage.confusions: Do not confuse with the historian Tacitus, whom the Historia Augusta implausibly makes his ancestor.

legends: IMP C M AN FLORIANVS AVG
coinage.text: Tacitus' half-brother (or praetorian prefect) held power for about 80 days in 276 before his troops killed him at Tarsus when Probus was proclaimed in the East. His coins come from most western and Balkan mints; the East struck for Probus.
coinage.rarity: Scarce.
coinage.confusions: None.

legends: IMP C M AVR PROBVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Probus' coinage is a specialist's paradise: a vast range of bust types, legends and field marks across eight mints. Busts show him laureate or radiate, helmeted with spear and shield, holding an eagle-tipped sceptre, in consular robes, or riding; some at Ticinum and Siscia are minor masterpieces. Common reverses include SOLI INVICTO (Sol in quadriga, facing), ADVENTVS AVG (emperor on horseback) and CONCORD MILIT. VIRTVS PROBI AVG puns on his name ('probus' = upright). He reasserted control of Gaul and planted vines on the Danube; his soldiers killed him at Sirmium in 282.
coinage.rarity: Common; rare bust varieties and gold are expensive.
coinage.confusions: Use RIC V.2 bust letters and the Bastien and Pink studies for mint and issue.
coinage.dating: Issue sequences (Pink's emissions) defined by field marks and officina letters.

legends: IMP C M AVR CARVS P F AVG
DEO ET DOMINO CARO INVIC AVG
coinage.text: Carus made his sons Carinus and Numerian Caesars and took the Persian capital Ctesiphon before dying in 283, reputedly struck by lightning. His coins include the famous DEO ET DOMINO CARO INVIC AVG with Carus jugate with Sol, a claim of divine kingship from Lugdunum, and consecration issues after his death. Carinus' wife Magnia Urbica and his infant son Nigrinian (DIVO NIGRINIANO) belong to the same dynasty.
coinage.rarity: Antoniniani common; Magnia Urbica scarce; Nigrinian rare.
coinage.confusions: Joint coins with Carinus.

legends: IMP C M AVR CARINVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Caesar under Carus and then Augustus in the West, Carinus defeated the usurper Julian at Verona and was killed by his own officers at the Margus (285) while winning against Diocletian. His coins are plentiful; his wife Magnia Urbica has scarce coins with VENVS VICTRIX. Gold of this dynasty is often finely engraved.
coinage.rarity: Common.
coinage.confusions: Caesar (NOB C) vs Augustus legends.

legends: IMP C M AVR NVMERIANVS AVG
coinage.text: Carus' younger son, Augustus in the East from 283. His death in a litter on the march back from Persia (reported concealed by his father-in-law, the prefect Aper) led to Diocletian's proclamation in November 284. A typical reverse shows the emperor receiving a globe from Jupiter (VIRTVS AVGG).
coinage.rarity: Common.
coinage.confusions: Caesar vs Augustus issues.

legends: IMP C M AVR IVLIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Governor of Venetia or Pannonia, proclaimed after Numerian's death, Julian struck at Siscia before Carinus defeated him near Verona. His coins include PANNONIAE AVG with two Pannoniae, echoing Decius. Scarce to rare.
coinage.rarity: Rare.
coinage.confusions: Do not confuse with Julian the Apostate.

coinage.t: Aes rude and aes signatum: money before coins
coinage.standard: by weight; bars c. 1.5-1.8 kg (about 5 Roman pounds)
coinage.text: For most of its early history Rome measured value in cattle and sheep (pecunia from pecus, the Twelve Tables' fines in sheep and oxen) and in weighed bronze. Shapeless lumps of aes rude are found in votive deposits from the 6th century onward. Then came cast bars with designs, aes signatum: the earliest carry a 'dry branch' (ramo secco) pattern and are Etruscan and Italic; the Roman series (Crawford RRC 3-12) includes bars with an eagle and Pegasus, a trident and caduceus, shields, and the famous elephant/sow bar, often connected with Pyrrhus' elephants (280-275) and the story that pigs terrified them. These bars were valued by weight and frequently broken; the per aes et libram ceremony of Roman law (mancipatio with scales and a piece of bronze) preserves the memory of weighed money in classical times. Why it matters: Rome entered coinage late and from a bronze-weight economy, which explains the heavy cast as and the long dominance of bronze accounting (the sestertius, 'two and a half asses', remained the unit of account long after the as shrank).
scholarship: Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

coinage.t: Aes grave: the cast libral as
coinage.standard: as of about one Roman pound (c. 270-330 g in different series); fractions marked by pellets (uncia = 1 pellet)
coinage.text: Rome's first official coinage was heavy cast bronze, aes grave, beginning in the early 3rd century (traditionally linked with the creation of the tresviri monetales, c. 289). The as weighed about a pound and its fractions were marked by value signs: S for the semis, four pellets for the triens, three for the quadrans, two for the sextans, one for the uncia. Early series show a range of deities (Janus, Mercury, Roma, Apollo, a wheel); the standard 'prow series' (Janus / ship's prow, from c. 225) fixed the iconography of Roman bronze for two centuries, and children in Macrobius' day still played 'heads or ships' (capita aut navia, Saturnalia 1.7.22). Cast coins were made in open or bivalve moulds and can show casting sprues. Parallel series were cast at allied centres (Luceria, Tuder, Hatria, Volaterrae). Identification: genuine aes grave has a granular cast surface with casting seams; most modern copies are lighter, too crisp, or have a sand-cast texture. Weight sequences are the key to dating them because the as was cut repeatedly: semilibral c. 217, sextantal c. 211, uncial in the mid-2nd century, semuncial in 91-89.

coinage.standard: Campanian didrachm c. 7.3 g
coinage.text: Pliny states that Rome first struck silver in 269 BC, in the consulship of Q. Ogulnius and C. Fabius, five years before the First Punic War. Modern scholarship accepts the date as a memory of a real event but disputes what it refers to: the Hercules / she-wolf and twins didrachm (ROMANO), the first silver struck at Rome itself rather than in Campania, or an antiquarian reconstruction.
