sites.summary: Town in Osrhoene near the Euphrates where, Ammianus says, a great annual fair in early September drew crowds of every rank to buy goods sent by the Indians and Chinese. Julian passed through in 363.

sites.name: Cremona fair
sites.summary: Latin colony of 218 BC whose market fair drew all of Italy. Tacitus notes that the fair was in progress when the Flavian army sacked the city in 69, swelling the number of victims.

sites.name: Campi Macri
sites.summary: Plain near Mutina where a great annual sheep and wool fair was held, mentioned by Varro and Strabo; the Po valley produced the fine wool of Mutina and Parma.

sites.name: Mamre (Terebinthus) fair
sites.summary: Annual summer fair at Abraham's oak near Hebron, attended by Jews, Christians and pagans. Jerome and the Chronicon Paschale say Hadrian sold Jewish captives here after the Bar Kokhba war. Constantine ordered the pagan altars removed and built a basilica c. 330; Sozomen describes the festival.

sites.name: Magdalensberg emporium
sites.summary: Hilltop trading town in Noricum where Italian merchants, many from Aquileia, bought Noric iron and gold before the annexation of 15 BC; graffiti record iron bars and gold ingots for the imperial house. Abandoned under Claudius for Virunum.

sites.name: Carnuntum amber market
sites.summary: Danube fortress where the Amber Road crossed the frontier. Pliny records that an eques under Nero travelled 600 miles from Carnuntum to the Baltic coast and brought back so much amber that the nets of the arena were knotted with it, including a lump of 13 pounds.

sites.name: Salinae at the Tiber mouth
sites.summary: Salt pans on both banks of the Tiber mouth, which tradition said Ancus Marcius took from Veii; the road that carried their salt inland was the Via Salaria. In 204 BC the censors Livius Salinator and Claudius Nero fixed the salt price, earning Livius his mocking cognomen.

sites.name: Salinae (Droitwich)
sites.summary: Brine springs worked into salt in Iron Age and Roman Britain; the Ravenna Cosmography names a Salinae here. Evaporation hearths and lead pans have been excavated.

sites.name: Hallstatt salt mine
sites.summary: The prehistoric salt mine that gave its name to the Early Iron Age; a Roman settlement in the valley below continued salt production under Noricum.

sites.name: Salt pans of maritime Venetia
sites.summary: Cassiodorus' letter of 537-538 to the tribunes of the maritime Venetians describes them living like water birds, bound to their boats, everyone eating alike, and growing rich on salt pans where 'instead of ploughs they roll cylinders'.

sites.name: Lake Tatta (Tuz Gölü)
sites.summary: Salt lake of central Anatolia. Strabo says it crusts salt so readily that a bird dipping its wings is dragged down, and that its salt was a source of revenue for the Galatian kings.

sites.name: See of Rome
sites.summary: Christians were in Rome by the 40s (Suetonius' riots 'at the instigation of Chrestus' under Claudius), Paul wrote to them c. 57, and Nero blamed them for the fire of 64. The letter 1 Clement (c. 96) speaks for the Roman church; Irenaeus later lists Linus, Anacletus and Clement as Peter's successors. A single ruling bishop is secure only from Anicetus (c. 155) or later. By the 4th century the bishop was a great landowner and, from Leo I, claimed primacy over all churches.

sites.name: See of Antioch
sites.summary: Where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11.26) and the base of Paul's missions. Ignatius, the first bishop known from his own writings, was taken to Rome under Trajan to die in the arena and wrote seven letters on the way insisting on obedience to one bishop. Eusebius makes Evodius his predecessor. Paul of Samosata was deposed here in 268. At Chalcedon (451) Antioch ranked third among the patriarchates.

sites.name: See of Alexandria
sites.summary: Eusebius' list from Mark's successor Annianus is legendary; the first historically secure bishop is Demetrius (189-232), who first sponsored then expelled Origen. By Nicaea (canon 6) the bishop ruled all the bishops of Egypt and Libya, and the 'pope' of Alexandria, from Athanasius to Cyril and Dioscorus, was the most powerful churchman in the East until Chalcedon split the Egyptian church.

sites.name: See of Jerusalem
sites.summary: The Jerusalem church was led by James, 'the Lord's brother', whom Paul met there and who presided at the apostolic council (c. 49); Josephus records his stoning in 62. After Hadrian's refoundation as Aelia Capitolina (135) the first gentile bishop was Mark. Subordinate to Caesarea until Juvenal won patriarchal rank at Chalcedon in 451.

sites.name: See of Carthage
sites.summary: Africa's primatial see. The Passion of Perpetua (203) names Bishop Optatus; Agrippinus held a council on rebaptism c. 220; Cyprian (248-258) left the richest archive of a 3rd-century bishop and was beheaded in 258. From 311 the see was split between Catholics (Caecilian) and Donatists (Majorinus, then Donatus).

sites.name: See of Lyon
sites.summary: The church of Lyon and Vienne, Greek-speaking and linked to Asia Minor, sent a letter describing the pogrom of 177, in which the 90-year-old bishop Pothinus died in prison. His successor Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies here, the first systematic attack on Gnosticism.

sites.name: See of Vienne
sites.summary: Co-author with Lyon of the letter on the martyrs of 177, but its first named bishop is Verus at Arles in 314. Vienne later fought Arles for metropolitan rank in Narbonensis.

sites.name: See of Smyrna
sites.summary: Ignatius wrote to Bishop Polycarp c. 110. Polycarp, who claimed to have known the apostle John, visited Anicetus in Rome over the date of Easter and was burned in the stadium c. 155-156 at 86 years old; the Martyrdom of Polycarp is the earliest martyr act.

sites.name: See of Ephesus
sites.summary: Paul's base for over two years and a centre of Johannine tradition. Ignatius praises its bishop Onesimus. Polycrates of Ephesus defended the Asian (Quartodeciman) Easter date against Victor of Rome c. 190. Host of the councils of 431 and 449.

sites.name: See of Magnesia on the Maeander
sites.summary: Ignatius' letter to the Magnesians names their young bishop Damas and urges them not to despise his youth.

sites.name: See of Tralles
sites.summary: Ignatius' letter to the Trallians names Bishop Polybius, who visited him at Smyrna.

sites.name: See of Philadelphia (Lydia)
sites.summary: One of the seven churches of Revelation. Ignatius, who passed through, praises its silent but authoritative bishop without naming him.

sites.name: See of Hierapolis in Phrygia
sites.summary: Papias (c. 120-130) collected oral traditions about the apostles, including the earliest statements on how Mark and Matthew were written. The tomb of the apostle Philip, venerated here, was found in 2011. Apollinaris, bishop c. 170, wrote an apology to Marcus Aurelius.

sites.name: See of Sardis
sites.summary: Melito, bishop c. 170, wrote an Apology to Marcus Aurelius and the homily On the Pascha, with its notorious charge of deicide against Israel, in a city where the synagogue was larger than any church.

sites.name: See of Laodicea on the Lycus
sites.summary: Bishop Sagaris was martyred c. 166 under the proconsul Servilius Paulus, Melito says. The Council of Laodicea (c. 363) issued canons on clergy and the biblical canon.

sites.name: See of Corinth
sites.summary: Paul's church of the letters to the Corinthians; 1 Clement (c. 96) rebukes it for deposing its presbyters. Bishop Dionysius (c. 170) wrote letters to Rome, Athens, Crete and Pontus, the first collected letters of a bishop.

sites.name: See of Athens
sites.summary: Dionysius of Corinth reports that Bishop Publius was martyred and Quadratus revived the church. Athens remained a pagan intellectual centre until Justinian's ban of 529.

sites.name: See of Gortyn
sites.summary: Metropolis of Crete; Dionysius of Corinth praised its bishop Philip, who wrote against Marcion.

sites.name: See of Knossos
sites.summary: Pinytus of Knossos replied to Dionysius of Corinth, urging solid teaching rather than milk; Eusebius admired his letter.

sites.name: See of Sinope
sites.summary: Hippolytus and Epiphanius say Marcion, the shipowner who founded a rival church c. 144, was the son of the bishop of Sinope, who excommunicated him for seducing a virgin (probably a metaphor for corrupting the church).

sites.name: See of Amastris
sites.summary: Dionysius of Corinth wrote to the churches of Pontus at Amastris under Bishop Palmas, who later presided over the Pontic synod on Easter c. 190.

sites.name: See of Anchialus
sites.summary: Thracian port whose bishop Sotas tried to exorcise the Montanist prophetess Priscilla, according to an anti-Montanist source in Eusebius.

sites.name: See of Caesarea Maritima
sites.summary: Metropolitan see of Palestine. Theophilus presided over a synod on Easter c. 190. Origen settled here in 231 and founded the school and library that Pamphilus expanded and Eusebius, bishop c. 313-339, used for his Ecclesiastical History.

sites.name: See of Tyre
sites.summary: Cassius of Tyre joined the Palestinian synod on Easter c. 190. Eusebius preached at the dedication of Paulinus' new basilica at Tyre c. 315, describing it in detail. Origen was buried at Tyre.

sites.name: See of Ptolemais (Acre)
sites.summary: Clarus of Ptolemais joined Theophilus of Caesarea and Cassius of Tyre in the Easter synod of c. 190.

sites.name: See of Edessa
sites.summary: Centre of Syriac Christianity. The legend of King Abgar's letter to Jesus was known to Eusebius. The Chronicle of Edessa records 'the temple of the church of the Christians' destroyed by flood in 201; Palut, said to have been consecrated by Serapion of Antioch, is the first named bishop. Rabbula (412-435) and the School of the Persians made it the hub of Syriac theology.

sites.name: See of Arles
sites.summary: Cyprian urged Pope Stephen to depose Marcianus of Arles c. 254 for his Novatianist rigorism. Marinus of Arles hosted Constantine's council of 314. In the 5th century the see claimed primacy over Gaul, and Caesarius (502-542) ran a model episcopal city.

sites.name: See of Lambaesis
sites.summary: Legionary base of III Augusta. Its bishop Privatus was condemned for heresy by a synod of 90 bishops c. 240, as Cyprian reports.

sites.name: See of Neocaesarea
sites.summary: Gregory the Wonderworker, a pupil of Origen, became bishop c. 240; Gregory of Nyssa's later Life claims he found 17 Christians on arrival and left 17 pagans at his death. His Canonical Letter deals with Christians who collaborated with Gothic raiders in the 250s.

sites.name: See of Caesarea in Cappadocia
sites.summary: Firmilian (c. 232-268) hosted Origen, sided with Cyprian against Rome on rebaptism, and presided at the first synod against Paul of Samosata. Basil (370-379) made the see the leader of Nicene orthodoxy in the East and built the Basileias poorhouse-hospital.

sites.name: See of Iconium
sites.summary: Bishop Celsus invited Origen, a layman, to preach, as Alexander of Jerusalem reminded Demetrius of Alexandria. A synod at Iconium c. 230 rejected heretical baptism.

sites.name: See of Bostra
sites.summary: Beryllus of Bostra taught that Christ had no divinity of his own before the incarnation; Origen was called in and argued him round at a synod c. 244.

sites.name: See of Arsinoe (Fayum)
sites.summary: Bishop Nepos wrote a millenarian Refutation of the Allegorists; Dionysius of Alexandria spent three days debating his followers in the Fayum villages c. 255 and persuaded them.

sites.name: See of Tarsus
sites.summary: Paul's home town. Helenus of Tarsus was one of the leading bishops whom Dionysius of Alexandria lists c. 251 and presided at the synods against Paul of Samosata.

sites.name: See of Legio and Asturica
sites.summary: Cyprian's council of 254 upheld the deposition of Basilides, who had obtained a certificate of sacrifice in the Decian persecution, the earliest evidence for organised churches in Hispania.

sites.name: See of Emerita
sites.summary: Martialis of Emerita was deposed with Basilides for apostasy in 254; Cyprian adds that he belonged to a pagan funerary college. Later the metropolis of Lusitania and the shrine of Eulalia.

sites.name: See of Tolosa
sites.summary: Saturninus was dragged to death by a bull after refusing to sacrifice, according to a 5th-century Passion that dates his mission to c. 250. Gregory of Tours lists him among seven bishops sent to Gaul under Decius.

sites.name: See of Lutetia (Paris)
sites.summary: Gregory of Tours places Dionysius' mission and martyrdom c. 250; the first solidly attested activity is a council at Paris in 360/361. Genovefa built the first basilica over his tomb c. 475.

sites.name: See of Hippo Regius
sites.summary: Theogenes of Hippo voted at Cyprian's council on baptism in 256. Augustine was ordained priest here in 391 against his will and was bishop from 395/6 until he died during the Vandal siege in 430.

sites.name: See of Cirta
sites.summary: Crescens of Cirta voted in 256. The minutes of the 303 confiscation of church property at Cirta, read at a trial of 320, list the bishop's chalices, tunics and stores of clothing, and reveal Bishop Silvanus as a traditor.

sites.name: See of Hadrumetum
sites.summary: Polycarpus of Hadrumetum voted at the council of 256. The town's catacombs hold around 15,000 burials.

sites.name: See of Thamugadi
sites.summary: Novatus of Thamugadi voted in 256. Under Optatus (c. 388-398), ally of the rebel Gildo, Timgad was a Donatist stronghold with one of the largest churches in Africa.

sites.name: See of Tarraco
sites.summary: Bishop Fructuosus was burned alive in the amphitheatre on 21 January 259 with his deacons Augurius and Eulogius, under Valerian's edict. A 6th-century basilica was built in the arena.

sites.name: See of Laodicea ad Mare
sites.summary: Eusebius, an Alexandrian deacon, and then Anatolius, the mathematician who devised a 19-year Easter cycle, were successive bishops of Laodicea after escaping the siege of the Alexandrian Bruchion c. 262.

sites.name: See of Corduba
sites.summary: Ossius (c. 295-357), the most influential Western bishop of his age, attended Elvira, advised Constantine from 312, carried his letter to Alexandria in 324, probably presided at Nicaea, and at nearly 100 was forced to sign the Arian formula of Sirmium in 357.

sites.name: See of Nicomedia
sites.summary: Diocletian's capital, where the Great Persecution began with the destruction of the church on 23 February 303. Bishop Anthimus was beheaded. Eusebius of Nicomedia, Arius' patron, baptised Constantine here in 337.

sites.name: See of Heraclea (Perinthus)
sites.summary: Metropolis of Thrace whose bishop Philippus was burned at Hadrianopolis in 304; Heraclea's bishop originally consecrated the bishop of Byzantium.

sites.name: See of Sirmium
sites.summary: Bishop Irenaeus was beheaded on 6 April 304. Imperial residence and site of four councils in 351-358 that produced the creeds of the Homoian party, including the 'Blasphemy of Sirmium' (357).

sites.name: See of Poetovio
sites.summary: Victorinus of Poetovio, martyred probably in 304, wrote the oldest surviving Latin commentary on the Apocalypse, with millenarian views Jerome toned down.

sites.name: See of Salona
sites.summary: Metropolis of Dalmatia; Bishop Domnius was martyred under Diocletian, whose palace was 5 km away. The great martyr cemeteries of Manastirine and Marusinac lie outside the walls.

sites.name: See of Iliberris (Elvira)
sites.summary: Host city of the synod of Elvira (c. 305), whose 81 canons, signed by 19 bishops, ban pictures in churches, marriages with pagans and Jews, and clerical sex.

sites.name: See of Toletum
sites.summary: Melantius of Toledo attended Elvira. In the Visigothic kingdom Toledo became the royal see, host of the councils from 400 and of the Third Council (589) at which Reccared converted.

sites.name: See of Thmuis
sites.summary: Phileas, a rich and learned bishop, wrote from prison describing the tortures in Alexandria and was beheaded c. 306; his trial transcript survives on papyrus (P. Bodmer XX).

sites.name: See of Lycopolis
sites.summary: Meletius of Lycopolis ordained clergy in other sees during the persecution, starting the Melitian schism that Nicaea tried to settle and that lasted into the 8th century.

sites.name: See of Siscia
sites.summary: Bishop Quirinus was drowned in the river at Savaria in 309 with a millstone around his neck, according to Jerome's Chronicle and his Passion.

sites.name: See of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
sites.summary: Papa bar Aggai (c. 310-329) asserted the primacy of the Sasanian capital over Persian bishops. Simeon bar Sabba'e was executed by Shapur II in 344. The Synod of Isaac (410) organised the Church of the East under a catholicos.

sites.name: See of Gaza
sites.summary: Silvanus, 'bishop of the churches around Gaza', was beheaded at the Phaeno mines in 311. Gaza remained largely pagan until Porphyry (395-420) won imperial orders to destroy the Marneion in 402.

sites.name: See of Emesa
sites.summary: Silvanus of Emesa was thrown to the beasts in 312, after 40 years as bishop, Eusebius says.

sites.name: See of Mediolanum
sites.summary: Merocles sat at the Roman synod of 313 and at Arles in 314. As imperial residence Milan became a leading see; Ambrose (374-397) baptised Augustine in 387 and forced Theodosius I into penance in 390.

sites.name: See of Capua
sites.summary: Proterius of Capua sat at Miltiades' synod of 313 on the Donatist case and was at Arles in 314.

sites.name: See of Ostia
sites.summary: Maximus of Ostia sat at the Roman synod of 313; by custom the bishop of Ostia consecrated the bishop of Rome. Augustine's mother Monica died at Ostia in 387.

sites.name: See of Florentia
sites.summary: Felix of Florentia sat at the Roman synod of 313 under Miltiades, the first attested bishop in Etruria.

sites.name: See of Ariminum
sites.summary: Stennius of Ariminum sat at the synod of 313. In 359 over 400 Western bishops met at Ariminum and were pressured into a Homoian creed.

sites.name: See of Beneventum
sites.summary: Theophilus of Beneventum sat at Miltiades' synod of 313, per Optatus' list of the Italian bishops.

sites.name: See of Augustodunum
sites.summary: Reticius of Autun, with Maternus and Marinus, was one of three Gallic bishops Constantine sent to judge the Donatists in Rome in 313. Jerome knew his commentary on the Song of Songs.

sites.name: See of Colonia Agrippina
sites.summary: Maternus of Cologne sat at Rome in 313 and Arles in 314; a 4th-century Christian community is attested by burials and the predecessor of St Gereon.

sites.name: See of Augusta Treverorum
sites.summary: Agricius attended Arles in 314. As imperial capital Trier hosted Athanasius in exile (335-337) and Priscillian's trial and execution (385).

sites.name: See of Londinium
sites.summary: Restitutus of London attended the Council of Arles in 314 with the bishops of York and probably Lincoln, a priest and a deacon: the first firm evidence of an organised British church.

sites.name: See of Eboracum
sites.summary: Eborius of York attended Arles in 314. At Ariminum in 359 three British bishops were so poor they accepted the imperial travel allowance the others refused, says Sulpicius Severus.

sites.name: See of Lindum (probably)
sites.summary: The Arles list has Adelfius 'from the city of the colony of the Londoners', usually emended to Lindum (Lincoln), possibly Camulodunum.

sites.name: See of Durocortorum
sites.summary: Imbetausius of Reims attended Arles in 314. Remigius of Reims baptised Clovis, by tradition at Christmas c. 496-508.

sites.name: See of Rotomagus
sites.summary: Avitianus of Rouen attended Arles in 314. Victricius (c. 386-407) wrote In Praise of the Saints on the relics he received.

sites.name: See of Burdigala
sites.summary: Orientalis of Bordeaux attended Arles in 314. A synod at Bordeaux in 384 condemned Priscillian, who appealed to the usurper Maximus.

sites.name: See of Massalia
sites.summary: Oresius of Marseille attended Arles in 314. John Cassian founded St Victor here c. 415.

sites.name: See of Vasio
sites.summary: Daphnus of Vaison attended Arles in 314; Vaison hosted councils in 442 and 529.

sites.name: See of Syracuse
sites.summary: Constantine's letter summoning Chrestus to Arles, with travel by public post, is quoted by Eusebius. The catacombs of San Giovanni are the largest outside Rome.

sites.name: See of Carales
sites.summary: Quintasius of Carales attended Arles in 314. Lucifer of Cagliari (d. 370), exiled for defending Athanasius, founded a rigorist schism.

sites.name: See of Aquileia
sites.summary: Theodore attended Arles in 314 and built the double basilica with its mosaic floor. Ambrose's council of Aquileia (381) deposed the Homoian bishops Palladius and Secundianus.

sites.name: See of Caesaraugusta
sites.summary: Valerius of Caesaraugusta attended Arles in 314; Cyprian's letter of 254 already praises a Felix of the city. A council here in 380 condemned Priscillian's practices.

sites.name: See of Ancyra
sites.summary: Host of the council of 314 on the lapsed. Marcellus of Ancyra, an extreme anti-Arian at Nicaea, was deposed in 336 for Sabellianism; the creed clause 'his kingdom will have no end' was added against him.

sites.name: See of Amaseia
sites.summary: Basileus of Amaseia attended Ancyra (314) and was executed under Licinius c. 322, an episode Eusebius cites as Licinius' persecution.

sites.name: See of Byzantium/Constantinople
sites.summary: A minor suffragan of Heraclea until Constantine's refoundation; Alexander (c. 314-337) prayed that Arius, due to be readmitted to communion in 336, should not be; Arius died suddenly the day before. The council of 381 gave its bishop second rank after Rome, and canon 28 of Chalcedon (451) equal privileges, which Rome rejected.

sites.name: See of Nicaea
sites.summary: Theognis of Nicaea signed the creed of 325 but not the anathemas and was exiled with Eusebius of Nicomedia, then recalled c. 328.

sites.name: See of Chalcedon
sites.summary: Maris of Chalcedon, an Arian sympathiser, attended Nicaea; old and blind, he later rebuked Julian to his face as an apostate. The council of 451 met in the martyrium of St Euphemia here.

sites.name: See of Nisibis
sites.summary: Jacob of Nisibis attended Nicaea; legend credits his prayers with saving the city in Shapur II's sieges. Ephrem the Syrian served him and his successors until Nisibis was ceded to Persia in 363.

sites.name: See of Damascus
sites.summary: Magnus of Damascus signed at Nicaea. The city's church of John the Baptist, built in the old temple of Jupiter under Theodosius, became the Umayyad mosque.

sites.name: See of Thessalonica
sites.summary: Paul's church of the Thessalonian letters; its first named bishop, Alexander, signed at Nicaea. From the late 4th century the bishop was papal vicar for Illyricum. Theodosius' massacre in the hippodrome (390) led to his penance before Ambrose.

sites.name: See of Serdica
sites.summary: Protogenes of Serdica signed at Nicaea and hosted the council of 343, which split into Western and Eastern assemblies excommunicating each other.

sites.name: See of Stobi
sites.summary: Budius of Stobi signed at Nicaea for Macedonia; the city's episcopal basilica had several rebuildings in the 4th-6th centuries.

sites.name: See of Larissa
sites.summary: Achillius of Larissa, metropolitan of Thessaly, signed at Nicaea.

sites.name: See of Trimithus (Cyprus)
sites.summary: Spyridon, a shepherd-bishop and Nicaea participant according to Rufinus and Socrates, became Cyprus' best known saint; his relics are now on Corfu. Epiphanius of Salamis (367-403) was the island's great metropolitan.

sites.name: See of Ptolemais (Pentapolis)
sites.summary: Secundus of Ptolemais refused to sign at Nicaea and was exiled with Arius. Synesius, a Neoplatonist who refused to give up his wife, was bishop from 410 and wrote on the nomad raids.

sites.name: See of the Bosporus
sites.summary: Domnus of Bosporus signed at Nicaea, the first bishop on the north shore of the Black Sea.

sites.name: See of Pityus
sites.summary: Stratophilus of Pityus, a frontier fort in Colchis, signed at Nicaea; John Chrysostom died on the way to exile there in 407.

sites.name: See of Aksum
sites.summary: Frumentius, a Tyrian shipwrecked as a boy and raised at the Aksumite court, was consecrated bishop by Athanasius c. 330-340; King Ezana's coins switch from pagan symbols to the cross. Constantius II wrote to the Aksumite kings demanding Frumentius' recall.

sites.name: See of Hadrianopolis
sites.summary: Eutropius of Hadrianopolis, an anti-Arian, was deposed c. 331 after Eusebius of Nicomedia's party accused him before Constantine's half-sister Basilina.

sites.name: See of Mursa
sites.summary: Valens of Mursa, with Ursacius the leader of Western Homoians, told Constantius II of his victory over Magnentius at Mursa (351) before the messengers arrived, claiming an angel had told him.

sites.name: See of Singidunum
sites.summary: Ursacius of Singidunum, a pupil of Arius, was a leading Homoian at Tyre (335), Sirmium and Ariminum.

sites.name: See of Caesarodunum (Tours)
sites.summary: Gregory of Tours, himself bishop from 573, lists Gatianus and then Litorius (c. 337) before Martin, the soldier-monk made bishop in 371, whose tomb made Tours the chief pilgrimage centre of Gaul.

sites.name: See of Ravenna
sites.summary: Severus signed at Serdica in 343. When Honorius moved the court to Ravenna in 402 the see rose rapidly: Peter Chrysologus, Neon's baptistery, and under Justinian the archbishops Maximian and Agnellus.

sites.name: See of Atuatuca Tungrorum
sites.summary: Servatius signed at Serdica (343) and attended Ariminum (359), the northernmost bishop on the continent; his see later moved to Maastricht, where his tomb became a cult centre.

sites.name: See of Philippi
sites.summary: Paul's first European church, to which Polycarp wrote c. 120 addressing presbyters, not a bishop. Porphyrius of Philippi is listed at Serdica. The octagonal church and great basilicas of the 5th-6th centuries dominate the site.

sites.name: See of Verona
sites.summary: Zeno of Verona (c. 362-372), probably an African, left 93 sermons. Verona later became a Gothic and Lombard royal city.

sites.name: See of Tomis
sites.summary: Bretanion of Tomis, the only bishop of Scythia, defied Valens to his face c. 368, according to Sozomen. Theotimus (c. 400) evangelised the Goths across the Danube.

sites.name: See of Octodurus
sites.summary: Theodore of Octodurus attended Ambrose's council of Aquileia in 381 and promoted the cult of the Theban Legion at Agaune; his see later moved to Sion.

sites.name: See of Avila
sites.summary: Priscillian, a lay ascetic made bishop of Ávila c. 381, was tried for sorcery before the usurper Maximus and beheaded at Trier in 385 with six followers, the first Christians executed for heresy by a Christian ruler; Martin of Tours and Ambrose protested.

sites.name: See of Bracara
sites.summary: Paternus of Braga renounced Priscillianism at the First Council of Toledo in 400. Under the Sueves Braga became a royal see; Martin of Braga converted them to Catholicism c. 560.

sites.name: See of Cyrrhus
sites.summary: Theodoret (423-c. 460) governed 800 parishes, wrote an Ecclesiastical History and the Religious History of Syrian ascetics, was deposed at Ephesus II (449) and restored at Chalcedon.

sites.name: Palladius and the Irish mission
sites.summary: Prosper records that in 431 Pope Celestine sent Palladius as 'first bishop to the Irish believing in Christ'. Patrick's Confessio describes his own mission later in the 5th century; Armagh's claim to be his see is 7th-century propaganda.

sites.name: Apostolic council of Jerusalem
sites.summary: Meeting of Paul and Barnabas with James, Peter and John over whether gentile converts must be circumcised. Acts presents a decree requiring only abstention from idol-meat, blood, strangled animals and fornication; Paul's own account in Galatians differs, and the Antioch incident followed.

sites.name: Council of Carthage on rebaptism
sites.summary: On 1 September 256, 87 African bishops under Cyprian voted one by one (the Sententiae episcoporum survive) that converts baptised by heretics or schismatics must be rebaptised, defying Pope Stephen. The precedent later underpinned Donatist theology.

sites.name: Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata
sites.summary: Bishops deposed Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch and a ducenarius in Zenobia's service, for adoptionist teaching and worldly display. Paul refused to leave the church house; after recovering Antioch, Aurelian ruled in 272 that it belonged to whomever the bishops of Italy and Rome recognised, the first imperial ruling in an internal church dispute.

sites.name: Synod of Rome under Miltiades
sites.summary: Constantine's first intervention in church affairs: Pope Miltiades with three Gallic and fifteen Italian bishops met in Fausta's house on the Lateran from 2 October 313 and acquitted Caecilian of Carthage. The Donatists appealed, leading to Arles.

sites.name: Council of Arles
sites.summary: Summoned by Constantine for 1 August 314, attended by some 33 bishops from Gaul, Britain, Spain, Italy and Africa. It rejected the Donatist appeal and issued 22 canons, including excommunication of soldiers who threw down their arms in peacetime.

sites.name: Council of Ancyra
sites.summary: Eastern bishops met after Maximinus Daia's death to set penances for those who lapsed in the persecution; its 25 canons include rules on clergy who sacrificed under torture and on bestiality.

sites.name: Council of Nicaea
sites.summary: Constantine's council, opened c. 20 May 325 in the palace at Nicaea, with some 250-300 bishops (tradition: 318). It condemned Arius, adopted a creed defining the Son as homoousios with the Father, fixed a common Easter date and ranked Alexandria, Antioch and Rome. Constantine paid for the bishops' travel by public post.

sites.name: Council of Tyre
sites.summary: Eusebian bishops deposed Athanasius on charges of violence against Melitians, including the murder of Arsenius, who was produced alive. Constantine exiled Athanasius to Trier anyway after he allegedly threatened to stop the Egyptian grain fleet.

sites.name: Dedication Council of Antioch
sites.summary: Some 97 bishops met at the dedication of Constantine's Golden Octagon in the presence of Constantius II and issued creeds avoiding homoousios, and 25 canons long used in both East and West.

sites.name: Council of Gangra
sites.summary: Anatolian bishops condemned the followers of Eustathius of Sebaste for extreme asceticism: rejecting marriage, encouraging slaves to leave masters and women to cut their hair and wear men's clothes. The date is disputed (c. 340-355).

sites.name: Council of Serdica
sites.summary: Called by Constans and Constantius II to reunite East and West; the Easterners refused to sit with Athanasius, withdrew to Philippopolis and excommunicated Pope Julius. The Westerners' canons gave Rome a role in appeals by deposed bishops.

sites.name: Council of Sirmium (the "Blasphemy")
sites.summary: A small council with Constantius II present issued a creed forbidding the terms ousia, homoousios and homoiousios; Hilary called it the 'blasphemy'. Ossius of Corduba and Pope Liberius were pressured into signing.

sites.name: Council of Ariminum
sites.summary: Over 400 Western bishops, detained at Ariminum until they signed, accepted a Homoian creed ('the Son is like the Father'), prompting Jerome's line that 'the whole world groaned and was amazed to find itself Arian'.

sites.name: Council of Seleucia in Isauria
sites.summary: The Eastern half of Constantius' twin council, held from 27 September 359 with about 160 bishops, split between Homoiousians and Homoians; delegates were then made to sign the Homoian creed at Constantinople.

sites.name: Council of Alexandria
sites.summary: Athanasius, back under Julian's amnesty, held a small synod whose Tome to the Antiochenes accepted different terminologies for the Trinity, preparing the Nicene reconciliation of 381.

sites.name: Council of Laodicea
sites.summary: Phrygian synod of uncertain date (c. 363-364) whose 60 canons ban Christians from keeping the Jewish Sabbath, celebrating with Jews, and wearing amulets, and include an early list of canonical books.

sites.name: First Council of Constantinople
sites.summary: Theodosius I's council of about 150 Eastern bishops reaffirmed Nicaea against Arians and Pneumatomachians, produced (or endorsed) the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed, ranked Constantinople second after Rome, and saw Gregory of Nazianzus resign as bishop.

sites.name: Council of Aquileia
sites.summary: Ambrose, with Gratian's support, conducted a hostile examination of the Homoian bishops Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus of Singidunum and deposed them; the stenographic minutes survive.

sites.name: Council of Hippo
sites.summary: African plenary council at which Augustine, still a priest, spoke on the creed; it issued a list of canonical scriptures including the deuterocanonical books, reaffirmed at Carthage in 397.

sites.name: Synod of Isaac (Seleucia-Ctesiphon)
sites.summary: With Yazdegerd I's permission and the help of the Roman envoy Marutha of Maypherqat, the Persian bishops accepted Nicaea and organised the Church of the East under the catholicos Isaac, independent of Antioch.

sites.name: Conference of Carthage
sites.summary: Honorius' commissioner Marcellinus presided over a three-day hearing between 286 Catholic and 279 Donatist bishops, whose roll-call records over 400 African sees. He ruled for the Catholics, and the edict of 412 outlawed Donatism.

sites.name: Synod of Diospolis
sites.summary: Fourteen Palestinian bishops acquitted Pelagius of heresy after he disowned the propositions charged against him; Augustine and the African church responded by securing his condemnation by Pope Innocent I in 417.

sites.name: Council of Ephesus
sites.summary: Cyril of Alexandria opened the council on 22 June 431 before the Antiochene bishops arrived, deposed Nestorius and proclaimed Mary Theotokos; John of Antioch's rival assembly deposed Cyril. Theodosius II eventually sided with Cyril; the reunion formula of 433 patched the split.

sites.name: Second Council of Ephesus (Latrocinium)
sites.summary: Dioscorus of Alexandria, backed by Theodosius II, rehabilitated Eutyches and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died after rough handling; Leo I's Tome was not read. Leo called it a robbery (latrocinium).

sites.name: Council of Chalcedon
sites.summary: Marcian's council of some 370 bishops, met from 8 October 451 in the church of St Euphemia, deposed Dioscorus, accepted Leo's Tome and defined Christ 'in two natures'. Canon 28 gave Constantinople equal privileges with Rome. The definition split the Eastern churches permanently: Egypt and much of Syria and Armenia rejected it.

sites.name: Councils of Dvin
sites.summary: Armenian church councils at the Persian-Armenian capital: the first (505/506) condemned the Church of the East's Nestorianism and accepted Zeno's Henotikon; the second (554) broke with Chalcedon, separating the Armenian church from Constantinople.

sites.name: Council of Agde
sites.summary: Thirty-five bishops of Visigothic Gaul under Caesarius of Arles met with Alaric II's permission months before Vouillé; its 47 canons on clergy, church property and penance became a reference collection.

sites.name: First Council of Orléans
sites.summary: Clovis' council of 32 bishops of the Frankish kingdom, held weeks before his death, set rules for church asylum, the ordination of slaves and royal control over making clergy.

sites.name: Second Council of Constantinople
sites.summary: Justinian's council condemned the Three Chapters (Theodore of Mopsuestia and writings of Theodoret and Ibas) to placate anti-Chalcedonians. Pope Vigilius, held in Constantinople, first refused then submitted; northern Italian sees went into schism.

sites.name: Third Council of Toledo
sites.summary: King Reccared and his Gothic nobles renounced Arianism before 62 bishops on 8 May 589, unifying the Visigothic kingdom with its Hispano-Roman Catholic majority. The council's creed included the Filioque.

sites.name: Monastery of St Antony (Inner Mountain)
sites.summary: Antony (c. 251-356) withdrew to a fort at Pispir on the Nile and then to the 'Inner Mountain' near the Red Sea, where disciples settled around him. Athanasius' Life of Antony (c. 360), quickly translated into Latin, made him the model of the hermit and helped convert Augustine.

sites.name: Nitria
sites.summary: Founded by Amoun c. 325 at the edge of the natron desert. Palladius found some 5,000 monks living here c. 390, with seven bakeries, doctors and a church; whips hung from palm trees for punishing offenders. Rufinus, Melania the Elder and Evagrius all passed through.

sites.name: Kellia
sites.summary: 'The Cells', founded c. 338 by Amoun and Antony for monks wanting more solitude than Nitria offered; Evagrius Ponticus lived here 385-399. Excavations since 1964 have mapped over 1,500 hermitages across 100 km2.

sites.name: Scetis (Wadi Natrun)
sites.summary: Desert valley settled by Macarius the Egyptian c. 330, home of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum). Sacked by Mazices raiders in 407, 434 and 444. Four monasteries survive in continuous use.

sites.name: Tabennisi and Pbow (Pachomian koinonia)
sites.summary: Pachomius, a former conscript, founded the first communal monastery at Tabennisi c. 323 and the headquarters at Pbow; by his death in 346 there were nine houses with several thousand monks under a written rule, organised by trades, with twice-yearly assemblies. Jerome translated the rule in 404. The Nag Hammadi codices were found nearby.

sites.name: White Monastery (Atripe)
sites.summary: Shenoute of Atripe (abbot c. 385-465) ruled a federation of some 4,000 monks and nuns, built the great church of c. 440, and led raids smashing pagan shrines; his Coptic writings are the core of Coptic literature.

sites.name: Lérins
sites.summary: Island monastery founded by Honoratus c. 410, a nursery of bishops for 5th-century Gaul: Hilary and Caesarius of Arles, Eucherius of Lyon, Lupus of Troyes, Faustus of Riez. Vincent of Lérins wrote his Commonitorium (434) here.

sites.name: Ligugé
sites.summary: Martin, former cavalry officer, founded this hermitage near Poitiers c. 361 under Hilary's patronage, the earliest known monastery in Gaul.

sites.name: Marmoutier
sites.summary: Monastery founded by Martin across the Loire from Tours after he became bishop: some 80 monks lived in caves and wooden cells, with no property, eating together, and copying books.

sites.name: Saint-Victor, Marseille
sites.summary: Founded c. 415 by John Cassian, who had lived in Egypt; his Institutes and Conferences transmitted Egyptian monasticism to the West and were prescribed reading in Benedict's Rule.

sites.name: Condat (Saint-Claude)
sites.summary: Founded c. 435 in the Jura by the brothers Romanus and Lupicinus; the Life of the Jura Fathers describes a growing network of houses and a rule combining Eastern and Lérinian models.

sites.name: Agaune (Saint-Maurice)
sites.summary: Shrine of the Theban Legion, whose martyrdom under Maximian Eucherius of Lyon narrated c. 440. In 515 the Burgundian prince Sigismund founded a monastery with the laus perennis, continuous chant by rotating choirs, the oldest continuously occupied abbey in the West.

sites.name: Monte Cassino
sites.summary: Benedict of Nursia founded the monastery c. 529 on the site of a temple of Apollo and wrote his Rule here. Gregory the Great's Dialogues (Book 2) narrate his life. Lombards sacked it c. 577-581; the monks fled to Rome with the autograph Rule.

sites.name: Subiaco
sites.summary: Benedict lived as a hermit in a cave (Sacro Speco) near Nero's dammed lakes at Subiaco c. 500-529 and founded twelve small monasteries before moving to Monte Cassino.

sites.name: Vivarium
sites.summary: Cassiodorus, retired from Ostrogothic service, founded Vivarium on his estate at Squillace with fishponds, baths and a scriptorium. His Institutions laid out a programme of sacred and secular reading and copying that shaped monastic libraries; its books reached the Lateran and Bobbio.

sites.name: Castellum Lucullanum
sites.summary: Lucullus' old villa at Naples, where the deposed Romulus Augustulus was pensioned off in 476. Severinus of Noricum's body was brought here c. 492 and a monastery founded, where Eugippius wrote the Life of Severinus and compiled excerpts of Augustine.

sites.name: Mar Saba (Great Lavra)
sites.summary: Lavra founded in 483 by Sabas in the Kidron gorge; Sabas led the Palestinian monks in support of Chalcedon. Persian-era raiders killed 44 monks in 614. Cyril of Scythopolis wrote the Lives of the Palestinian monks.

sites.name: Monastery of St Catherine, Sinai
sites.summary: Justinian fortified the monastery at the Burning Bush between 548 and 565, as dated by inscriptions on the church roof beams; Egeria had visited monks here in 383/4. Its apse mosaic of the Transfiguration and the pre-iconoclast icons, including the Christ Pantokrator, are unique survivals.

sites.name: Mor Gabriel (Qartmin)
sites.summary: Syriac monastery in Tur Abdin founded in 397, said to have received endowments from Arcadius and Theodosius II; Anastasius funded its great church in 512. Still active.

sites.name: Iona
sites.summary: Founded by the Irish prince-monk Columba in 563; from here missions went to the Picts and, in 635, Aidan to Northumbria. Adomnán's Life of Columba (c. 700) describes the community.

sites.name: Whithorn (Candida Casa)
sites.summary: Bede says Ninian built a stone church here dedicated to Martin, called 'the white house'. The Latinus stone (c. 450) is the earliest Christian memorial in Scotland.

sites.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
sites.summary: Constantine ordered Hadrian's temple of Venus removed in 326 to expose the rock tomb of Christ, and built a basilica (the Martyrium) and the rotunda of the Anastasis, dedicated in 335. The legend of Helena's discovery of the True Cross appears by the 390s. Egeria (384) describes the liturgy; the Persians took the Cross in 614 and Heraclius restored it in 630.

sites.name: Abu Mena
sites.summary: Shrine of the soldier-martyr Menas in the Mareotis, which grew into a pilgrim town with a great basilica under Arcadius and Zeno, baths, inns, and workshops making the clay flasks for holy water stamped with Menas between two camels, found from Marseille to Britain.

sites.name: Tomb of Martin at Tours
sites.summary: Martin died in 397 and was buried outside Tours. Bishop Perpetuus built a large basilica c. 470; Clovis came here after Vouillé (507) and received the consular insignia. Gregory of Tours recorded hundreds of miracles at the tomb.

sites.name: Qal'at Sim'an
sites.summary: Simeon the Stylite lived on a column here from c. 423 until his death in 459, preaching to pilgrims from Gaul to Persia. Zeno's government built around the column a cross-shaped martyrium of four basilicas (c. 476-490), the largest church in the East before Hagia Sophia.

sites.name: Sergiopolis (Resafa)
sites.summary: Desert fort where the soldier-martyr Sergius was buried. Anastasius renamed it Sergiopolis and Justinian walled it; the saint was venerated by Arab tribes and by Khosrow II, who sent gold crosses after his restoration in 591.

sites.name: Hagios Demetrios, Thessalonica
sites.summary: Basilica of the city's soldier-saint, rebuilt after a fire c. 620. The Miracles of St Demetrius credit him with defending the city from the Avar and Slav sieges of 586 and 615-618.

sites.name: Basilica of St John, Ephesus
sites.summary: Shrine on the Ayasoluk hill over the tomb of John the Evangelist, rebuilt by Justinian and Theodora as a domed cross basilica. The Seven Sleepers' cave nearby drew pilgrims after their 'awakening' in the reign of Theodosius II.

sites.name: Shrine of Felix at Nola (Cimitile)
sites.summary: Paulinus, a senator and consul, gave away his fortune and settled at the tomb of the confessor Felix c. 395, building a basilica complex and writing annual poems on the saint's feast; bishop of Nola 409-431.

sites.name: Tomb of Peter (Vatican necropolis)
sites.summary: The presbyter Gaius (c. 200) said he could show 'the trophies of the apostles' on the Vatican and the Ostian Way; excavations of 1940-49 found a small aedicula of c. 160 in a pagan cemetery, over which Constantine built Old St Peter's by cutting into the hill.

sites.name: Catacomb of Callixtus
sites.summary: The first official cemetery of the Roman church, administered by the deacon Callixtus under Zephyrinus. Its 'Crypt of the Popes' holds the tombs of nine 3rd-century bishops; Pope Sixtus II, seized while preaching in a nearby cemetery and beheaded with four deacons in 258, was buried here. Damasus decorated it with verse inscriptions.

sites.name: Martyrs of Lyon
sites.summary: In 177 a mob and the governor tortured and killed about 48 Christians in the amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, including the slave Blandina, who outlasted everyone, the deacon Sanctus and the old bishop Pothinus; their ashes were thrown into the Rhône.

sites.name: Martyrdoms of Carthage (Perpetua, Cyprian)
sites.summary: The young noblewoman Perpetua, whose prison diary survives, and the slave Felicity died in the amphitheatre on 7 March 203 at games for Geta's birthday. Cyprian was beheaded at the Ager Sexti on 14 September 258; his Proconsular Acts record the trial.

sites.name: Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
sites.summary: Forty soldiers of legio XII Fulminata were left to freeze on a frozen lake near Sebaste c. 320 under Licinius. Basil and Gregory of Nyssa preached on them and their relics spread across the East.

sites.name: Shrine of Thecla, Seleucia (Meryemlik)
sites.summary: Cave shrine of Paul's legendary female disciple Thecla south of Seleucia, visited by Egeria in 384, who found monks and virgins there; Zeno built a great basilica in thanks for regaining his throne (476).

sites.name: Shrine of Cyrus and John at Menouthis
sites.summary: Cyril of Alexandria moved the relics of the martyrs Cyrus and John here c. 414 to supplant a popular healing shrine of Isis; Sophronius of Jerusalem later recorded 70 miracles. The site is now under Abukir Bay.

sites.name: Shrine of Alban at Verulamium
sites.summary: Britain's protomartyr, a citizen of Verulamium beheaded for sheltering a priest, under Decius or Diocletian. Germanus of Auxerre visited the tomb in 429; Gildas and Bede tell the story. The abbey stands on the hill of execution.

sites.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis
sites.summary: Genovefa built a church over Denis' tomb north of Paris c. 475; the Merovingian queen Arnegundis (d. c. 580) was buried there, and Dagobert I made it the royal abbey.

sites.name: Shrine of Eulalia at Emerita
sites.summary: The twelve-year-old Eulalia, burned in 304, became the patron of Lusitania; Prudentius wrote her hymn, and Hydatius credits her with the drowning of the Suevic king Hermigarius in the Guadiana after he insulted her in 429.

sites.name: Martyr cemetery of Manastirine, Salona
sites.summary: Cemetery outside Salona where Bishop Domnius and other Diocletianic martyrs were buried, the core of a basilica complex; the bishops of Salona were buried around them until the city fell to Avars and Slavs c. 614.

sites.name: Basilica of Crispina at Theveste
sites.summary: Crispina, a woman of Thagara, was beheaded at Theveste in December 304. A huge pilgrimage basilica with a monastery and hostels was built on her shrine in the late 4th century.

sites.name: Babylas at Daphne
sites.summary: Gallus Caesar moved the relics of Bishop Babylas (d. 250) to the grove of Apollo at Daphne c. 351. In 362 Julian had them removed because the oracle was silenced; days later the temple of Apollo burned, which pagans blamed on Christians and Christians on God.

sites.name: Wondrous Mountain of Simeon the Younger
sites.summary: Simeon Stylites the Younger stood on columns from childhood until 592; the monastery around his pillar southwest of Antioch drew pilgrims selling clay eulogia tokens stamped with his image.

sites.name: Edessa: Abgar's letter and the Mandylion
sites.summary: Egeria (384) was shown the gates through which Abgar's letter from Jesus had been carried, a letter that protected the city. Evagrius credits a miraculous image of Christ with saving Edessa from Khosrow I's siege of 544, the first mention of the Mandylion.

sites.name: Shrine of Julian at Brioude
sites.summary: Tomb of the soldier-martyr Julian, killed under Decius or Diocletian, Gaul's second shrine after Tours; the emperor Avitus was buried here in 456. Gregory of Tours wrote a book of his miracles.

sources.w: De passione et virtutibus sancti Iuliani

sites.name: Oracle of Apollo at Delphi
sites.summary: Rome consulted Delphi as early as the tradition of Tarquin's sons, and in 216 BC sent Fabius Pictor after Cannae. Sulla plundered its treasures in 86 BC. Plutarch, priest here c. 95-125, wrote on why the oracle now spoke in prose and had only one Pythia where once there were three. The Pythian games and oracle lingered into the 4th century; the 'last oracle' to Julian's physician Oribasius is probably a later Christian invention. Theodosian legislation of 391-392 closed it.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia
sites.summary: The games went on under Rome: Sulla moved the 175th Olympiad (80 BC) to Rome, and Nero competed in 67 in a special postponed festival, winning the chariot race despite falling out. The last attested victor is the Armenian boxer Varazdates (385). The traditional end of the games under Theodosius I in 393 is late and uncertain; a fire under Theodosius II (c. 426) is reported. Phidias' Zeus was taken to Constantinople, where it burned in the Lauseion fire of 475.

sites.name: Oracle of Apollo at Didyma
sites.summary: The colossal unfinished Hellenistic temple near Miletus. Caligula wanted to finish it for his own cult. In 303 Diocletian consulted the oracle, which replied that 'the just on earth' prevented true prophecy, a response that Constantine later remembered as the trigger of the Great Persecution. Julian made himself prophet of the shrine; Christian chapels were later built inside.

sites.name: Oracle of Apollo at Claros
sites.summary: Colophon's oracle, at its height in the 2nd century AD. The prophet drank from a sacred spring in an underground chamber beneath the temple; Tacitus tells of Germanicus' visit in AD 18 and the prediction of his early death. Inscriptions record delegations from cities as far as Britain and Dalmatia seeking verse oracles against the Antonine plague.
scholarship: Parke, The Oracles of Apollo in Asia Minor (1985)

sites.name: Sanctuary of Demeter at Eleusis
sites.summary: Home of the Mysteries, into which Romans eagerly sought initiation: Sulla, Cicero, Augustus (31 BC), Hadrian (124/5 and again as epoptes), Lucius Verus, Marcus Aurelius and Commodus (176). Marcus rebuilt the sanctuary after the Costoboci raid of 170. Valentinian I's ban on night rituals in 364 was waived for Eleusis by the proconsul Praetextatus. Eunapius says Alaric's Goths, guided by Christian monks, sacked it in 396.

sites.name: Oracle of Ammon at Siwa
sites.summary: The desert oracle that greeted Alexander as son of Zeus. By Strabo's day it was almost abandoned, he says, because the Romans preferred the Sibylline books and Etruscan haruspicy. Pausanias saw Pindar's hymn inscribed there. Siwa's Christianisation is obscure.

sites.name: Heliopolis (Baalbek) sanctuary
sites.summary: The largest temple complex of the Roman world, built over 150 years on a colony of Augustus: the Temple of Jupiter Heliopolitanus (begun late 1st century BC, finished under Nero), with 20 m columns resting on a podium including the Trilithon blocks of c. 800 tonnes, and the 2nd-century 'Temple of Bacchus'. Macrobius says Trajan tested the oracle by sending sealed blank tablets. Theodosius built a basilica in the great court.

sites.name: Artemision of Ephesus
sites.summary: One of the Seven Wonders, rebuilt after Herostratus' arson of 356 BC. Its right of asylum was confirmed by Caesar and Augustus, who limited its extent. Paul's preaching provoked the silversmiths' riot ('Great is Artemis of the Ephesians'). Goths sacked it c. 262. The temple was quarried in late antiquity; tradition, probably false, has its columns reused in Hagia Sophia.

sites.name: Pessinus, sanctuary of the Great Mother
sites.summary: Phrygian temple-state of Cybele and her galli. In 204 BC, following a Sibylline oracle, Rome obtained from Attalus I the goddess's black aniconic stone and brought it to the Palatine, received by Scipio Nasica as 'best man in Rome' and Claudia Quinta. Julian visited in 362 and wrote his hymn to the Mother of the Gods.

sites.name: Comana Pontica (Ma-Enyo)
sites.summary: Temple-state of the goddess Ma, with, Strabo says, over 6,000 temple servants and a priest second only to the king. Strabo's maternal kinsman Dorylaus held the priesthood under Mithridates VI; Pompey gave it to Archelaus, Caesar to Lycomedes. A festival city frequented by merchants and prostitutes, which Strabo compares to Corinth.

sites.name: Comana in Cappadocia
sites.summary: Original seat of Ma-Enyo, whose cult Sulla brought to Rome as Bellona. Strabo says the priest held power second to the king and the temple owned over 6,000 servants of both sexes.

sites.name: Temple of Atargatis at Hierapolis Bambyce
sites.summary: Temple of the Syrian Goddess described by Lucian (or his imitator) in De Dea Syria: eunuch galli who castrated themselves in ecstasy, sacred fish in the lake, and two phallic towers climbed twice a year. Crassus plundered the treasury in 54 BC before Carrhae.

sites.name: Temple of Elagabal at Emesa
sites.summary: Shrine of the sun god Elagabal, worshipped as a black conical stone, whose hereditary priests were the family of Julia Domna. The boy priest Varius Avitus became emperor in 218 and took the stone to Rome. Aurelian credited the god with his victory at Emesa over Zenobia in 272.

sites.name: Doliche (Jupiter Dolichenus)
sites.summary: Hilltop sanctuary of the Commagenian Baal on Dülük Baba Tepesi, origin of a cult spread by soldiers to the Rhine, Danube and Hadrian's Wall. Excavations since 2001 confirmed the temple, destroyed when Shapur I took Doliche c. 253, after which the cult faded in the West too.

sites.name: Temple of Jerusalem
sites.summary: The Second Temple, rebuilt from 520-515 BC. Pompey entered the Holy of Holies in 63 BC; Crassus robbed it in 54. Herod rebuilt it from 20/19 BC on a platform of 14 ha. Josephus says over a million died in the siege of 70, when Titus' troops burned the Temple on 9-10 Ab. Its menorah appears on the Arch of Titus, and the fiscus Iudaicus diverted the Temple tax to Jupiter Capitolinus. Julian's rebuilding attempt failed in 363.

sites.name: Temple of Onias at Leontopolis
sites.summary: Jewish temple founded c. 160 BC by the priest Onias IV in the nome of Heliopolis (Tell el-Yahudiya), with Ptolemaic consent. After the fall of Jerusalem, Vespasian ordered it closed in 73, fearing it would become a new focus of revolt.

sites.name: Mount Gerizim
sites.summary: Holy mountain of the Samaritans. Their temple was destroyed by John Hyrcanus c. 111/110 BC; Hadrian built a temple of Zeus Hypsistos. In 484, after a Samaritan revolt, Zeno built a church of the Theotokos on the summit; the great revolt of 529 under Justinian ended in massacre.

sites.name: Temple of Isis at Philae
sites.summary: The last functioning temple of the old Egyptian religion. A treaty of Diocletian allowed the Blemmyes and Nobades to worship here; the last hieroglyphic inscription is dated 24 August 394 and the last demotic graffito to 452. Procopius says Justinian ordered Narses to close it c. 535-537, imprison the priests and send the cult statues to Constantinople.

sites.name: Serapeum of Alexandria
sites.summary: Ptolemaic temple of Sarapis on its acropolis, holding Bryaxis' great statue and the 'daughter library'. In 391, after riots, Theophilus' Christians with imperial backing demolished it and smashed the statue: Rufinus describes the axe-blow and the mice running from the head. Its fall was a defining moment for both pagans and Christians.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis
sites.summary: Latin federal sanctuary on Lake Nemi, served by the rex Nemorensis, a runaway slave who won the office by killing his predecessor (the starting point of Frazer's Golden Bough). Caligula's two great ships were moored on the lake; recovered in 1929-32, they burned in 1944.

sites.name: Jupiter Latiaris on Mons Albanus
sites.summary: Summit of Monte Cavo, site of the Feriae Latinae, at which the consuls had to preside before leaving for their provinces. Generals refused a triumph in Rome could celebrate one here (first by Papirius Maso in 231 BC). The paved Via Sacra to the summit survives.

sites.name: Fanum Voltumnae
sites.summary: Federal sanctuary of the Twelve Etruscan Peoples near Volsinii, where they met in council and debated aid to Veii (Livy). Excavations at Campo della Fiera, Orvieto, since 2000 are the best candidate. Constantine's Hispellum rescript (333-337) allowed the Umbrians to hold their festival at home instead of at Volsinii.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia
sites.summary: Terraced sanctuary of the late 2nd century BC climbing the hillside of Praeneste, where oracular lots (sortes) carved on oak were drawn by a boy. Its Nile mosaic is the finest Hellenistic floor in Italy. Cicero mocks the lots; Tiberius tried and failed to suppress them, and Domitian consulted the goddess every year.

sites.name: Lavinium (Penates and Thirteen Altars)
sites.summary: Ritual centre of the Latins, where Rome's consuls and dictators sacrificed to the Penates and Vesta on entering office. The Thirteen Altars and the heroon claimed as Aeneas' tomb were excavated from 1955.

sites.name: Asclepieion of Epidaurus
sites.summary: Healing sanctuary of Asclepius. In 292 BC, during a plague, a Roman embassy brought back a sacred snake, which swam ashore on the Tiber Island where Asclepius' temple was built. Inscribed cure tablets record dream healings.

sites.name: Asclepieion of Pergamon
sites.summary: Rebuilt in the 2nd century with a round temple modelled on the Pantheon. Aelius Aristides spent years here as an incubant and recorded his dreams in the Sacred Tales; Galen trained here and treated gladiators. Caracalla visited for treatment in 214.

sites.name: Asclepieion of Cos
sites.summary: Terraced healing sanctuary near the home of the Hippocratic school. Claudius' doctor Gaius Stertinius Xenophon, a Coan (who Tacitus says helped poison him), got the island tax immunity in 53.

sites.name: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace
sites.summary: Mystery sanctuary of the Cabiri, whose initiation protected sailors. Perseus of Macedon fled here after Pydna in 168 BC and was captured. Romans traced their Penates to Samothrace; Germanicus tried to visit for initiation in AD 18 but was turned back by contrary winds.

sites.name: Oracle of Zeus at Dodona
sites.summary: The oldest Greek oracle, consulted by inscribed lead tablets. Sacked by Aetolians in 219 BC and devastated with the rest of Epirus in 167, when Aemilius Paullus enslaved 150,000 Epirotes; restored under Augustus.

sites.name: Temple of Aphrodite at Aphrodisias
sites.summary: City privileged by Octavian, who wrote that he had chosen it from all Asia; the archive wall preserves his letters. The temple of Aphrodite was converted into a church c. 500 by moving its columns outward, and the city was renamed Stauropolis.

sites.name: Plutonium of Hierapolis
sites.summary: Cave gate of Hades emitting lethal carbon dioxide. Strabo tested it with sparrows that died instantly, while castrated galli could enter unharmed; Dio says he tried it too. Rediscovered in 2013 with the temple, theatre seats and pool.

sites.name: Temple of Athena Ilias
sites.summary: Rome's claimed mother-city. Ilium got tax privileges after 190 BC and from Caesar, a supposed descendant of Aeneas. Fimbria sacked it in 85 BC, boasting he had taken in 11 days what Agamemnon needed 10 years for. Julian visited in 354 and found a bishop tending the pagan shrines.

sites.name: Oracle of Glycon at Abonuteichos
sites.summary: Alexander of Abonuteichos created the oracle of Glycon, a human-headed snake (a puppet, says Lucian), in the 150s. Its fame reached Rome: Marcus Aurelius followed its advice to throw two lions into the Danube, and the senator Rutilianus married Alexander's daughter. Coins of the town show Glycon into the 3rd century.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Aphrodite at Paphos
sites.summary: Aphrodite's birthplace sanctuary, worshipped as a conical stone. Titus visited in 69 on his way to Judaea and consulted the priest about his future; Tacitus describes the cult and the rule that no blood touched the altar.

sites.name: Temple of Bel, Palmyra
sites.summary: Dedicated on 6 April AD 32, the great temple of Palmyra's chief god combining Greek columns with a Near Eastern cella. Aurelian's troops looted it in 273 and he paid for its repair. Converted to a church, later a mosque; blown up by ISIS in 2015.

sites.name: Temple of the Moon at Carrhae (Harran)
sites.summary: Ancient centre of the moon god Sin. Caracalla was murdered on 8 April 217 riding from Edessa to the moon temple at Carrhae; Julian sacrificed there in 363. Harran stayed pagan beyond the end of Roman rule, its 'Sabians' surviving into the 11th century.

sites.name: Temple of Mercury on the Puy de Dôme
sites.summary: Mountain-top temple of Mercury Dumias of the Arverni. Pliny says the Greek sculptor Zenodorus spent ten years and 40 million sesterces making a colossal bronze Mercury for the Arverni before Nero summoned him to make the Colossus.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Apollo Grannus at Grand
sites.summary: Healing sanctuary in the Vosges, probably the 'most beautiful temple in the world' where, according to the panegyric of 310, Constantine saw Apollo and Victory offering him laurel wreaths promising 30 years of rule: the pagan precursor of his Christian vision of 312. Its astrological diptych of ivory survives.

sites.name: Fontes Sequanae (source of the Seine)
sites.summary: Healing spring of the goddess Sequana with a temple and portico. Over 200 wooden ex-votos of body parts and pilgrims, preserved in the mud, and a bronze of the goddess in a duck-shaped boat were excavated in 1963.

sites.name: Temple of Sulis Minerva, Bath
sites.summary: Temple and spa over the hot spring, built in the Flavian period. The sacred spring yielded 130 curse tablets asking the goddess to punish thieves of cloaks, rings and money, and around 12,000 coins.
scholarship: Tomlin, in Cunliffe (ed.), The Temple of Sulis Minerva at Bath II (1988)

sites.name: Temple of Nodens, Lydney Park
sites.summary: Late Roman healing sanctuary above the Severn with temple, guest-house, baths and long abaton for incubation, excavated by Mortimer and Tessa Wheeler in 1928-29, with J.R.R. Tolkien contributing a note on the name Nodens. A curse tablet asks Nodens to recover a stolen ring.

sites.name: Nehalennia sanctuaries (Domburg and Colijnsplaat)
sites.summary: Coastal temples of the goddess Nehalennia at the Scheldt mouth. Over 240 altars, dredged from the sea since 1970, were set up by traders in wine, salt, fish sauce and pottery crossing to Britain, thanking her for safe passage.

sites.name: Tophet of Carthage (Salammbô)
sites.summary: Precinct of Baal Hammon and Tanit with thousands of urns of infant and animal cremations under stelae. Whether they were child sacrifices, as Greek and Roman writers and the Hebrew Bible claim, or a cemetery for infants, is a long debate; recent analysis favours sacrifice. Saturn's cult continued the tradition under Rome.
sites.debate: Sacrifice (Stager, Xella et al. 2013) versus infant cemetery (Schwartz et al. 2010).

sites.name: Temple of Caelestis at Carthage
sites.summary: Temple of Juno Caelestis, Romanised Tanit, the chief goddess of African Carthage. Elagabalus brought her statue to Rome to marry Elagabal. Bishop Aurelius turned it into a church c. 399, and Quodvultdeus says it was razed in 421.

sites.name: Hispellum rescript
sites.summary: Constantine's rescript allowed the Umbrians to build a temple to the gens Flavia at Hispellum and hold their festival there, on condition that it was not polluted by 'the deceits of contagious superstition', meaning sacrifice. Imperial cult survived Christianisation as a civic honour.

sites.name: Temple of Augustus at Tarraco
sites.summary: In AD 15 Tiberius allowed the Spaniards to build a temple to Augustus at Tarraco, 'setting an example for all provinces'. Quintilian preserves Augustus' joke when told a palm had sprouted on his altar there: 'that shows how often you light it'. The provincial cult complex covered the upper town.

sites.name: Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum
sites.summary: Provincial cult centre of the Three Gauls at the confluence of Rhône and Saône, inaugurated by Drusus on 1 August 12 BC (or 10 BC). Each year delegates of the 60 Gallic civitates met in the concilium Galliarum and elected a priest. Its amphitheatre was the site of the martyrdom of Blandina and companions in 177.

sites.name: Ara Ubiorum (Cologne)
sites.summary: Altar of Rome and Augustus for Germania, founded as the counterpart of Lugdunum when the province was meant to reach the Elbe. In AD 9 its priest, the Cheruscan Segimundus, tore off his fillets and joined Arminius.

sites.name: Temple of Roma and Augustus at Pergamon
sites.summary: In 29 BC Octavian allowed the koinon of Asia to build him a temple at Pergamon (with Roma), and Bithynia one at Nicomedia, the first provincial imperial cult temples, for provincials only; Romans were to worship Roma and Divus Julius at Ephesus and Nicaea. The temple has not been securely located.

sites.name: Temple of Roma and Augustus at Nicomedia
sites.summary: Bithynia's provincial imperial cult temple, authorised together with Pergamon in 29 BC. Pliny the Younger, governing Bithynia c. 110, conducted the loyalty sacrifices that Christians refused, prompting his famous letter to Trajan.

sites.name: Temple of Augustus and Roma at Ancyra
sites.summary: Temple of the provincial cult of Galatia whose walls carry the best copy of Augustus' Res Gestae in Latin and Greek, discovered by Busbecq's party in 1555 and published by Mommsen. Later a church.

sites.name: Temple of Divus Claudius, Camulodunum
sites.summary: Temple of the deified Claudius in the veteran colony, built at the Britons' cost and seen as 'a citadel of eternal domination'. Boudica's rebels besieged the last defenders in it for two days in 60. Its podium vaults survive under Colchester Castle.

sites.name: Temple of Tiberius, Livia and the Senate at Smyrna
sites.summary: In AD 26 eleven cities of Asia competed before the Senate for the right to build a temple to Tiberius, Livia and the Senate; Smyrna won over Sardis by citing its ancient loyalty, including a temple to Roma in 195 BC.

sites.name: Temple of the Sebastoi, Ephesus
sites.summary: Ephesus' first provincial neokorate temple, dedicated in 89/90 to the Flavian emperors; a colossal head and forearm of Titus (or Domitian) survive. Neokoros ('temple warden') titles became prizes in the rivalry of Asian cities.

sites.name: Altar of the Numen of Augustus at Narbo
sites.summary: The plebs of Narbo vowed an altar to the numen of Augustus in AD 11; the inscription sets out the dates of annual sacrifices, including Augustus' birthday, and the rules modelled on the altar of Diana on the Aventine.

sites.name: Mithraea of Ostia
sites.summary: Ostia has around 18 known mithraea, the densest cluster anywhere. The Mithraeum of the Seven Spheres and the Mithraeum of Felicissimus, whose floor mosaic shows the symbols of the seven grades of initiation (Raven to Father), are key evidence for the cult's structure.
scholarship: Becatti, Scavi di Ostia II: I mitrei (1954)

sites.name: Mithraeum under San Clemente
sites.summary: Late 2nd-century mithraeum in a courtyard of a Roman house, beneath the 4th-century basilica of San Clemente. It preserves the cult relief of Mithras killing the bull and benches for the meal, overlaid by the Christian church in one of Rome's most vivid stratigraphies.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Santa Prisca
sites.summary: Aventine mithraeum with painted processions of the grades and verse inscriptions, one possibly dated by consuls to 202. The paintings were damaged in antiquity, perhaps by Christians.
scholarship: Vermaseren & van Essen, The Excavations in the Mithraeum of the Church of Santa Prisca (1965)

sites.name: Mithraeum at Carrawburgh (Brocolitia)
sites.summary: Small mithraeum outside the fort on Hadrian's Wall, with three altars dedicated by prefects of the First Cohort of Batavians. It was desecrated in the early 4th century, perhaps by Christians. The nearby well of Coventina yielded over 13,000 coins.

sites.name: London Mithraeum (Walbrook)
sites.summary: Mithraeum built c. 240 beside the Walbrook stream, found in 1954, when 30,000 people queued to see it. Its marble heads of Mithras, Serapis and Minerva were buried in the 4th century. Rebuilt on its original site beneath the Bloomberg building in 2017.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Dura-Europos
sites.summary: Founded c. 168 by Palmyrene archers of the Roman garrison and enlarged c. 240, with paintings of Mithras as a mounted hunter and of two Magi-like figures. Moved to Yale. With the synagogue and church it shows three religions within metres of each other.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Capua
sites.summary: Underground mithraeum with the best surviving fresco of the tauroctony and scenes of initiation (blindfolded initiates kneeling before a mystagogue).

sites.name: Carnuntum: the altar of 308
sites.summary: Carnuntum had several mithraea. At the conference of November 308, Diocletian, Galerius and Licinius restored a mithraeum and dedicated an altar to the Unconquered Sun Mithras, 'protector of their rule'.

sites.name: Mithraea of Poetovio
sites.summary: Five mithraea at the customs station of Poetovio, the first run by customs slaves of the portorium Illyricum, the third by soldiers of legions V Macedonica and XIII Gemina in Gallienus' reign.

sites.name: Mithraea of Nida (Heddernheim)
sites.summary: Civil settlement north of Frankfurt with at least four mithraea, one with a double-sided rotating relief, evidence of the cult's popularity in the Rhine provinces.

sites.name: Mithraeum of Huarte (Hawarte)
sites.summary: Mithraeum near Apamea with 4th-century paintings of Mithras fighting demons, found in 2000 beneath a church built over it, probably c. 400, a direct case of Christian supersession.

sites.name: Synagogue of Dura-Europos
sites.summary: House synagogue rebuilt in 244/245 with walls covered in biblical paintings (Moses, Exodus, Ezekiel's valley of bones), overturning the idea that Judaism banned figural art. It was buried in the rampart built against the Sasanian siege of 256, which preserved it. Now in Damascus.

sites.name: Synagogue of Sardis
sites.summary: The largest ancient synagogue known, a converted hall of the bath-gymnasium complex, 80 m long, with over 80 donor inscriptions, many by city councillors. It shows a wealthy, integrated Jewish community until the city's destruction in 616.

sites.name: Synagogue of Ostia
sites.summary: Found in 1961 near the ancient shore, the oldest synagogue building in Europe, with a 1st-century phase and a 4th-century Torah shrine; an inscription honours Mindius Faustus for the ark. Jews of Ostia served the port trade.

sites.name: Synagogue of Capernaum
sites.summary: Limestone synagogue of the 4th-5th century over a basalt 1st-century building, perhaps the synagogue where the Gospels place Jesus' teaching. Opposite it a church was built over the 'house of Peter'.

sites.name: Synagogue of Delos
sites.summary: Building near the shore identified as a synagogue of the 2nd-1st century BC, among the oldest in the diaspora; an inscription of Samaritans of Delos was found nearby.

sites.name: Synagogue of Gamla
sites.summary: One of the earliest synagogue buildings in the land of Israel, destroyed when Vespasian stormed Gamla in 67 after a siege; Josephus says 4,000 died and 5,000 threw themselves from the cliffs.

sites.name: Hammath Tiberias and the rabbinic academies
sites.summary: Synagogue with a 4th-century mosaic of the zodiac around Helios in his chariot. Tiberias was the seat of the Jewish patriarchate and the academy where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled c. 400.

sites.name: Synagogue of Beth Alpha
sites.summary: 6th-century synagogue mosaic signed by Marianos and his son Hanina, with the binding of Isaac, a zodiac and a Torah shrine, found by kibbutzniks in 1928.

sites.name: Sepphoris
sites.summary: Galilean city where Judah ha-Nasi completed the Mishnah c. 200. A 5th-century synagogue mosaic has a zodiac and the binding of Isaac; the 'Mona Lisa of Galilee' Dionysian mosaic shows a pagan elite alongside.

sites.name: Synagogue of Stobi
sites.summary: Inscription of Claudius Tiberius Polycharmus, 'father of the synagogue', who gave the ground floor of his house for the synagogue while keeping the upper floor for his family.

sites.name: Synagogue of Naro (Hammam Lif)
sites.summary: Synagogue near Carthage whose mosaic, found in 1883, has a Latin dedication by Juliana 'for her salvation', menorahs and marine scenes; part is in the Brooklyn Museum.

sites.name: Great Synagogue (Diplostoon) of Alexandria
sites.summary: Rabbinic sources describe a vast double-colonnaded synagogue where officials signalled the responses with flags. Philo records the attacks on the Alexandrian synagogues in 38. It was destroyed in the Diaspora revolt of 115-117.

sites.name: Christian house of Dura-Europos
sites.summary: The earliest securely identified church building: a house adapted c. 232 with a baptistery painted with the Good Shepherd, Adam and Eve, the healing of the paralytic, Christ walking on water and the women at the tomb. Buried in 256.

sites.name: Prayer hall of Kefar Othnay (Megiddo)
sites.summary: Christian prayer hall in a Roman army camp, found in 2005, with a mosaic of c. 230 naming 'the God Jesus Christ' and the donor Akeptous, and a centurion Gaianus who paid for the floor.

sites.name: Theodorian basilica of Aquileia
sites.summary: Twin halls built by Bishop Theodore (who signed at Arles in 314) with the largest early Christian floor mosaic in the West: Jonah, the Good Shepherd, donors' portraits and marine scenes, preserved beneath the medieval cathedral.

sites.name: Double cathedral of Trier
sites.summary: Twin basilicas built from c. 330 over a palace whose painted ceiling, perhaps showing Fausta or Helena, was smashed and buried. The core of the present cathedral is a 4th-century square hall.

sites.name: Lullingstone villa house-church
sites.summary: Upper room of a Kentish villa painted c. 350-370 with chi-rho monograms and praying figures (orantes), the earliest Christian wall painting in Britain.

sites.name: Hinton St Mary mosaic
sites.summary: 4th-century villa mosaic in Dorset with a bust of a man before a chi-rho, probably the earliest portrait of Christ in Britain, beside Bellerophon killing the Chimaera.

sites.name: Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
sites.summary: Built under Constantine c. 333 over the cave of the Nativity, with an octagon above the grotto; rebuilt under Justinian after the Samaritan revolt of 529. Jerome and Paula founded monasteries here in 386, where Jerome made the Vulgate.

sites.name: San Vitale, Ravenna
sites.summary: Octagonal church begun under Bishop Ecclesius and funded by the banker Julianus Argentarius, consecrated in 547 by Maximian. Its apse mosaics of Justinian and Theodora with their courts are the defining images of the reconquest.

sites.name: Sant'Apollinare in Classe
sites.summary: Basilica consecrated in 549, also funded by Julianus Argentarius, with an apse mosaic of St Apollinaris amid sheep and a jewelled cross in a starry sky.

sites.name: Etchmiadzin cathedral
sites.summary: Mother church of Armenia at Vagharshapat, by tradition founded by Gregory the Illuminator after Tiridates III's conversion (c. 301 or 314), rebuilt in 483/484. Armenia's adoption of Christianity probably preceded Constantine's.

sites.name: Svetitskhoveli, Mtskheta
sites.summary: Royal church of Iberia (eastern Georgia), traditionally founded after King Mirian's conversion by the captive woman Nino c. 330s, a story Rufinus heard from the Iberian prince Bacurius.

routes.name: Alexandria to Puteoli and Portus: the grain fleet
routes.days: 50-70 westbound against the etesian winds; 9-20 eastbound (record 6 days Messina strait to Alexandria)
routes.summary: The annona's lifeline. Ships of 340 tonnes and more (Lucian's Isis was about 55 m long, carrying grain for a year for Athens) left Alexandria in spring, beat north to Lycia (Paul's ship at Myra) and crept west along Crete before the open crossing to Sicily, reaching Puteoli, and after 64 Portus. Seneca describes Puteoli turning out for their topsails. Return voyages ran before the wind: Pliny records Galerius reaching Alexandria from the Sicilian strait in 7 days and Balbillus in 6. Claudius guaranteed shippers against storm losses and gave privileges to those building ships of 10,000 modii.
scholarship: Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World (1971)

routes.name: Alexandria to Constantinople grain run
routes.days: 15-25 northbound through the Aegean, subject to the Hellespont current
routes.summary: From 332 the Egyptian grain went to the New Rome; Justinian's Edict 13 fixes the quota at 8 million artabas (about 240,000 tonnes). Fleets wintered if delayed: Justinian built a granary on Tenedos so ships held up by the north wind at the Hellespont could unload. The Persian conquest of Egypt in 618-619 ended the free bread ration in Constantinople.

routes.name: Carthage to Portus: the African grain fleet
routes.days: 2-4 (Pliny: Ostia to Africa in 2 days)
routes.summary: The shortest of the annona runs. Josephus has Africa feeding Rome for eight months of the year. The navicularii of Africa had offices at Ostia's Piazzale delle Corporazioni. Gildo's revolt of 397-398 and the Vandal capture of Carthage in 439 showed how fragile Rome's dependence was.

routes.name: Italian wine to Gaul (Dressel 1)
routes.summary: In the late Republic tens of millions of Dressel 1 amphorae of Campanian and Etruscan wine went to Gaul via Massalia and Narbo, many on to the Atlantic by the Aude-Garonne route. Diodorus says the Gauls traded a slave for a jar of wine. Wrecks like the Grand Congloué and Madrague de Giens (c. 70-50 BC, 6,000-7,000 amphorae) map the trade.
scholarship: Tchernia, Le vin de l'Italie romaine (1986)
Tchernia, Pomey & Hesnard, L'épave romaine de la Madrague de Giens (1978)

routes.name: Narbo to Burdigala: the Gallic isthmus
routes.days: 8-12 by river and road
routes.summary: Strabo's isthmus: goods went up the Aude from Narbo, overland to Tolosa and down the Garonne to the Atlantic, avoiding the voyage around Spain. Toulouse's rivers yielded Dressel 1 amphorae by the thousand, and Tolosa's sacred gold (aurum Tolosanum) was what Caepio stole in 106 BC.

routes.name: Arelate and Narbo to Ostia
routes.days: 3-5 (Pliny: Ostia to Narbonensis in 3 days)
