routes.summary: Gaulish wine in Gauloise 4 amphorae, and goods brought down the Rhône, reached Ostia in a few days with the mistral behind them. The Arles-Rhône 3 barge and river guilds handled the transfer at Arelate. In 418 Honorius made Arles the seat of the council of the Seven Provinces partly because, as the edict says, everything the world produces came there by sea and river.

routes.name: Baetican oil to Rome
routes.days: 7-10 (Pliny: Gades to Ostia in 7 days)
routes.summary: Dressel 20 amphorae of oil, stamped at the kilns and labelled at Hispalis, went down the Baetis and along the Spanish coast to Portus, then up the Tiber to the Emporium, where the empties built Monte Testaccio. An alternative route ran through the Strait of Bonifacio. Under the Severans the trade became largely fiscal, managed by the prefect of the annona.

routes.name: The Atlantic route: Baetica to Britain and the Rhine
routes.summary: How Baetican oil reached the armies of Britain and the Rhine is debated: up the Rhône-Rhine corridor or round Iberia by sea. Wrecks and the lighthouse of Brigantium (Tower of Hercules, A Coruña, 2nd century) support an Atlantic leg, at least to Britain and the Rhine mouth.
routes.debate: Atlantic versus Rhône-Rhine supply of the northern armies (Remesal versus Carreras and others).

routes.name: Rhône-Saône-Moselle-Rhine corridor
routes.days: 30-45 upstream to the Rhine army; downstream much faster
routes.summary: The great internal artery of Gaul: Rhône barges to Lugdunum, the Saône to Cabillonum, a portage to the Moselle and down to the Rhine. In AD 58 the legate Lucius Antistius Vetus planned a canal linking Saône and Moselle so that ships could go from the Mediterranean to the North Sea; jealousy of the governor of Belgica stopped it. Guilds of nautae of the Rhône and Saône were among the richest men of Lugdunum.

routes.name: The Danube
routes.days: 40-60 upstream; c. 25 downstream from Regensburg to the delta
routes.summary: Frontier and highway, patrolled by the Pannonian and Moesian fleets. Tiberius' and Trajan's engineers cut a towpath into the cliffs of the Iron Gates (Tabula Traiana, AD 100) and a canal to bypass the cataracts (101); Apollodorus' bridge at Drobeta (105) was the longest of the ancient world. In late antiquity Valentinian I and Justinian rebuilt the river forts.

routes.name: Berenike to Muziris: the monsoon run
routes.days: 30 to Ocelis, then 40 across the open sea; return from December on the northeast monsoon
routes.summary: Pliny gives the itinerary: Coptos to Berenike in 12 days, then about 30 days to Ocelis or Cane, then 40 days with the Hippalus wind to Muziris, leaving in July and returning in December or January. He complains that India drains 50 million sesterces a year from the empire. The Muziris papyrus shows a single ship's cargo valued at nearly 7 million sesterces, on which the 25% import tax (tetarte) was paid at Alexandria.
scholarship: McLaughlin, Rome and the Distant East (2010)

routes.name: Myos Hormos to Barygaza along Arabia
routes.days: 60-90 including coastal stages
routes.summary: Strabo saw up to 120 ships a year leave Myos Hormos for India. The Periplus describes the route along the incense coast past Cane, the Gulf of Oman and across to Barygaza, where royal pilots met ships at the Narmada estuary and guided them through the tidal bore.

routes.name: Coptos to Myos Hormos desert road
routes.days: 6-7 by camel caravan, travelling at night
routes.summary: Road of about 180 km through the Wadi Hammamat with watered forts (hydreumata) every 30 km, guarded by soldiers; the ostraca from the forts record passes, rations and attacks by desert raiders. The Coptos tariff of AD 90 priced the passes.

routes.name: Coptos to Berenike desert road
routes.days: 12 (Pliny), by night stages
routes.summary: Pliny lists the water stations on the 257-mile road and says most travel was by night because of the heat. The forts of Didymoi and Dios have yielded thousands of ostraca on army logistics, prostitutes and escorts.

routes.name: The Nile: Alexandria to Coptos
routes.days: 12-20 upstream with the north wind; 8-12 downstream with the current
routes.summary: Grain moved down from the nomes to Alexandria by state barges; Indian cargoes moved down from Coptos. The north wind let boats sail upstream while the current carried them down. The canal from Schedia linked the Canopic branch to Alexandria, where every cargo paid duty.

routes.name: The Incense Road: Hadramawt to Gaza
routes.days: 65 stages (Pliny), about 70-90 days
routes.summary: Frankincense from Dhofar and the Hadramawt went by camel through Shabwa (where a tenth was taken for the god), Timna, Marib and Najran, up the Hijaz to Dedan and Hegra and through Nabataean Petra to Gaza. Pliny gives 65 camel stages from Thomna to Gaza and says the cost was multiplied by fees and payments at every stop. Aelius Gallus' expedition of 26-25 BC to seize the source failed.

routes.name: Palmyrene caravan route to the Gulf
routes.days: 30-40 across the desert and down the Euphrates
routes.summary: Palmyrene merchants organised caravans from the Euphrates to Vologesias and Spasinou Charax, where their agents shipped goods to India. Dozens of honorific inscriptions, dated 19-266, thank caravan leaders (synodiarchs) for protecting the convoys. Zenobia's revolt and Aurelian's sack of 273 ended the system.

routes.name: The Amber Road
routes.days: about 30 from Carnuntum to the Baltic
routes.summary: Baltic amber travelled from the Sambian coast up the Vistula and through Moravia to the Danube at Carnuntum and down to Aquileia, whose workshops carved it. Pliny records a Neronian expedition 600 miles from Carnuntum to the amber coast. Ptolemy names Calisia (Kalisz) on the route.

routes.name: Western Silk Road: Antioch to Bactra
routes.days: 150-200 from Antioch to Bactra
routes.summary: The Roman end of the overland silk trade, through Zeugma or Nisibis to Seleucia-Ctesiphon and the Iranian plateau, with the Parthians and then Sasanians as middlemen. Isidore of Charax listed the Parthian stations. After 298 trade with Persia was channelled through Nisibis; a law of 408/9 limited exchange to Nisibis, Callinicum and Artaxata. Justinian tried to bypass Persia via Aksum, and c. 552 monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople.

routes.name: Rome to Constantinople by the Via Appia, Traiana and Egnatia
routes.days: 25-35 for an official with the cursus publicus; couriers 10-14
routes.summary: The trunk route of the eastern empire: the Via Appia and Trajan's Via Traiana (109) to Brundisium, a day's crossing of the Adriatic to Dyrrachium, then the Via Egnatia (built c. 146-120 BC) across Macedonia and Thrace. The cursus publicus provided changes of animals every 8-12 miles and lodging every 25-35; normal official travel was about 50 Roman miles a day. Tiberius once covered 200 miles in a day and a night to reach his dying brother.

routes.name: Rome to Constantinople by the Danubian diagonal
routes.days: 30-40 for officials; Itinerarium Burdigalense counts about 1,300 Roman miles from Aquileia to Constantinople
routes.summary: The military highway of the late empire, linking Italy with the Danube capitals Sirmium, Naissus and Serdica. The Bordeaux pilgrim of 333 recorded every change station (mutatio) and night stop (mansio) along it. Constantius II, Julian and Theodosius moved armies along this road, and Attila's campaigns of 441-447 devastated it.

routes.name: Bosporan and Pontic grain to Constantinople
routes.summary: The northern Black Sea exported grain, salt fish and slaves through Panticapaeum and Chersonesus. Arrian's Periplus (c. 131) describes the coast for Hadrian. In late antiquity Chersonesus and the Bosporus remained imperial outposts supplying Constantinople.

routes.name: Gesoriacum to Rutupiae
routes.days: 1 (about 12 hours)
routes.summary: The standard crossing to Britain, used by Claudius' invasion fleet of 43 and the Classis Britannica. A monumental arch at Richborough greeted arrivals. Caligula's lighthouse at Boulogne and the pharos at Dover marked the route.

routes.name: British grain to the Rhine
routes.summary: Traders who sailed between the Rhine-Scheldt mouths and Britain set up altars to Nehalennia at Colijnsplaat and Domburg. In 359 Julian built 600 ships to carry British grain up the Rhine to feed the cities of Gaul devastated by the Alamanni.

routes.name: Puteoli to Delos: the Republican slave route
routes.summary: Italian negotiatores at Delos supplied the slaves that worked Italian estates; Lucilius called Puteoli a 'little Delos'. Strabo says the slave market of Delos could take in and dispatch 10,000 slaves in a day, fed by Cilician pirates. The trade collapsed after the sacks of 88 and 69 BC and Pompey's pirate war of 67.

routes.name: Luna to Portus: the marble ships
routes.summary: Carrara marble came down to the beach at Luna and was shipped on heavy lapidariae naves to Portus and up the Tiber to the marble wharf (Marmorata) below the Aventine, where unfinished blocks and columns were stockpiled.

routes.name: Proconnesus to Ravenna: prefabricated churches
routes.summary: Proconnesian capitals, column shafts, chancel screens and ambos were made in standard sizes and shipped as kits for churches across the Mediterranean; Ravenna's San Vitale and Sant'Apollinare in Classe used them, and the Marzamemi wreck off Sicily (6th century) carried a whole church's furnishings.
scholarship: Kapitän, The Church Wreck off Marzamemi (1969)

routes.name: Mons Claudianus to the Nile
routes.days: 5-7 hauling columns on wagons
routes.summary: Columns of up to 200 tonnes were hauled 120 km from the quarry to the Nile at Kaine on huge wagons pulled by teams of animals; a papyrus letter asks the prefect for fodder for the animals moving a 50-foot column. Then by river barge to Alexandria and by special ship to Portus.

routes.name: Via Hadriana: Antinoopolis to Berenike
routes.summary: Built by Hadrian in 137 from his new city of Antinoopolis to the Red Sea and south along the coast to Berenike, with cisterns, stations and forts, as its foundation inscription records.

sources.w: Inscriptiones Graecae ad res Romanas pertinentes

routes.name: Oea to Garama: the Garamantian road
routes.days: 30 (Ptolemy: Julius Maternus reached the Garamantes from Leptis)
routes.summary: Lucius Cornelius Balbus triumphed over the Garamantes in 19 BC; Septimius Flaccus and Julius Maternus later travelled from Leptis to Garama and beyond. Roman amphorae, glass and fine wares are found in Garamantian tombs, and the Garamantes supplied slaves and 'carbuncle' stones.

routes.name: The tin route: Ictis to Massalia
routes.days: about 30 overland from the Atlantic coast to the Rhône mouth (Diodorus)
routes.summary: Diodorus, drawing on Pytheas via Posidonius, says the Britons brought tin to the island of Ictis at low tide; merchants carried it to Gaul and then on horseback across the country in 30 days to the mouth of the Rhône and Massalia. Strabo mentions Corbilo on the Loire as an emporium. The route lost importance once Spanish tin and Roman Britain took over.

routes.name: Via Nova Traiana: Bostra to Aila
routes.summary: Paved road built in 111-114 by Claudius Severus after the annexation of Arabia, running 'from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea', as its milestones say. It channelled the incense trade and supplied the frontier forts.

routes.name: Trajan's Canal: the Nile to the Red Sea
routes.summary: The old pharaonic and Ptolemaic canal through the Wadi Tumilat and the Bitter Lakes was re-dug by Trajan from Babylon (Old Cairo) to Clysma. It was used in late antiquity and reopened by Amr ibn al-As c. 641-643 to ship Egyptian grain to Arabia.

routes.name: Up the Tiber: Portus to the Emporium
routes.days: 2-3 towed upstream (35 km)
routes.summary: Barges (naves caudicariae) were hauled upriver by teams of oxen and men along towpaths to the Emporium and Porticus Aemilia (193 BC) below the Aventine. Procopius describes the towpath still in use in 537, when Vitigis' Goths cut Rome off from Portus.

routes.name: Constantinople to Sicily and Rome by sea
routes.days: 20-40 westbound
routes.summary: The sea route that linked the two capitals: Belisarius' fleet of 533 took this way to Sicily and Africa, and Pope Vigilius was brought along it to Constantinople in 545-547. Procopius describes the 533 fleet's stops at Abydos, Methone and Zacynthus.

tours.title: How a city-state took Italy
tours.summary: From the expulsion of the kings to the first army sent outside Italy: how one Latin town out of dozens became master of the peninsula in 245 years, by war, colonies, roads and a uniquely flexible system of alliances.

stops.title: A middling city loses its kings
stops.text: Start here, on the Tiber ford, around 509 BC by the Varronian reckoning. Rome is already the largest city of Latium, perhaps 25,000 to 40,000 people, and its territory of roughly 800 square kilometres is about a third of Old Latium. The first treaty with Carthage, which Polybius copied from a bronze tablet, shows Rome speaking for the coastal towns of Ardea, Antium, Circeii and Tarracina. Now the Tarquins are driven out and replaced by two annually elected magistrates, and the enormous Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, one of the largest in the Mediterranean, is dedicated by a consul instead of a king. Keep that number in mind: two magistrates, one year. Rome will conquer Italy with commanders who change every twelve months, and its institutions will be shaped by that constraint at every step.

stops.title: Partners, not masters: the Latin treaty
stops.text: After the battle at Lake Regillus in 496, where legend put Castor and Pollux in the Roman line, Rome made peace with the Latin League. The Foedus Cassianum, inscribed on a bronze column that Cicero could still read in the Forum, promised peace 'as long as heaven and earth remain where they are', mutual military aid, and equal shares of booty. For a century Rome fought as one partner among many, against the Aequi on Mount Algidus and the Volsci in the southern hills, and new 'Latin colonies' were founded jointly. Notice the logic, because it never disappears: allies supplied soldiers, not tribute, and were paid in land and plunder. Rome's power would always be measured in men it could call to arms rather than in money it could collect.

stops.title: Veii: doubling the state
stops.text: Fifteen kilometres north of Rome stood Veii, an Etruscan city as large as Rome, which controlled the right bank of the Tiber and the salt road. The wars with Veii lasted most of the 5th century and ended, tradition says, with a ten-year siege modelled suspiciously on Troy. Livy has Camillus take the city through a tunnel and 'invite' Veii's goddess Juno Regina to a new temple on the Aventine. What is not legendary is the result: Rome annexed the whole territory, roughly doubling its land, and created four new voting tribes on it in 387. The long siege also forced a change that would matter for centuries: soldiers were paid a stipendium for the first time, so that citizen farmers could stay in the field through winter.

stops.title: The Gauls in the Forum
stops.text: Six years after Veii, a Gallic war band of Senones crushed the Roman army at the Allia on 18 July, a date kept as a day of ill omen for ever after. The city was sacked; only the Capitol held, saved in the story by Juno's sacred geese. The Gauls left after receiving a ransom of a thousand pounds of gold, with Brennus throwing his sword on the scales and saying 'vae victis'. Polybius dates the sack to 387/386. The damage was severe but brief, and the response was revealing. Within a decade Rome built a circuit wall of nearly 11 kilometres in tufa from the quarries of conquered Veii, enclosing about 426 hectares, the largest fortified city in Italy. Rome recovered faster than its neighbours, and the trauma of 390 made the Gauls Rome's nightmare for three centuries.

stops.title: The settlement of 338: a new kind of empire
stops.text: The Latins rose against Rome's growing dominance in 340 and lost. The peace of 338 is the single most important constitutional act in the conquest of Italy. Rome dissolved the Latin League and treated each city separately. Some, like Lanuvium, Aricia and Nomentum, were absorbed with full Roman citizenship. Others, like Tibur and Praeneste, stayed nominally independent allies bound to Rome alone, forbidden to trade or intermarry with one another. The Campanian cities received 'citizenship without the vote', a halfway status that gave Rome their soldiers. The bronze rams of Antium's warships were mounted on the speakers' platform in the Forum, which is why it was called the Rostra. Divide, bind each community separately, offer a ladder towards citizenship: that formula would carry Rome through the rest of Italy.

stops.title: Humiliation in the mountains
stops.text: Rome's next opponents were the Samnites, a federation of hill peoples in the central Apennines who were at least as numerous as the Romans. In 321 both consular armies marched into a defile near Caudium and found it blocked at both ends. Gavius Pontius let them go after they had passed under a yoke of spears, stripped to their tunics, leaving 600 knights as hostages. The Senate repudiated the treaty. The lesson was military and logistical: the old phalanx was useless in mountain valleys, and Roman armies needed bases. The more flexible manipular legion is usually dated to these wars, and Rome began to ring Samnium with fortified colonies, at Luceria in 314, Saticula, Interamna and later Venusia, each of several thousand settlers.

stops.title: The first great road
stops.text: In 312 the censor [[appius_claudius_caecus|Appius Claudius]] began two works that made the Roman way of conquest visible: Rome's first aqueduct, and a road 132 Roman miles long from the Porta Capena to Capua. The Via Appia ran straight across the Pontine marshes on embankments and was later extended to Beneventum, Venusia, Tarentum and Brundisium. It was a military artery, letting legions reach Campania in a week and supplying the colonies planted along it, but it also tied Campania, the richest region of Italy, to Rome. Watch the named roads on the map from here on: Via Valeria, Flaminia, Aurelia, Aemilia. Each was built to hold newly conquered ground, and almost every one carries the name of the magistrate who built it during his term of office.

stops.title: Sentinum: the battle for Italy
stops.text: In 295 the Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls finally combined against Rome. The decisive clash came at Sentinum in Umbria, with perhaps 36,000 Romans and allies against a still larger coalition, the largest battle yet fought in Italy. The Etruscans and Umbrians had been drawn off by a diversion, but the Gauls' chariots broke the Roman left. There the consul Publius Decius Mus, like his father in 340, performed the devotio: he dedicated himself and the enemy to the gods of the underworld and rode to his death in the Gallic ranks. Livy gives 25,000 enemy dead; the Greek historian Duris of Samos, writing within living memory, gave 100,000. After Sentinum no coalition could stop Rome from finishing the war, and the Samnites made peace in 290.

stops.title: Pyrrhus and the price of victory
stops.text: Tarentum, the richest Greek city of the south, invited the best general of the age to fight Rome. [[pyrrhus|Pyrrhus]] of Epirus landed with about 25,000 men and 20 elephants, the first the Romans had seen, and won at Heraclea in 280 and at Ausculum in 279. His losses at Ausculum gave the language 'Pyrrhic victory'. His envoy Cineas reported that the Senate was 'an assembly of kings' and that fighting Rome was like fighting a hydra, because the citizen levy simply replaced every army destroyed. When the Senate wavered, the old, blind Appius Claudius had himself carried into the Curia and declared that Rome would not negotiate while a foreign army stood in Italy. That refusal to accept a peace after a lost battle became a Roman principle.

stops.title: Beneventum: the south falls
stops.text: Pyrrhus spent three years in Sicily fighting Carthage and returned to Italy weakened. In 275 Manius Curius Dentatus met him near Maleventum in Samnium, and this time the elephants panicked and trampled their own side. Pyrrhus sailed home, and Rome renamed the place Beneventum, 'good result' instead of 'bad result', and settled a Latin colony there in 268. Tarentum surrendered in 272 with its Epirote garrison. Look at the map now: everything south of a line from Pisa to Ariminum belongs to a single system, about 150 communities bound to Rome by separate treaties. Ptolemy II of Egypt sent an embassy in 273 to establish friendly relations. The Hellenistic world had noticed that a new great power existed in the west.

stops.title: Across the strait
stops.text: In 264 a band of Campanian mercenaries who had seized Messina, the Mamertines, asked Rome for help against Syracuse and Carthage. Polybius says the Senate hesitated and the people, hoping for plunder, voted for war. For the first time a Roman army crossed the sea. Rome had no fleet, no provinces and no experience of overseas war, but it had the manpower of all Italy. Polybius' figures for 225 show what that meant: about 700,000 infantry and 70,000 cavalry liable for service among Romans and allies. The system built since 338, which turned defeated enemies into soldiers, was about to be tested against the richest state in the western Mediterranean. Continue with the tour 'Rome against Carthage'.

tours.title: Rome against Carthage
tours.summary: A century of war between the land power of Italy and the sea power of North Africa, from the first Roman fleet to the burning of Carthage.

stops.title: A fleet from nothing
stops.text: Four years into the war, Rome realised it could not take Sicily while Carthage ruled the sea. According to Polybius it built 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes in sixty days, copied from a Carthaginian warship that had run aground, and trained the rowers on benches set up on the beach. Knowing their crews could not out-manoeuvre the Carthaginians, the Romans fitted a boarding bridge with a spike, the corvus, which turned a sea battle into an infantry fight. At Mylae in 260 the consul Gaius Duilius captured or sank around 50 ships. He received the first naval triumph, a column decorated with the bronze rams of the captured ships in the Forum, and the lifelong right to be escorted home at night by a torch-bearer and a flute player.

stops.title: The largest sea battle of antiquity
stops.text: In 256 Rome went for Africa itself. Off Cape Ecnomus on the south coast of Sicily, 330 Roman ships carrying perhaps 140,000 men met 350 Carthaginian ships; by the number of men engaged it may be the largest naval battle ever fought. Rome won and the consul Regulus landed near Carthage, which sued for peace. Regulus offered terms so harsh that Carthage hired a Spartan mercenary, Xanthippus, who used elephants and cavalry to destroy the Roman army on the plain near Tunis in 255. Then the sea took its share: the fleet that evacuated the survivors was caught by a storm off Camarina, and Polybius says 284 of 364 ships were lost. Roman admirals lost more men to weather in this war than to the enemy.

stops.title: The Aegates: victory on borrowed money
stops.text: By 242 the treasury was empty and the war in Sicily was stalled around the Carthaginian strongholds of Lilybaeum and Drepana and Hamilcar Barca's mountain base at Eryx. Rich citizens lent the state the money for 200 new quinqueremes, built on a captured fast Rhodian design, to be repaid only if the war was won. In March 241 Lutatius Catulus caught a Carthaginian supply fleet off the Aegates islands, weighed down with grain for Hamilcar, and destroyed it. Carthage gave up Sicily and agreed to pay 3,200 talents over ten years. Sicily became Rome's first overseas province. Three years later, while Carthage fought its own mutinous mercenaries, Rome seized Sardinia too. Polybius thought that act of opportunism, more than anything, made a second war inevitable.

stops.title: Saguntum
stops.text: Carthage rebuilt its power in Spain. Hamilcar, his son-in-law Hasdrubal and then his son Hannibal turned the silver mines and peoples of the south into a Barcid kingdom, with New Carthage as its capital. A treaty of 226 fixed the Ebro as the limit of Carthaginian expansion, but Saguntum, south of the Ebro, had become a friend of Rome. In 219 Hannibal besieged it for eight months and took it. In 218 a Roman embassy in the Carthaginian senate made the famous gesture: its leader, a Fabius, held up a fold of his toga and said that in it he carried peace and war, and they could choose. The Carthaginians said he could give whichever he liked. He shook out war. The legal case on both sides has been argued ever since.

stops.title: Over the Alps
stops.text: Rome planned to fight in Spain and Africa. Hannibal took the war to Italy instead. He left New Carthage in spring 218 with, Polybius says, 90,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry and 37 elephants, crossed the Pyrenees, the Rhône and in October the Alps, losing men to Gallic ambushes, snow and falls on the icy descent. He reached the Po valley with 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, figures Polybius took from an inscription Hannibal himself set up at Cape Lacinium. Which pass he used is one of the oldest arguments in ancient history: Col de la Traversette, Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis and the Little St Bernard all have defenders. Turn on the campaign layer to follow his route, then watch what happened to the first Roman armies that met him.

stops.title: Trasimene: an army vanishes in the fog
stops.text: After beating the Romans at the Ticinus and the Trebia in 218, Hannibal crossed the Apennines through the flooded Arno marshes, losing an eye to infection. In June 217 the consul Gaius Flaminius followed him along the north shore of Lake Trasimene in the morning mist. Hannibal had hidden his whole army on the hills above the narrow road. About 15,000 Romans died, many driven into the lake, and Flaminius was killed by a Gallic horseman. Rome appointed a dictator, Quintus Fabius Maximus, who refused battle and shadowed Hannibal, wearing him down and protecting the allies. Romans called him Cunctator, the delayer, first as an insult and later as the highest praise. Ennius wrote that 'one man, by delaying, restored the state'.

stops.title: Cannae
stops.text: Impatient with delay, Rome raised the largest army in its history, eight double-strength legions and as many allies, perhaps 86,000 men, and sent both consuls against Hannibal in Apulia. On 2 August 216, near the village of Cannae on the Aufidus, Hannibal let his centre of Gauls and Spaniards fall back while his African infantry closed in from the flanks and his cavalry sealed the rear. Polybius says 70,000 Romans died; Livy gives 48,200. The consul Aemilius Paullus and some 80 senators were among them. It became the textbook double envelopment, studied by Schlieffen. Then look at what did not happen: Capua and much of the south went over to Hannibal, but not one Latin colony did. Rome refused to ransom its prisoners and kept fighting.

stops.title: Syracuse and the engineer
stops.text: Hiero II of Syracuse had been Rome's loyal ally for half a century. When he died in 215 the city went over to Carthage, and in 213 Marcus Claudius Marcellus attacked by land and sea. He met the most ingenious defence in ancient history. Archimedes' machines dropped stones on the ships, and his iron claw lifted their prows out of the water and dropped them. The famous burning mirrors are a much later legend. Marcellus took the city in 212 when the guards on the Epipolae plateau were drunk at a festival of Artemis; Archimedes, absorbed in a geometric problem, was killed by a soldier. Marcellus shipped the city's statues and paintings to Rome. Cato and Polybius saw the beginning of a fatal Roman taste for Greek art in that plunder.

stops.title: Scipio takes New Carthage
stops.text: After his father and uncle were killed in Spain in 211, the 25-year-old Publius Cornelius Scipio was given a proconsular command by the people although he had held no senior office. In 209 he marched on New Carthage, the Barcid capital, in a single dash. He knew from local fishermen that the lagoon behind the city became fordable when the evening wind drove the water out, and told his men Neptune had promised him help. While the walls were attacked from the isthmus, a party waded across the lagoon and found the wall unguarded. Scipio captured the arsenal, the mint, the treasury and the Spanish hostages, whom he sent home with gifts. The war in Spain turned, and at Ilipa in 206 Carthage lost the peninsula.

stops.title: The Metaurus: the march that saved Rome
stops.text: In 207 Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal crossed the Alps with a second army. His letter announcing the rendezvous was captured. The consul Gaius Claudius Nero, watching Hannibal in the south, did something no consul was supposed to do: he left his province without orders, took 7,000 picked men and marched north, perhaps 400 kilometres in about a week, while the towns along the road fed his men. He slipped into his colleague's camp at night. On the Metaurus river Hasdrubal realised from the doubled trumpet calls that both consuls faced him, tried to retreat and was trapped and killed. Nero rode back south and had Hasdrubal's head thrown in front of Hannibal's outposts. Hannibal is said to have recognised in it the fate of Carthage.

stops.title: Zama
stops.text: Scipio invaded Africa in 204, burned the Carthaginian camps, won the Numidian prince [[masinissa|Masinissa]] to his side and forced Carthage to recall Hannibal after fifteen years in Italy. They met near Zama in 202, the exact site still unknown. Hannibal opened with 80 elephants; Scipio arranged his maniples in columns with lanes for the beasts to run through. The battle was decided when Masinissa's and Laelius' cavalry returned to strike Hannibal's last line from behind. The peace of 201 left Carthage independent but harmless: 10,000 talents over fifty years, a fleet of only ten triremes, no war anywhere without Rome's permission. Rome kept Spain, which would cost it two centuries of fighting, and Scipio took the name Africanus.

stops.title: Carthago delenda est
stops.text: Carthage recovered so well that it offered to pay off its indemnity early. [[cato_the_elder|Cato]] ended every speech by saying that Carthage must be destroyed, and once showed the Senate fresh figs picked in Carthage three days before. When Carthage defended itself against Masinissa in 150, Rome declared war. The Carthaginians surrendered their weapons, 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults, and were then ordered to abandon their city and move ten miles from the sea. They refused and held out for three years. In spring 146 Scipio Aemilianus broke in and fought six days through the streets. About 50,000 survivors were sold. The territory became the province of Africa. The ploughing of the ruins with salt is a modern invention.

tours.title: Conquering the Greek East
tours.summary: How Rome, drawn across the Adriatic by Illyrian pirates, broke the Hellenistic kingdoms in seventy years and inherited Alexander's world.

stops.title: First steps across the Adriatic
stops.text: Rome's first military venture east of Italy was a police action. Illyrian ships under Queen [[teuta|Teuta]] were raiding Italian traders, and in 230 a Roman envoy was murdered. In 229 both consuls crossed the Adriatic with 200 ships and 22,000 men. Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus and the Illyrian tribes of the coast placed themselves under Roman protection. What happened next matters more than the fighting: Roman envoys travelled to the Aetolian and Achaean leagues, to Athens and to Corinth to explain the war, and Romans were admitted to the Isthmian Games in 228. For the Greeks, Rome had stepped onto their stage. For Philip V of Macedon, a Roman protectorate on his western coast was an intolerable intrusion.

stops.title: A treaty that shocked the Greeks
stops.text: When Philip V allied with Hannibal after Cannae, Rome fought him cheaply, by finding Greek allies. The treaty of 211 with the Aetolian League survives in part on a stone from Thyrrheion in Acarnania. Its terms were brutal: any city taken jointly would go to the Aetolians, but its movable property and people would go to Rome. The sack of Aegina in 210 showed what that meant, as its inhabitants were sold as slaves. Greek opinion never forgot it, and Polybius treats Roman conduct in this war as barbarous. The war ended with the Peace of Phoenice in 205, a draw that left Philip intact. Rome had learned that it could manage the Greek East through local allies who would ask it to intervene again.

stops.title: The legion meets the phalanx
stops.text: Rome went back to war with Philip in 200, scarcely recovered from Hannibal, at the request of Pergamon and Rhodes. The young consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus brought Philip to battle in 197 on the 'dog's head' hills of Thessaly, in fog. Polybius uses the battle to compare the two systems. On level ground the Macedonian phalanx, sixteen ranks deep with pikes over five metres long, was irresistible from the front. But it could not turn or cross broken ground. An unnamed military tribune took twenty maniples from the victorious Roman right and struck the advancing Macedonian right in the rear. The phalanx could not respond and was destroyed. Philip kept his throne but lost his fleet, his garrisons in Greece and his freedom to make war.

stops.title: The freedom of the Greeks
stops.text: At the Isthmian Games of 196, before a crowd from every Greek state, a herald read out the Senate's decision: the Greeks formerly ruled by Philip were to be free, without garrisons, without tribute, under their own laws. The crowd, Plutarch says, shouted so loudly that crows flying overhead fell dead. In 194 Flamininus withdrew every Roman soldier from Greece. This was not altruism. 'Freedom of the Greeks' was the standard slogan of Hellenistic kings, and Rome used it to deny Greece to Philip and to [[antiochus_iii|Antiochus III]]. It also created a world of cities that saw Rome as their patron and appealed to it in every dispute. Freedom granted by Rome could be defined, and withdrawn, by Rome.

stops.title: Magnesia: the Seleucid giant falls
stops.text: Antiochus III, who had marched to India and back, crossed to Greece in 192 at the invitation of the Aetolians. The Romans drove him out at Thermopylae, followed him into Asia, and in late 190 met him near Magnesia under Mount Sipylus. Lucius Scipio was the nominal commander, his brother Africanus the real adviser, and King Eumenes II of Pergamon the hero of the day. The Seleucid army, perhaps 70,000 strong with scythed chariots, war elephants and a phalanx of 16,000, was larger than the Roman force. Eumenes' cavalry and archers stampeded the chariots back into their own lines, and the phalanx, surrounded, was shot down. Antiochus' son Antiochus IV spent fourteen years as a hostage in Rome.

stops.title: Apamea: Asia Minor redrawn
stops.text: The peace signed at Apamea in Phrygia in 188 is one of the harshest of antiquity. Antiochus surrendered everything north of the Taurus mountains, paid 15,000 talents over twelve years, gave up his elephants and all but ten warships, and handed over twenty hostages. Rome took no territory. It gave the lands to its friends: most of western Asia Minor went to Pergamon, Lycia and Caria to Rhodes. This was the pattern for the next half-century: Rome won the war, then left behind client states, swollen by its gifts, which competed for its favour. The indemnity money began to flow into Rome; in 187 Manlius Vulso's army returned from Asia with, Livy complained, bronze couches, female lute players and the first professional cooks.

stops.title: Pydna: the end of Macedon
stops.text: Philip's son Perseus was a capable king who rebuilt Macedonian strength and popularity in Greece, and Rome decided to finish the kingdom. On 22 June 168, the day after a lunar eclipse that allows the date to be fixed, Lucius Aemilius Paullus met him at Pydna near Mount Olympus. Paullus later admitted that the advancing phalanx was the most frightening sight of his life. But on the uneven ground near the river the line opened gaps, Roman maniples worked into them, and in about an hour 20,000 Macedonians were dead. Perseus was led in Paullus' triumph and died in custody. Macedon was split into four republics forbidden to trade or intermarry with one another. The dynasty of Philip II and Alexander was over.

stops.title: The circle in the sand
stops.text: In the same summer, Antiochus IV invaded Ptolemaic Egypt and stood at Eleusis, a suburb of Alexandria, with the kingdom in his grasp. A Roman envoy, Gaius Popillius Laenas, met him there and handed him a tablet with the Senate's demand that he leave Egypt. When the king asked for time to consult his advisers, Popillius drew a circle around him in the sand with his vine stick and told him to answer before he stepped out of it. Antiochus agreed. The news of Pydna had arrived a few days before. Without a single Roman soldier present, the greatest king in Asia withdrew. Polybius, who tells the story, makes it the moment at which Roman power over the whole Mediterranean became plain to everyone.

stops.title: The year of terror
stops.text: After Pydna Rome changed tone. In 167 the Senate ordered Paullus to punish Epirus, which had sided with Perseus. In a single day his soldiers sacked seventy towns, and 150,000 people were sold into slavery, perhaps the largest single enslavement recorded in antiquity. Rhodes, which had tried to mediate, lost its territories in Asia and was ruined commercially when Rome made Delos a free port. A thousand leading Achaeans suspected of disloyalty were deported to Italy, among them [[polybius|Polybius]], who would spend seventeen years in Rome and write the history of how all this had happened. Booty from Macedon was so great that Roman citizens paid no direct tax, the tributum, from 167 until 43 BC.

stops.title: Corinth
stops.text: In 146 the Achaean League, misjudging both its strength and Roman patience, went to war against Rome over its right to coerce Sparta. The consul Lucius Mummius defeated the Achaeans at Leucopetra and entered Corinth, one of the richest cities in Greece. The men were killed, the women and children sold, and the city razed, in the same year as Carthage. Polybius, who arrived soon after, saw soldiers playing dice on famous paintings thrown on the ground. Mummius was so ignorant of art that he warned the shippers that if they lost the statues they would have to replace them with new ones. Macedonia became a province, Greece was placed under its governor, and Corinth stayed empty for a century until Caesar refounded it.

stops.title: A kingdom by will
stops.text: In 133 Attalus III of Pergamon died and left his kingdom to the Roman people. The motive is unclear: perhaps to forestall a civil war, perhaps because he expected Rome to take it anyway. Aristonicus, a claimant who promised freedom to slaves and the poor in a 'City of the Sun', resisted until 129. The province of Asia that followed was the richest Rome had acquired, and its revenues became a political prize at once. Tiberius Gracchus proposed to use the royal treasure to fund his land reform, and his brother Gaius later gave the collection of Asia's tithe to Roman tax-farming companies, the publicani. Their greed would make Rome hated across the Aegean, a hatred that exploded under Mithridates in 88.

stops.title: Pompey reorders the East
stops.text: The conquest ended with one man. Given extraordinary commands against the pirates in 67 and against Mithridates in 66, [[pompey|Pompey]] swept through the East, ended the Seleucid dynasty, took Jerusalem and entered the Holy of Holies, and in 63 redrew the map. New provinces of Bithynia-Pontus and Syria were created, Cilicia enlarged, and a ring of client kings, from Galatia to Judaea to Armenia, was bound to Rome and to Pompey personally. He claimed to have raised the annual revenues of the state from 50 to 85 million denarii. Egypt alone remained, nominally independent until Octavian took it in 30 BC. Alexander's world was now Rome's, and it had been won as much by Roman politicians competing for glory as by any plan.

tours.title: The fall of the Republic
tours.summary: A century of escalating violence, from the murder of a tribune in 133 to the battle that left one man in control of the Roman world.

stops.title: The first blood
stops.text: The empire had made Rome rich and its peasant soldiers poor. Long service abroad ruined small farms, the rich bought up or simply occupied public land worked by slaves, and the census showed fewer men qualified for the legions. In 133 the tribune [[tiberius_gracchus|Tiberius Gracchus]] passed a law to reclaim public land above 500 iugera and distribute it in small lots. To do it he deposed a fellow tribune who vetoed him, and proposed to use the Pergamene bequest to fund the scheme. When he stood for a second tribunate, his cousin Scipio Nasica, the chief priest, led senators armed with chair legs out of the Temple of Fides and clubbed him and about 300 supporters to death. It was the first political killing in Rome's assembly in nearly four centuries.

stops.title: Gaius Gracchus and the emergency decree
stops.text: Ten years later Tiberius' younger brother [[gaius_gracchus|Gaius]] came back with a full programme: subsidised grain for citizens, new colonies including one on the site of Carthage, roads, a jury law that gave the courts for extortion to the equestrian class, and a plan to give the Latins citizenship. When rioting broke out in 121, the Senate for the first time passed what came to be called the senatus consultum ultimum, urging the consul Opimius to see that the state came to no harm. Opimius attacked Gracchus' followers on the Aventine with archers from Crete. Gaius had a slave kill him in a sacred grove; his head was paid for with its weight in gold. Some 3,000 of his supporters were executed. Opimius then rebuilt the Temple of Concord.

stops.title: Marius opens the legions
stops.text: The war against Jugurtha in Numidia exposed the Senate as corrupt and incompetent; Jugurtha is supposed to have called Rome 'a city for sale'. In 107 the people elected a new man, Gaius Marius, consul and gave him the command by law, overriding the Senate. Marius enlisted volunteers from the capite censi, citizens too poor to meet the property qualification. It was not quite a revolution, since the qualification had been falling for a century, but it changed the relationship between soldier and state. Poor volunteers looked to their general for land when they were discharged, and generals needed political power to get it for them. Marius went on to destroy the Cimbri and Teutones and to hold five consecutive consulships, a thing without precedent.

stops.title: The allies revolt
stops.text: Rome's Italian allies had supplied half or more of its soldiers for two centuries without a vote in its decisions. When the tribune Livius Drusus, who promised them citizenship, was murdered in 91, the Marsi, Samnites and others rose. The war began at Asculum in Picenum, where the people killed a Roman praetor and every Roman in the town. The rebels founded a state called Italia, with a capital at Corfinium, a senate, consuls and coins showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf. It was a ferocious war fought between men trained in the same army. Rome won it by giving way: the lex Julia of 90 and later laws offered citizenship to all who stayed loyal or laid down their arms. Italy south of the Po became Roman.

stops.title: Sulla marches on Rome
stops.text: In 88 the consul [[sulla|Sulla]] was given the command against [[mithridates_vi|Mithridates]] of Pontus, who had just ordered the massacre of perhaps 80,000 Romans and Italians in the province of Asia. A tribune transferred the command to Marius by a vote of the people. Sulla went to his six legions in Campania, told them they would lose the rich eastern campaign, and marched them on Rome. All his officers but one quaestor refused to follow. It was the first time a Roman army had taken the city by force. Sulla outlawed Marius, passed his laws and left for Greece. The rule that had held since the kings, that armed soldiers did not enter the pomerium, was broken, and it would be broken again within a year.

stops.title: The proscriptions
stops.text: After three years in the East, Sulla came back and fought his way to Rome through a civil war that ended at the Colline Gate in November 82. He then did something new: he posted lists in the Forum of men who could be killed by anyone, with a reward of two talents, and whose property would be sold at auction. The sons and grandsons of the proscribed were barred from office. Perhaps 520 names appeared on the first lists, and thousands of men died before the killings stopped, many for their estates rather than their politics; the young [[crassus|Crassus]] made a fortune buying confiscated property. Sulla made himself dictator, enlarged the Senate to about 600, crippled the tribunate, and settled his veterans on land taken from Italian towns.

stops.title: Cicero and the conspirators
stops.text: In 63 the consul was [[cicero|Cicero]], a new man from Arpinum. His rival Catiline, a bankrupt patrician twice defeated at the polls, planned an armed rising with discontented veterans and the indebted. Cicero exposed him in the Senate with the speech that begins 'How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?' Five conspirators who stayed in Rome were arrested after envoys of the Allobroges handed over incriminating letters. On 5 December the Senate debated their fate. Caesar argued for life imprisonment; Cato for death. Cicero had them strangled that night in the Tullianum and announced 'vixerunt': they have lived. He called himself the saviour of the country, but executing citizens without trial would drive him into exile five years later.

stops.title: Three men and the state
stops.text: Pompey returned from the East in 62, disbanded his army, and found the Senate refusing to ratify his settlement or give his veterans land. Crassus wanted relief for the tax-farmers of Asia. [[julius_caesar|Caesar]] wanted a consulship and a great command. In 60 they made a private pact. As consul in 59 Caesar passed their programme by violence and ignored his colleague's religious obstruction, and the law of Vatinius gave him Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul for five years, with Transalpine Gaul added by the Senate. The scholar Varro called it 'Trikaranos', the three-headed monster. The triumvirate showed that three determined men with money, veterans and popularity could run Rome around the institutions.

stops.title: The Rubicon
stops.text: Caesar spent nine years conquering Gaul, gaining a battle-hardened army devoted to him, a fortune, and enemies in Rome who planned to prosecute him the moment he became a private citizen. Crassus died at Carrhae in 53, and Pompey drew closer to the Senate. In January 49 the Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army and passed the emergency decree against him. On the night of 10 January he crossed the Rubicon, the small river that marked the boundary of his province, with a single legion. Suetonius and Plutarch report the words 'the die is cast', which Plutarch says he spoke in Greek, quoting the playwright Menander. Pompey, with no army ready in Italy, abandoned Rome and then the peninsula.

stops.title: Pharsalus
stops.text: Caesar secured Spain, then crossed to Greece in winter, was nearly destroyed at Dyrrachium, and followed Pompey into Thessaly. On 9 August 48 at Pharsalus, Pompey had perhaps 45,000 infantry and 7,000 cavalry against Caesar's 22,000 and 1,000. Pompey planned to crush Caesar's right with his cavalry. Caesar had foreseen it and placed a fourth line of six cohorts behind his cavalry, with orders to strike upward at the riders' faces with their javelins. The cavalry fled and the Pompeian line was rolled up. Caesar, looking at the dead senators, said: 'They wanted it'. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on the beach. Caesar would win more battles at Thapsus and Munda, and be killed by his own senators on the Ides of March 44.

stops.title: The Ides of March
stops.text: Dictator for life from February 44, Caesar had reformed the calendar, enlarged the Senate to 900, planned a war against Parthia and filled the city with building projects. About sixty senators, led by Brutus and Cassius, many of them men he had pardoned, decided that the Republic could only be restored by killing him. On 15 March he was stabbed 23 times in the meeting hall of the Senate in Pompey's theatre complex, at the foot of Pompey's statue. The assassins had made no plan for what came next. Antony used Caesar's funeral to turn the crowd against them, and Caesar's will named as his heir an 18-year-old great-nephew, Gaius Octavius, who took the name Caesar at once.

stops.title: Actium
stops.text: The heirs of Caesar destroyed the assassins at Philippi in 42 and then turned on each other. Octavian held the West; Antony held the East, with Cleopatra as his partner and queen. Octavian made the war a crusade of Italy against a foreign queen. On 2 September 31, at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, Antony's fleet, blockaded and wasting from disease and desertion, tried to break out. Agrippa's lighter ships pressed it, and in the afternoon Cleopatra's squadron of sixty ships hoisted sail and broke through to the open sea; Antony followed. The rest of the fleet surrendered, and the land army went over to Octavian a week later. Both lovers killed themselves at Alexandria the following summer. Continue with 'Augustus builds an empire'.

tours.title: Augustus builds an empire
tours.summary: How Octavian, sole master of the Roman world at 33, turned a military dictatorship into a durable monarchy disguised as a restored Republic, and pushed the empire to the Danube, the Elbe and the Atlantic.

stops.title: The treasure of the Ptolemies
stops.text: Start in Alexandria in August 30 BC. With Antony and Cleopatra dead, Octavian took Egypt not as an ordinary province but as a personal possession. It was governed by an equestrian prefect, and no senator could enter it without his permission. Egypt's grain fed Rome for about four months of the year, and the treasury of the Ptolemies paid for everything that followed. Octavian used it to settle perhaps 120,000 veterans in colonies in Italy and the provinces, buying land instead of confiscating it as in 41. He also kept a standing army for the first time: 28 legions, about 150,000 citizen soldiers, with a similar number of auxiliaries. Interest rates in Rome reportedly fell from 12 to 4 per cent when the gold arrived.

stops.title: The Republic restored
stops.text: On 13 January 27 Octavian handed the state back to the Senate and people. The Senate immediately gave much of it back to him: a ten-year command over the provinces with armies, Spain, Gaul, Syria, Egypt, and on 16 January the name Augustus, 'the revered one', together with a golden shield listing his virtues and laurels for his door. The Senate kept the peaceful provinces, governed by proconsuls chosen by lot. Augustus remained consul every year. Contemporaries understood the reality perfectly well. The genius of the arrangement was that it allowed senators to keep their honours, their careers and their self-respect while one man controlled the armies, the money and the appointments that mattered.

stops.title: The last conquest of Spain
stops.text: Augustus went to Spain himself in 26 to finish a war begun two centuries earlier. The Cantabri and Astures of the northern mountains held out in hillforts like Aracillum, whose siege earthworks have been excavated near Reinosa. The emperor fell ill and retired to Tarraco, leaving the fighting to his legates; the war dragged on until Agrippa crushed the last revolt in 19, after troops in Spain had become so demoralised that he stripped a legion of its name. The reward was the gold of the northwest, worked on a colossal scale at mines like Las Médulas, where whole mountains were brought down by water channelled from the hills. Augusta Emerita was founded for the veterans in 25, and the peninsula was finally reorganised into three provinces.

stops.title: The settlement of 23
stops.text: In 23 Augustus nearly died of illness and handed his signet ring to Agrippa, and a conspiracy was uncovered among the elite. He responded with a second settlement that defined the principate for three centuries. He gave up the annual consulship, freeing a place for senators. In exchange he received tribunician power for life, which gave him the right to propose laws, veto any act and claim the tribunes' sacrosanctity, and a greater proconsular power (imperium maius) over all provincial governors. Emperors would count their years by tribunician power from now on, as you can see on their coins as TR P. It was a typically Augustan solution: no new office, just a combination of old powers held by one man without the offices that went with them.

stops.title: Victory without a battle
stops.text: During his eastern tour Augustus achieved the propaganda coup of his reign. Phraates IV of Parthia, facing a Roman army in Armenia under Tiberius and a rival claimant at Roman disposal, returned the legionary standards lost by Crassus at Carrhae in 53 and by Antony's generals, together with surviving prisoners. No battle was fought. Augustus celebrated it as if it were a conquest: coins showed a kneeling Parthian offering a standard, an arch was built in the Forum, and the breastplate of the Prima Porta statue shows the handover at its centre. The standards were later deposited in the temple of Mars Ultor. Rome and Parthia would compete for Armenia for centuries, but the Euphrates had been accepted as a practical border.

stops.title: A new age
stops.text: In June 17 Augustus held the Secular Games, a festival supposed to happen once every saeculum, the longest human lifespan, which the priests calculated at 110 years. The ritual protocol has survived in an inscription found by the Tiber in 1890. Over three nights and days there were sacrifices to the Moirai, to the goddesses of childbirth, to Mother Earth, and then to Jupiter, Juno, Apollo and Diana. On the last day a chorus of 27 boys and 27 girls sang a hymn written for the occasion by Horace, the Carmen Saeculare, which survives. It marked the start of a new golden age, and it came a year after the Julian laws on marriage and adultery, which penalised the unmarried and childless among the upper classes.

stops.title: To the Danube
stops.text: Augustus' stepsons Tiberius and Drusus completed the conquest of the Alps in a single campaign in 15. Drusus came up the Adige valley from Italy, Tiberius from Gaul via Lake Constance, where he fought a naval battle; together they reached the upper Danube. The trophy at La Turbie above Monaco, erected in 7-6 BC, lists 45 Alpine peoples conquered. For the first time land communication between Italy and Gaul and the Danube lands was secure. In the following years Tiberius conquered Pannonia, and Drusus led armies from the Rhine as far as the Elbe, where he died in 9 BC after a fall from his horse. A province between the Rhine and the Elbe seemed only a matter of time.

stops.title: The altar of peace
stops.text: When Augustus returned from Gaul and Spain in 13 BC, the Senate voted an altar to the Augustan Peace on the Campus Martius; it was dedicated on 30 January 9 BC. Its marble screens are the most sophisticated statement of the new order. A procession of the imperial family moves along the sides, Agrippa, Livia, the children; this is the first time Roman state art shows children and women of a ruling house. On the front panels, a goddess, perhaps Tellus, Italia or Pax, nurses twins among plants and animals, and Aeneas sacrifices on arriving in Latium. The lower register is covered with acanthus scrolls full of insects, lizards and birds. The altar was rebuilt in the 1930s from fragments, some recovered from beneath a palazzo.

stops.title: The Forum of Augustus
stops.text: On 5 February 2 BC Augustus was named 'father of his country', and in the same year he dedicated his forum and the Temple of Mars Ultor, vowed forty years earlier at Philippi. The forum, closed by a firewall 30 metres high, was a lesson in history. In the exedrae stood statues of Aeneas and the Alban kings on one side, Romulus and the great men of the Republic on the other, each with an inscription describing his career, and in the centre a four-horse chariot dedicated to Augustus. The message was that Augustus was the culmination of Roman history. Here the Senate met to decide on war and triumphs, and boys put on the toga of manhood. Augustus' own grandsons and heirs were dead within six years.

stops.title: Paying for the army
stops.text: The great unsolved problem was money for veterans. After 13 BC soldiers received cash instead of land, and in AD 6 Augustus created a military treasury, the aerarium militare, starting it with 170 million sesterces of his own. It was funded thereafter by a 5 per cent tax on inheritances and a 1 per cent tax on auction sales, paid by Roman citizens, who had paid no direct tax since 167 BC. Service was fixed at sixteen, then twenty years for legionaries, with a discharge bonus of 12,000 sesterces. The army was now a professional standing force, recruited increasingly in the provinces. That same year a revolt broke out in Pannonia and Illyricum that took three years and half the army to suppress.

stops.title: Varus, give me back my legions
stops.text: In September AD 9, Publius Quinctilius Varus, governor of the new territory between the Rhine and the Elbe, was led into a trap by [[arminius|Arminius]], a Cheruscan prince who held Roman citizenship and equestrian rank. Over several days of rain, on forest tracks and along a turf rampart at the foot of the Kalkriese hill, three legions, the XVII, XVIII and XIX, with six cohorts and three cavalry wings were destroyed. Their numbers were never used again. Suetonius says Augustus beat his head against a door, crying 'Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!' Germanicus avenged the defeat in AD 14-16, but Rome never again tried to rule east of the Rhine. Augustus advised his successor to keep the empire within its existing bounds.

stops.title: The record of his achievements
stops.text: Augustus died at Nola on 19 August AD 14, a month short of 76. His last words to his friends, according to Suetonius, were a line from a comedy: if he had played his part well, they should applaud. He left a text to be inscribed on bronze pillars in front of his mausoleum, the Res Gestae, 'things accomplished'. The best surviving copy is on the temple of Rome and Augustus in Ancyra, in Latin and Greek. It lists his honours, his donations, his building and his conquests, and ends with the claim that after 27 BC he 'excelled all in authority, but had no more power than his colleagues in each office'. It is the most brilliant piece of political misdirection in Roman history. His successor, Tiberius, was already in power.

tours.title: Life on the frontier
tours.summary: Soldiers, walls, letters and sieges: what it meant to garrison the edge of the Roman world, from the mutinies of AD 14 to Diocletian's eastern forts.

stops.title: The soldiers' complaint
stops.text: When Augustus died, the three legions in summer camp in Pannonia mutinied. Tacitus gives their spokesman, a former theatre claqueur named Percennius, a speech that is our best summary of a soldier's grievances. Men were kept thirty or forty years under the standards, many maimed, and discharged to swampy or mountain land. Pay was ten asses a day, out of which they bought their clothing, weapons and tents, and bribed centurions for leave. One centurion was nicknamed 'Bring me another' for the vine sticks he broke on soldiers' backs. The German legions mutinied too. The mutiny in Pannonia collapsed when a lunar eclipse frightened the men. The crisis shows the frontier army as a community with its own interests, and a power emperors would always have to buy.

stops.title: Revolt on the Rhine
stops.text: In the civil wars of 69 the Rhine frontier collapsed from within. Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and commander of auxiliaries, led his people and their neighbours in revolt. The Batavians, a small tribe in the Rhine delta, paid no taxes but supplied about 5,000 men to the Roman army, including the emperor's mounted bodyguard; they knew the army from the inside. Two understrength legions held out in the fortress of Vetera near Xanten through the winter, eating their horses and mules, before surrendering in March 70; they were massacred after leaving the camp. Other legions swore allegiance to an 'empire of the Gauls'. The lesson Rome drew was to stop stationing auxiliary units in their homelands and to keep legions apart.

stops.title: At the end of the world
stops.text: In 83 the governor Agricola, Tacitus' father-in-law, brought the Caledonians to battle at Mons Graupius, somewhere in northeast Scotland, possibly near Bennachie. Tacitus gives the Caledonian leader Calgacus the most famous anti-Roman speech in Latin: 'they make a desert and call it peace'. Note how the battle was fought. Agricola placed his 8,000 auxiliary infantry in front and kept the legions in reserve behind the line: 'a great glory if the victory could be won without shedding Roman blood'. Batavian and Tungrian cohorts fought their way uphill with short swords. Tacitus claims 10,000 Caledonians killed for 360 Romans. Agricola's fleet sailed around the north of Scotland, proving Britain an island. Within four years most of Scotland was given up.

stops.title: A fortress left unfinished
stops.text: At Inchtuthil on the Tay, legio XX began a full legionary fortress of about 22 hectares around 82-83, with barracks for a whole legion, a hospital, workshops and granaries, but no headquarters building yet. Around 87, before it was finished, troops were withdrawn from Britain for the Danube wars of Domitian, and the fortress was dismantled. The army left nothing useful to the enemy. Excavators in the 1950s found a pit containing about 875,000 iron nails, around ten tonnes, buried deep so the Caledonians could not forge them into weapons. The nails, the largest over 35 cm long, were sold to the public and are now in museums around the world. Inchtuthil shows how fast frontier policy could change when the emperor needed soldiers elsewhere.

stops.title: Letters from Vindolanda
stops.text: At the fort of Vindolanda, south of the later Wall, waterlogged rubbish preserved hundreds of wooden writing tablets from about 90 to 120. They are the most intimate source for life on any Roman frontier. Claudia Severa, wife of a fort commander, invites her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday, adding in her own hand the earliest known writing in Latin by a woman. Someone sends socks, two pairs of sandals and underpants. A merchant complains that he was beaten. Officers order beer for the men. An intelligence report notes that the Britons, whom it calls 'Brittunculi', little Brits, fight without armour and the cavalry do not use swords. A strength report shows that of 752 men of the First Cohort of Tungrians only 296 were present.

stops.title: A bridge over the Danube
stops.text: For his second war against Decebalus, Trajan had his architect Apollodorus of Damascus build a bridge across the Danube at Drobeta, below the Iron Gates. It had twenty masonry piers carrying a timber superstructure over a river more than a kilometre wide, and was the longest arch bridge in the world for a thousand years. Cassius Dio, who saw the piers, could hardly believe it had been built. In the gorge upstream, a road was cut into the cliff face and carried on cantilevered beams, and the Tabula Traiana inscription still records it, moved above the waters of a modern dam. Trajan's Column shows the bridge in the background of a sacrifice. Hadrian reportedly removed the superstructure to stop barbarians using it.

stops.title: The desert frontier
stops.text: In 106, while Trajan finished off Dacia, the governor of Syria annexed the Nabataean kingdom with almost no fighting. The new province of Arabia was garrisoned by legio III Cyrenaica at Bostra, and between 111 and 114 the governor built the Via Nova Traiana, as its milestones proclaim, 'from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea', from Bostra to Aila on the Gulf of Aqaba. This frontier did not face an organised enemy across a river. It watched nomads, protected caravan routes and water sources, and collected customs. Papyri from soldiers in Arabia survive: one, Julius Apollinaris, writes home in 107 that he has a cushy job as a clerk in headquarters while others cut stones all day.

stops.title: The Wall
stops.text: Hadrian visited Britain in 122 and, in the words of his biographer, 'was the first to build a wall, 80 miles long, to separate Romans from barbarians'. The first plan was a stone wall 10 Roman feet wide from Newcastle to the Irthing, a turf wall beyond it to the Solway, with a small fort every Roman mile and two turrets between. The forts for whole units were added on the line only later, and the plan was changed several times. South of the wall ran the Vallum, a ditch with mounds, marking a military zone. The Wall was a barrier with gates, a way of controlling movement and taxing trade, rather than a fighting platform. Three legions built it, and their building stones still carry the names of their centuries.

stops.title: The emperor inspects the troops
stops.text: On 1 July 128 Hadrian watched the exercises of legio III Augusta and its auxiliaries at Lambaesis in Numidia. His speeches, inscribed on a monument on the parade ground, survive in part, and they read like the remarks of a demanding drill instructor. He praises the legion for its performance although one cohort is detached and the unit sends men every year to other legions. He criticises cavalry for chasing too fast and failing to keep formation. He compliments one unit for building in a single day a stone wall that would normally take much longer. Hadrian made a cult of discipline: Dio says he inspected weapons, food and the soldiers' private lives. Lambaesis became the permanent base of the African legion and the capital of Numidia.

stops.title: The turf wall in Scotland
stops.text: Antoninus Pius, who never left Italy as emperor, still wanted a military victory, and in 142 his governor Lollius Urbicus advanced into Scotland and built a new wall between the Forth and the Clyde, about 40 Roman miles long. It was made of turf on a stone base, with forts much closer together than on Hadrian's Wall. The legions that built it set up 'distance slabs' recording the length each had completed, carved with scenes of victory and sacrifice; about twenty are known, most in the Hunterian Museum in Glasgow. The Antonine Wall was held for barely twenty years before the army returned to Hadrian's line, around 160. Pius took the title imperator for the campaign, the only time in his reign.

stops.title: Dura-Europos: a siege frozen in time
stops.text: Dura-Europos on the Euphrates was a frontier town of the Roman East, garrisoned by the Cohors XX Palmyrenorum, whose duty rosters and records survive on papyrus. Around 256 the Sasanian Persians besieged it. To strengthen the walls, the defenders filled the streets behind them with earth, burying houses, a church with the earliest datable Christian paintings, a synagogue with painted walls of biblical scenes, and a Mithraeum. The Persians dug mines under the walls; the Romans dug countermines. In one tunnel archaeologists found about twenty Roman soldiers and one Persian, and the evidence suggests that the Persians burned bitumen and sulphur to fill the tunnel with toxic smoke: possibly the earliest archaeological evidence of chemical warfare. The town fell and was never reoccupied.

stops.title: Diocletian's eastern road
stops.text: After the crisis of the third century, Diocletian rebuilt the eastern frontier on a new plan. The Strata Diocletiana was a military road running from the Euphrates through Palmyra to Damascus and south to Arabia, lined with forts about a day's march apart, many of them square enclosures of around 50 to 70 metres with corner towers. Legions were now smaller, perhaps 1,000 to 2,000 men, and the army had grown much larger overall. Soldiers on such frontiers were increasingly settled troops, the limitanei, with families and land around the forts. At Palmyra a legion camp was built over part of Zenobia's city. Many of these forts are still visible in the Syrian and Jordanian desert, like Qasr Bshir, whose building inscription dates it to 293-305.

tours.title: The empire at its height (AD 117)
tours.summary: Trajan's reign and the year of his death: the largest extent the empire ever reached, what held it together, and why his successor gave part of it back at once.

stops.title: Feeding the children of Italy
stops.text: Start in an Italian country town. Trajan expanded a scheme begun by Nerva, the alimenta, under which the state lent money to Italian landowners at about 5 per cent interest, secured on their estates, and the interest paid monthly allowances to poor children. The great bronze tablet from Veleia near Piacenza, the largest Latin inscription on bronze to survive, lists 51 mortgaged estates and payments for 263 boys and 35 girls; boys got 16 sesterces a month, girls 12. Historians argue whether the aim was charity, raising future soldiers, or propping up Italian agriculture against provincial competition. Either way it is a sign of the confidence and the paternalism of the age. Trajan was awarded the title Optimus, 'the best', by the Senate in 114.

stops.title: Dacia: the last great conquest
stops.text: Trajan fought two wars against the Dacian king [[decebalus|Decebalus]], in 101-102 and 105-106. In 106 the royal capital of Sarmizegetusa in the Orăştie mountains fell, Decebalus cut his own throat to avoid capture, and his head was displayed on the steps of the Capitol. A treasure the king had hidden under the bed of a diverted river was betrayed to the Romans; the Byzantine writer Lydus, quoting Trajan's doctor Crito, claims five million pounds of gold and ten million of silver, certainly a gross exaggeration. Dacia became a province, garrisoned by legions at Apulum and colonised by settlers 'from the whole Roman world', according to Eutropius. The gold mines of the Apuseni mountains were run by Dalmatian miners, whose wax tablets survive at Alburnus Maior.

stops.title: A governor writes to the emperor
stops.text: Around 110 Trajan sent the senator Pliny the Younger to sort out the finances of Bithynia and Pontus. The 120 letters between the two in Book 10 of Pliny's correspondence are the best evidence for how the empire was actually run. Pliny asks whether Nicomedia may form a fire brigade of 150 men (no: such clubs become political), how to finish a theatre at Nicaea that is already cracking, whether a canal can be dug to the sea, and what to do with Christians denounced to him. Trajan's replies are brisk: do not hunt Christians, ignore anonymous accusations, but punish those who refuse to sacrifice. The letters show a governor with few staff, cities competing in expensive buildings, and an emperor expected to decide everything.

stops.title: The Forum of Trajan
stops.text: With the spoils of Dacia, Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus built the last and largest of the imperial fora, cutting away the saddle of land between the Capitol and the Quirinal. It contained a colonnaded square with a gilded equestrian statue of Trajan, the Basilica Ulpia, the largest basilica in Rome, two libraries, one Greek and one Latin, and, beyond, the Column. On the hillside behind rose Trajan's Markets, a terraced complex of about 150 rooms used for offices and shops. When the emperor Constantius II visited Rome in 357, Ammianus says, he was struck dumb by the Forum of Trajan, 'a construction unique under the heavens', and said all he could copy was the horse.

stops.title: A war in a spiral
stops.text: Dedicated in May 113, the column is 100 Roman feet high and its height marked how much of the hill had been cut away. A frieze about 200 metres long winds 23 times around it, with some 2,500 figures narrating the Dacian wars: river crossings, fort building, the emperor addressing troops, sacrifices, Dacian women torturing prisoners, the suicide of Decebalus. The soldiers spend more time building than fighting. The reliefs were originally painted and probably impossible to read from the ground beyond the lowest turns, which has led scholars to debate who they were meant for. Trajan's ashes were placed in the base in a golden urn. A statue of Saint Peter has stood on top since 1587.

stops.title: The harbour that fed Rome
stops.text: A city of perhaps a million people needed roughly 200,000 to 400,000 tonnes of grain a year, mostly shipped from Egypt and Africa. Claudius began a harbour at Portus, north of the Tiber mouth, but its huge basin was exposed: Tacitus records 200 ships sunk in a storm inside it in 62. Around 110-113 Trajan added an inner basin in the shape of a hexagon, each side about 358 metres, surrounded by warehouses, and linked to the Tiber by a canal. The hexagon is still visible as a lake on aerial photographs near Fiumicino airport. From here barges were hauled upriver to Rome's warehouses below the Aventine, where the broken oil amphorae were dumped in a hill of sherds, Monte Testaccio, built from some 53 million vessels.

stops.title: Into Armenia
stops.text: In 114 Trajan used a Parthian intervention in Armenia as the pretext for war. At Elegeia, the Armenian king Parthamasiris laid his diadem at Trajan's feet expecting to be crowned again, as in Nero's time. Trajan refused and annexed the kingdom. Parthamasiris was killed by his escort shortly after. Armenia was made a province, and Trajan's armies went on into northern Mesopotamia, taking Nisibis and Edessa. The Senate voted him the title Optimus and then Parthicus. The war was a break with a century of Roman policy, which had kept Armenia as a buffer under a Parthian prince with a Roman crown. Watch the empire's borders on the map grow to their widest point over the next two years.

stops.title: The revolt of the Diaspora
stops.text: While Trajan was in Mesopotamia, Jewish communities rose against their gentile neighbours and Roman authorities in Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus in 115-117. Under a leader called Lukuas or Andreas, Cyrene's temples were destroyed; papyri from Egypt mention battles near Hermopolis and estates ruined, and the Jewish quarter of Alexandria was devastated. Dio gives casualty figures of 220,000 in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus, impossible numbers that show the terror the revolt caused. Jews were afterwards banned from Cyprus on pain of death. Trajan sent Marcius Turbo with land and sea forces to crush it. The revolt destroyed the great Jewish community of Alexandria, and it drew troops away from the eastern conquests at the decisive moment.

stops.title: To the Persian Gulf
stops.text: In 116 Trajan sailed down the Euphrates, crossed to the Tigris and took the Parthian winter capital of Ctesiphon, capturing the king's daughter and his golden throne. He went on to the head of the Persian Gulf at Charax, where, Dio says, he watched a ship leaving for India and said that if he were younger he would have gone on to India like Alexander. New provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria were declared and coins proclaimed 'Parthia captured'. This is the moment of the empire's greatest extent, about five million square kilometres from the Tyne to the Gulf. It lasted months. Revolts broke out across the conquered territory, a Roman general was killed, and Trajan failed to take the desert city of Hatra. He crowned a Parthian client king, Parthamaspates, and turned back.

stops.title: Death at Selinus
stops.text: Trajan fell ill in Syria, probably from a stroke, and set off for Rome. He died at Selinus on the Cilician coast in early August 117, aged 63. His wife Plotina announced that he had adopted Hadrian, the governor of Syria and his cousin's son, on his deathbed; the letter of adoption was signed by Plotina, and the servant who could have confirmed it died suddenly days later. Dio's father, governor of Cilicia in 117, believed the adoption was faked. Trajan's ashes were taken to Rome and buried in the base of his Column, the first emperor buried inside the city boundary. Later senates acclaimed new emperors with the wish that they might be 'luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan'.

stops.title: Hadrian gives it back
stops.text: [[hadrian|Hadrian]]'s first decision was to abandon Mesopotamia and Assyria, which were in revolt, and to give Armenia back to a client king. His biographer says he followed Cato's advice on Macedon: let what cannot be held go free. He was attacked for it; four senior consulars associated with Trajan were executed in 118 for an alleged plot, and Hadrian never fully won back the Senate. But the decision set the pattern of his reign: consolidation behind defined frontiers, palisades in Germany and the Wall in Britain, long tours of inspection, and investment in the cities. The empire of AD 117 was a high-water mark. From here the question was not how far Rome could expand but how much it could afford to defend.

tours.title: Crisis and recovery (235-305)
tours.summary: Fifty years of military anarchy, invasion, plague and inflation, and the reconstruction of the state by soldier-emperors from the Balkans.

stops.title: The end of the Severans
stops.text: In March 235 soldiers at Mogontiacum on the Rhine murdered the young emperor Severus Alexander and his mother Julia Mamaea, whom they despised for preferring to buy off the Germans rather than fight them. They proclaimed Maximinus, a giant Thracian of humble origin who had risen through the ranks; he was the first emperor never to set foot in Rome. Over the next fifty years there would be about twenty recognised emperors and many more usurpers, and only one or two died in their beds. The underlying problem was structural: wars on two fronts at once, against the new Sasanian dynasty in Persia from 224 and against stronger Germanic confederations on the Rhine and Danube, and an army that made and unmade emperors.

stops.title: The year of six emperors
stops.text: Maximinus' heavy taxation provoked a revolt among the landowners of Africa, who proclaimed the elderly proconsul Gordian and his son in early 238. The Senate backed them. Within three weeks the governor of Numidia had crushed them at Carthage. The Senate then chose two of its own, Pupienus and Balbinus. Maximinus marched on Italy, but the city of Aquileia closed its gates and held out; the townspeople, it was said, cut off the women's hair for bowstrings. His starving army murdered him and his son in their tents. In Rome the praetorian guard then killed Pupienus and Balbinus and made the 13-year-old [[gordian_iii|Gordian III]] emperor. Six emperors in one year: the Senate's last serious attempt to choose a ruler had failed.

stops.title: A Roman emperor on a Persian rock
